DEDICATION POEM

The First Ones

Undaunted by the treeless sea of grass
they dreamed,
Lured by the promises of
ample land
prosperity
freedom.
In canvas ships drawn by stalwart teams,
poor in goods . . .
rich in hope . . .
the First Ones dreamed.

Moving along invisible trails
they came,
Naive of perils too soon met:
relentless winds
fickle rainfall
paralyzing snows.
Carting their lives in dusty wagons,
some courageous . . .
others desperate . . .
the First Ones came.

Rising to the challenge of the land
they stayed,
Persevering to survive through
fire and drought
deprivation and lack
loneliness and despair.
Rolling up their sleeves, shouldering their plows,
determined . . .
and tough . . .
the First Ones stayed.

Building their churches and homes
they grew,
Into counties and towns replete with
railways and stores
government and schools
problems and joy.
Striving to improve and willing to work
with vision . . .
and fortitude . . .
the First Ones grew.

Bending to the dictates of time
they died,
Leaving a legacy rich in
tillage and trees
friendship and faith
kuchen and kraut.
Having borne children to carry on
with courage . . .
and conviction . . .
like the First Ones.

by Dianne P. Rood

WE REQUEST
that you forgive us if we have erred. We made every effort to be accurate, but
much of our material has come from memories and family records, and such are
seldom infallible. We checked and double-checked the material, but our attempts
are likely imperfect. If your family was omitted, it was unintentional. We
sent our request for data far and wide, and worked with the materials you
provided. We have compiled YOUR book, and we hope the result is as satisfying
to you as the project was challenging to us.

IN MEMORIAM
This book was completed despite the absence of one of the committee's charter
members, Gretchen Hilgemann. Her enthusiasm had been a valuable igniting spark
and there were times when her keen mind and cooperative spirit were sorely
missed. We hope she would have endorsed our product.

                        CITY OF LEOLA HISTORY

The vast untamed prairie, the abundance of wildlife, the virgin soil and the
promise of a better future were strong attractions for settlers seeking land
and a good life, and the Leola area had these all.

In 1883, a group of men gathered at Ordway, a starting point for settlers north
of Aberdeen, heading northwest looking for homesteads. Among them were Tarquin
Franklyn, John Murrie, Andrew Williams, S. P. Harden brook, Walter Cavanaugh,
John Hooker, H. A. Moulton, his son, Louis, and Captain E. D. Haynes, who were
looking for a suitable town site. The town site was established and named
Leola, in honor of Captain Haynes' small daughter. Haynes had served Leola as
surveyor before it was established.

        Leola Jones, nee Haynes.

Surveyor Kline came into the township now known as Leola on August 30th and
finished surveying September 23rd. Here they found Phillip Morteau, Fred Junge,
and Henry Z. Moulton in Section 17, and S. P. Hardenbrook, E. D. Haynes, and A.
Williams in Section 20. Of these original owners, Fred Junge filed his claim
March 3, 1884, for the land which lies north of Highway 10 and west of the
courthouse block. H. Z. Moulton filed his claim February 27, 1884, for the land
which lies north of the highway and includes the courthouse block east. S. P.
Hardenbrook filed his receipt on March 3, 1884 for the NE 1/4 of Section 20,
which lies south of Highway 10 and east of the Peavey Lumber Yard. March 4, J.
R. Murrie filed covering the NW 1/4 of the section south of Highway 10, west of
the Peavey corner. W. Cavanaugh filed March 3, 1884 for the NE 1/4 of Section
21, which is now Grimes Addition, east of Highway 45. April 12, 1884, E. D.
Haynes filed on section of land that is now the Greenmound Cemetery, located in
the SE 1/4 of Section 20, Leola Township.

Leola was platted in April and the plat was filed May 1, 1884. This original
plat included the area designated for the county seat: bound by Elm Street to
the north, Sherman to the east, Main to the south, and Broadway to the west,
with the center of Broadway and Main being the quarter corner between sections
17 and 20. A gala celebration was held to christen the town on May 1, 1884. But
Leola was not the first town in the county; Koto was established in 1883.

Land north of the Leola dam which now is the city park, was originally owned by
George L. Twombly, who filed on the NE 1/4 of Section 17 on September 17, 1884.
Andrew Williams, McPherson County's first judge, filed on the SW 1/4 of Section
20 November 6, 1884. The West Hill addition, south of Highland Park, was added
the same year. John Myson Hooker filed his claim for the SE 1/4 of Section 18
on August 15.

On August 27, 1887, more land was surveyed by E. J. Herman of Ellendale, ND and
the Hardenbrook addition was adjoined from the southeast, and the northwestern
addition was added from the west. Highland Park was added in 1888, northwest of
the original plat, at the request of Beach and Cornwall, C. N. Herreid, and P.
O. Kriebs. Leola grew rapidly as more settlers began moving in. Young Leola
soon had a town pump, a number of frame buildings with false fronts and
scrollsaw trimmings, and board walks. Main Street was busy with a post office,
a newspaper known as the Leola Blade, which opened in 1885, a livery stable,
saloon, Boucher Brothers Abstract Company, (the first insurance company,
established in 1885); Moulton's store, and A. J. Clayton's blacksmith shop.
During this early era, Leola celebrated the birth of Worth Charles Turner as
the first baby born, December 7, 1884, and the first marriage ceremony, on
April 20, 1887, of Joseph Bowles (32) and Mary May (28), whose marriage
certificate was signed by Charles N. Herreid, Judge of the Probate Court. Deeds
were being filed and lots snatched up. Deeds in 1884 cost $1.25/acre.

Accompanying business growth was the emergence of such organizations as the
Masonic Lodge, Order of the Eastern Star, Modern Woodmen of America, Odd
Fellows, and Rebekah Lodge.

The first newspapers were the Leola Pioneer Banner and the McPherson County
Standard. After they passed out of existence, two new ones were started: the
Northwest, which appears to have been started April 1884, and may have been a
continuation of the Pioneer Banner. It was published by W. W. Cornwall and
Beach. The other, the Leola Blade was run by lawyers C. N. Herreid and L. T.
Boucher, and its first publication was about 1887. The Northwest was called the
Democrat paper and the Leola Blade, the Republican. Herreid and Boucher moved
to Eureka in 1893 and with them went the Northwest paper. The Herald was
started in Eureka, in October 1892, by Geidt and M. O. Ronayne. It was brought
to Leola about a year later when the Leola Blade moved to Eureka. Andrew
Williams became the publisher of the Herald when Geidt and Ronayne became
disenchanted with politics. In October 1896, the Herald (by then owned by O. J.
Roe and Charles Turner) was moved back to Eureka when the owner saw visions of
the west-end city becoming the county seat. Three months later Charles Turner
became the sole owner of the Herald and moved back to Leola permanently.

Several outstanding community leaders emerged from this period in Leola's
history. A progressive, far-sighted man named Charles N. Herreid came to Leola
in 1882 at the age of 27 and used his knowledge of government to help set up
the county's government. He served as its first clerk and register of deeds,
later becoming county judge and in 1892 being named lieutenant governor. He
served as national committeeman from 1898 to 1900, and during this period he
served on the board of trustees of the State University in 1897 and on the
board of regents from 1898 to 1900. C. N. Herreid from McPherson County served
as governor of South Dakota from 1901 to 1903.

A second outstanding citizen was John J. Hepperle, who served as city auditor,
mayor, county treasurer, register of deeds, and county commissioner. He became
president of the First State Bank of Leola and his political aspirations led
him to the state senate.

John Friedrich (Fred) Junge was one of South Dakota's first legislators. His
six children took an active part in the development of Leola. One daughter,
Caroline (Junge) Haynes was the mother of Leola, for whom the town was named.
Another daughter, Phrene Junge was a leader in the community. She worked for
John J. Hepperle in the First State Bank, served in the post office, and was
secretary in many of the county offices, later becoming county treasurer. One
son, Albert, owned a dry-goods store; another son, Frank, ran a feed and
implement store, then a grain elevator, eventually becoming postmaster. A third
son, Xavier, ran the Junge Feed and Implement store which later merged with the
Valentine Feed and Implement (where Curt's Repair is now). Fred himself served
as county sheriff from 1887 to '90 and as postmaster from 1893 to '97.

Settlement of any town in that era was hard work, often made more difficult by
weather and natural disasters, notably fire. Winters were long and hard and on
January 12, 1888, a reprieve from the stormy weather was welcomed by all. On
that day warm winds blew and men did the morning chores in their shirt sleeves.
By midmorning winds had risen and temperatures dropped. Rural and townspeople
were caught unawares in a raging blizzard. Roads in the area were soon blocked.
People were stranded by the suddenness and severity of the storm, and complete
isolation set in upon the area for several days.

Bela Dexter had left for Frederick early in the morning to purchase coal. On
the return trip he became lost in the blizzard and passed within 20 rods of his
home and did not know it until he came upon a field he recognized. It was
one-half mile southwest of the farmstead. He then unhitched the horses and
turned them to face the wagon box. He fastened blankets over them and wrapped
grain sacks around their legs. By moving around he kept from freezing to death.
He spent the remainder of the night there and when morning came, a lull in the
storm enabled him to find his way home.

The next year on April 2, 1889, a fire raged through Leola carried by winds
estimated at 80 mph; about 80 buildings were destroyed. Possibly the fire
started from a smoldering straw pile that had been burned the previous month by
Eben Daugherty in the Arena valley, northwest of Leola. The day Eben lit the
straw there was no fire hazard, as a drizzling rain fell, which turned to snow.
The straw had burned to a depth of about three feet and apparently smoldered
for two weeks before coming to life again on that tragic day in April. It is
said the fire was spread by dry buffalo chips being blown about in the strong
wind.

One man, C. W. Old, died from burns after he lost his bearings and became
separated from his team of oxen.

Leola's citizens organized and began to rebuild their town. Aberdeen and other
towns came to their aid as business people heard of the destruction, and on the
third day at least four loads of goods were sent to Leola. Lumber and materials
were hauled in from Ipswich and Westport as every man and boy bent to the task
of rebuilding. Buildings went up fast and more were built in 30 days than ever
before on record in South Dakota. Some of the new buildings were the residences
of the Cornwalls, Rev. Hahn, Moulton, Roe, and Hardenbrook, and business
places, such as Frank Child's Wagon Shop on Main Street, MacNamire's Photo
Studio, and also Methodist and Presbyterian churches.

The gay '90's in Leola were a bustling and active time. The first bank was
chartered in 1894 and known as Turner's Bank. There was an opera house, and it
was not uncommon to see males stomping around together if female partners were
not available. Traveling medicine shows came and stayed for a week, enacting a
play each night after the troupe sold their items. People held big political
rallies with free kegs of beer and torch-lit parades during these years. Many
small businesses were opened.

Each town of course, had its saloon. Leola was no exception, with Odenbach's
the first. In 1902, however, a vigilante committee formed for destroying the
demon rum. This did not daunt the saloon keeper, however, who immediately
applied to the county commission for a liquor license and quickly resumed his
business.

Changes and improvements were rapid. In March 1902, a second bank, the Leola
Equity Exchange Bank was opened. A large crowd greeted the first train
Christmas Day 1906. Establishing a library in Leola was on the minds of local
residents and as early as June 1, 1901 a benefit was held. A third bank, the
First State Bank, was established by Mr. Reagan and Mr. Hooper of Eureka. Small
businesses changed hands and relocated frequently. On June 2, 1908 a German
school opened for the summer, a new real estate firm was opened, and "the Leola
Commercial Club materialized for the purpose of continued improvements in
Leola." Twenty carloads of stock (the first big shipment) were shipped via the
M. & St. L. Railroad. On September 24, John Dexter drove into town with the
first automobile in the county.

Although Leola had been in existence for quite some time, it was not an
incorporated body until July 1907. Members of the first board were James
Clayton, 1st District; Fred F. Pietz, 2nd District; Michael Krause, 3rd
District; John J. Hepperle, Clerk; and John Johnstone, Treasurer. More land was
added to the town as Grimes addition was added on May 25, 1907; Kenwood, July
7, 1908; Pleasantville, April 29, 1909; and Hohm Park, July 10, 1918.

In 1908 the town had two banks, three general stores, one drugstore, two
hardware stores, one hardware and furniture store, one feed store, two hotels,
one restaurant, one harness shop, one blacksmith shop, two livery and feed
barns, two farm machine dealers, one city meat market, two saloons, one barber
shop, one pool hall, one printing office, two lawyers, one painter and paper
hanger, two real estate dealers, several carpenters, one mason, two dray lines,
one opera house, three churches, one school, four coal dealers, one wood yard,
three elevators, three lumberyards, and a telegraph and telephone system.

Progress in Leola was always aimed at improving living circumstances here, and
in 1909 the Leola school was constructed. The city began operating a municipal
light plant in the winter of 1911. The lights were on from 6 p.m. to 12 a.m.
Prior to 1901, many Leolans had to carry water from the well. The city council
and Perry Conahan, mayor, striving to improve this situation, decided to have
two wells drilled in the late '40s. Future supply of water was assured. In 1917
a 50,000-gallon storage tank was built atop a 100-foot tower, and fire fighting
equipment was added to the fire department. The council hired a marshal to
enforce the laws and arrest all persons driving vehicles over 12 mph within the
city limits.

The first theatre in Leola was started by Claude Chittick and Rod Ronayne.
Shows were scheduled on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday evenings each week, with
a matinee on Saturday afternoon. A large cylinder gasoline engine with fly
wheels about a yard in diameter pulled a dynamo to furnish the electricity for
the movie-picture machine. The vibrations from this one-cylinder engine were
felt by the spectators throughout the building and were synchronized to the
quick jerking movements of Charlie Chaplin. This proved to be no hindrance to
patronage and the business flourished.

Traveling vaudeville shows were another social attraction, as well as husking
bees and school socials. The Chatauqua, a series of meetings with education and
entertainment was extremely popular. Youngsters acted out scripts as Indians,
cowboys, or fairies.

Prior to 1919 Leola had a president and a board of trustees as the governing
officials in city government. In May 1919, John V. Hohman became Leola's first
mayor, and councilmen replaced trustees. The American Legion Roy S. Hickman
Post 78 held its first meeting and elected officers that same year. The
population then was 600.

December 9, 1920 Leolans enjoyed an improvement in their electric service.
Electric lights came on an hour earlier in the afternoon; six street lights
were added, and a beacon was mounted atop the city water tower. The Leola city
council established a dump ground in April 1921, and a sewer bond was passed in
1922. A municipal light and power plant was also added.

Leola covered 30 acres of land, including residential and business areas, when
the Lundquist subdivision was added April 25, 1927, named after Dr. Gilbert C.
Lundquist, who had donated the land that embraces the Leola Dam. Dr. Lundquist
aroused W.P.A. interest in providing a recreation area for the people. It was
declared a state game refuge in October 1927.

Two lots in Pleasantville addition were donated by Charlie Fosler for use in
establishing a hospital for Leola. Solicitation of funds began in 1945 and
continued until 1952. The hospital opened in March 1952, it closed briefly in
1955 and reopened in 1956. Two resident doctors, J. F. Malloy and Karlis
Zvejnieks, had established their offices in Leola. The hospital needed many
improvements and since there would no longer be a doctor in Leola its doors
were closed in 1965.

The 1950's saw the following improvements: Roy S. Hickman Post 78 built a
Legion Hall in 1951; new street lights were installed by MDU in 1954; ambulance
service was added to the fire department in 1955; and in 1958 a farm fire truck
was added. The bakery, Gamble Store, and the Leola Legion (L & L) Bar, were
built, replacing the buildings that had been destroyed in the fire on February
11, 1959.

In 1959 Leola celebrated its 75th birthday. The program on the preceding page
portrays the '59 celebration. The 1960's saw the installation of dial
telephones as well as the addition of lights to the ball park. A new well was
drilled to compensate for a water shortage, and yielded 130-140 gallons per
minute.

The Leola Hospital stockholders met June 3, 1965 to decide whether to operate
the hospital or relinquish their holding without compensation to city
ownership. When the doctor decided to leave the Leola area, the Leola citizens
resolved not to put forth the effort to raise the money to meet state
specifications. Landmark losses continued when the Leola Leader was razed in
November 1965, and a fire destroyed the Central Lumber building as well as
Clint Blumhardt's TV shop and John Voegele's shoe repair shop.

        Kenwood Manor.

The need for housing for Leola's elderly citizens brought about the
construction of Kenwood Manor, a four-plex apartment building, in 1974, a
second unit was built later. During that same year the Senior Citizens Center
was opened in the former Masonic Temple hall. Another four-plex for the
elderly, "The Village," was built in 1977.

        The Village.

Leola citizens recognized the need for a municipal building, and on March 3,
1975 the city council asked for bids for construction of a building to house
the council, the finance officer, public rest rooms, and a community room. The
building was completed in June. On September 5 bids were let again, for
construction of a city swimming pool. Westgate, Inc. of Bismarck had the
accepted low bid of $114,950. The new pool was to be at Broadway and Williams,
where the hospital had been located. Dedication of the new pool was June 7,
1976. Playground equipment was added adjacent to the pool in 1977. A bond was
asked for in that same year for a building to house the library, doctor's and
dentist's office. The building was completed, and Dr. Marvel, DDS, opened his
office and Dr. John McFee moved from the bank basement to his new office. The
library was transported from the basement of the courthouse to occupy the south
section of the new building.

        Leola Swimming Pool.

        Library Building.

Celebration of the nation's Bicentennial was held in Leola with an all-school
reunion in July, 1976, the second of its kind. The first had been held in 1968,
when all classes gathered for a three-day reunion.

The Community Alliance Committee was organized in 1979 to provide the framework
for planning and expanding the community by bringing in new businesses,
expansion of existing businesses, and growth of homes.

In 1981 new lights were installed at the baseball field. Water rates were
increased to include sewer and dump ground fees. Manpower for the dump ground
and other city maintenance work is provided by the Green Thumb Projects, a
federal project for employing low-income elderly. The city also employs several
CETA workers each summer.

A carnival will be available all three days of the centennial. Other events
include crafts and displays at the Leola Senior Citizens Center.

Planning for the Centennial celebration had its beginning in 1982. Bake sales,
dances, 4-H Achievement Day supper, raffles have been projects of Centennial
Boosters as fund raising events. Modern Woodmen of America, represented by Art
Breitag, sponsored a pancake feed to raise centennial dollars, on June 26,
1983. Proceeds were matched by the Modern Woodmen Insurance Company and
barbecue grills were purchased for the Leola City Park. A picnic shelter
building was erected at the city park, and a slide will be added to the city
park in 1984.

The 1980 U.S. Census reported 640 residents in Leola, and although there is a
regrettable outflow of our young people from this area, we are proud to note a
gradual influx of young adults and continued stable enrollment in our school
over the past several years. The air is still clean, the people still friendly,
and the possibilities of a good life still exist here

        City Council (L-R) Milbert Zelmer, Eugene Weisenburger, John Stolle,
        Floyd Meidinger, Mayor, George Zacher, Patty Schaible, Reinhold
        Glaesman, and Ernest Jasmer.

                Leola's Police Department

        Albert Norris (A. N.) Bell.      Anthony (Tony) Koppy.

Albert Norris (A. N.) Bell came to Leola in 1910. Beginning in 1918 he was
hired by the town board to be in charge of the municipal light plant and also
serve as the town's marshal; a post he held for three years.

Anthony (Tony) Koppy, a long time Leola businessman, came to Leola in 1917.
After WWI, he was hired by the city to be in charge of the powerhouse and water
system in combination with the marshal duties. A parttime job, on call 24 hours
per day.

Tony went into business for himself for several years, after which he sold his
business. Again in 1941, Tony was hired to his former position of taking care
of the light plant, pump house and marshal duties. Tony was mainstay at the
pump house for many years prior to 1949.

        Walter (Walt) Hoeft.          Harold Haux

Walter (Walt) Hoeft accepted employment with the city of Leola in 1949 as
police chief and also was in charge of the pump house water system. In 1963 he
gained a new title, "Water Commissioner," and in 1967 was awarded a citation of
meritorious service to the community by Post No. 78 of the American Legion as
part of its program to "Recognize Police Achievement," Walt retired in 1970.

Harold Haux, began his career in Leola in 1956, when he took over the body shop
owned by Ed Rueb. On May 1, 1962, Harold accepted the position as chief of
police, at which he is still employed.

Others have been employed in the department throughout these many years, a
complete record was not available.

                Sports

Athletic competition was not laid to rest during the summer or after high
school graduation at Leola. Various forms of competition have been carried on
in Leola's winning tradition for many years.

The Leola Independent basketball program for players out of high school has
been a tradition at Leola. Numerous high school and college athletes have come
home to play for the Indee's in competition for different titles.

        Trophies.

One highlight was the 1948 team with Lloyd Turnwall and Harold Heibel, Allen
and Edwin Hilgeman, Gene Ganser, Gus Kolb, Herbert Frost, Irvin Kulm, Keith
Heibel, Earl Swanson as team members and Walt Conahan as manager. They won the
1948 State Legion Championship at Rapid City and went on to compete in the
National Tourney at Jeffersonville, IN. Many good ball teams have competed for
different titles on the amateur basketball level here at Leola.

Summer activities include the baseball program presently handled by the Leola
Athletic Association which was formed in 1978. A number of league and tourney
championships have been crowned in the Pee Wee and Midget baseball leagues.
Some of these little leaguers have gone on to greater things as did the Leola
teener team in winning the 1978 State VFW Teener Baseball Championship at
Eureka by eliminating Brandon Valley 3 to 1, Eureka 12 to 2, and Clark in the
championship game 4 to 0. That was a grand finale for a team who had a very
respectable season of 23 wins and 3 losses.

Several outstanding Jr. Legion teams have represented Leola well at the State
Legion Tourney over the years. After playing Jr. Legion ball many went on to
play for the Leola Mallard amateur team which played in the Northern League for
several years.

The Leola Mallard team was a direct descendant of many good local baseball
teams going back to the 1920's with names like Holmes, Heibel, Brown, Hepperle,
Serfoss, Reiner, Hoff, Lubka, Schuchardt, Krause, Loney, Lohman, Mock, Morris,
Parmeter, Fox, and many others leading their teams in competition.

In recent years a men's softball team known as the "Brewers" has gone on to
represent Leola in various leagues and tournaments around the state.

Summer events are not limited to just the men since the formation of a girls
softball team, which is presently competing very well in a strong Aberdeen City
League. Summer activities in Leola have increased with the addition of the new
park with swimming pool, tennis court, horse shoe, badminton, and volleyball
areas.

        Back Row: Jody Hoffman, Miles Blumhardt, Mike Waltman, Craig Zenker,
        Jeff Schnaidt, Kevin Steckler. Pick-up players: Mark Voegele, Ipswich;
        Kermit Cantwell, Barnard; and Tim Geffre. Front Row: Clint Blumhardt,

                Weather . . . Or Not

Temperature and precipitation have been recorded daily in Leola for over 50
years for the United States Department of Commerce National Weather Service.

First records were kept by John Porter in the latter '20's throughout 1930.
Calvin C. Hilgeman continued from 1949 to 1960. Wayne Nesby kept records in
1960 which later was taken over by Walt Hoeft who kept records until 1972.
Since September 1972 Rudolph Opp has been weather observer. Rudolph sends the
daily reports to the Sioux Falls weather service each Saturday. At the end of
the month he sends the daily reports to the Department of Commerce at
Asheville, NC. Equipment, record books and supplies are furnished by the
Department of Commerce. It takes 15 minutes each day, 7 1/2 hours each month
which in turn equals 90 hours each year that Rudy volunteers his time.

Mr. Opp, now a retired farmer, has watched the weather closely for many years.
He recalls the variety of South Dakota weather. He remembers, when on June 12,
1943, a tornado destroyed all of the buildings but the house on the Jacob
Becker farm 3 1/2 miles northwest of Leola. Also, a tornado that struck
southwest of Leola damaging buildings on farms in 1956.

        1920 Leola Stockyards.

Both in poetry and story, descendants of early settlers, recall the "Blizzard
of '88" and the devastating tornado of 1896. Although the area has had its
share of blocked roads, high snow level, bitter colds and rampaging storms in
more recent times, modern conveniences and facilities make it hard for us to
grasp the suffering early pioneers endured under similar conditions.

        The vicious winter of 1951-52. A team of horses struggling to get to a
        hay stack. Richard Jasmer waiting for Ernest to get there.

The blizzard of 1966 was called "a killer out of the west." Reports indicated
that it was one of the worst in history, having lasted the longest period of
time. Up to 23 inches of snow fell with winds from 40 to 50 miles per hour and
gusts up to 70 miles per hour whipped snow into impassable drifts.

Many farmers were isolated during the blizzard. Some of the farm buildings were
covered with snow while the prairie was swept almost clean by the same wind
that caused the drifts.

Livestock losses were heavy, approximately 1,000 head in McPherson County. The
heavy snow and high winds killed livestock in barns, in feedlots and on the
range. Roofs collapsed under the weight of the snow, killing cattle trapped
inside.

Drifts piled up in the corrals. The cattle either walked out over them to
wander with the storm or they were caught under the pile of snow and
suffocated. On the range the animals wandered blindly, eyes frozen shut and
long icicles hanging from their nostrils. One herd wandered blindly into town.
Dead cattle were strewn about the prairie with their feet sticking out of the
snowdrifts. Those that survived were suffering from frozen limbs, extreme
exposure, lack of food and water.

        Cow on Highway No. 10--Blizzard of '66.

According to weather bureau reports only 11 statewide storms of its kind were
recorded. They listed an April storm in 1873, a February storm in 1881, the
January blizzard of 1888, a March storm in 1892, a November storm in 1896 and
1940, a January storm in 1949 and a February storm in 1955.

The following is how a Leola farmer Gerald Hoffman remembers the blizzard of
'66. "On Wednesday morning about 9:30 a.m. on March 3, 1966, a light snow was
beginning to fall. As the day progressed, it snowed heavier with the wind
blowing out of the northeast. It continued to snow during the night with the
wind getting stronger. I was still able to get to the cows and get them well
fed, on Thursday. With a rope I led the herd bulls into the barn. Toward
evening on Thursday the storm got so bad I could not go out in it.

"Most of the cow herd was outside in the trees for shelter. No cattle were lost
in the choking storm. I was able to get to the barn twice on Friday by
following a board fence and was able to take care of the cattle in the hip roof
barn. On Saturday noon when the storm subsided, I fed the cattle that I could
get to. The cattle were all iced over with about four to five inches of ice on
their nostrils. Instead of eating hay, they laid down on it to rest.

        Highway No. 10 in front of the Highway Cafe and Peavey Lumber
        Yard.

"Some of the cows along the trees and windbreak kept packing the snow until
they were on top of 20 feet of snow. To get them off this snow bank, I had to
tie ropes and cables together and pull them off one at a time with the tractor.

"Three bull calves were lying on top of the trees melted down with their backs
low, but after getting them up and taking the snow off their nostrils they
survived.

"The cattle wanted water, but with no electricity there wasn't any until about
one o'clock on Sunday morning. The electricity had gone out sometime on
Thursday. The water tanks had to be shoveled out of the snow. Some of the
cattle that were in the barn had to be shoveled out before they could get out
of the barn.

"After hours of hard work, the cattle got fed and bedded down.

"There is a saying that blizzards aren't what they used to be, but I consider
this was an 'Old Time' blizzard."

That same year in the month of August in '66 a wide swath of destruction hit
northwest of Leola and the Long Lake area. On highway 101 south of Long Lake,
about a quarter of a mile of blacktop was rolled up like a rug by the storm.
The storm was the third in the northwest area that year. Complete farms were
wiped out. Machinery and cars were demolished. Trees were uprooted. Some
farmers reported the loss of cattle, hogs and poultry.

Some crops received extensive damage in the tornado area. Two deaths were
reported.

        1968 tornado tail's destruction at the Ernest Jasmer farm.

June 20, 1968 brought more storms into the Leola area. Hail and tornado tails
accompanied by high winds raised havoc in Leola and destroyed crops on farms
southwest of Leola. Many roof tops were damaged and windows facing west were
smashed.

Storms usually follow a very hot humid day, often times accompanied by hail.

The 1982-83 winter was recorded as the warmest on record.

An extreme cold spell plagued the midwest in mid-December, 1983. For nine
straight days temperatures were recorded below zero in Leola. A - 32 degrees
was recorded on December 23, with a high for the day - 17 degrees. Wind chill
factors anywhere between - 80 and - 100 degrees during wind gusts that reached
30 miles per hour or more.

Anyone who has been around the Dakotas knows and dreads the "sun dogs" of
winter. When temperatures drop below zero, ice crystals in the air reflect the
sun's rays to create the optical phenomenon. A halo generally colored red on
the inside, then orange, yellow, and white on the outside are the luminous
rings around the sun and moon. In South Dakota we don't always like the weather
we get--but we take what we get--weather . . . or not.

        Cattle at Kappes farm after the deadly tornado.

                        STEPPING STONES 1884-1984

The little village of Leola blossomed in 1885 with the following business
establishments which in turn developed into what it is today.

Leola's first store stood at the corner of Main and Broadway on the present
site of Walt's Standard.

A. G. Clayton's blacksmith shop, one of the earlier ones, was located where the
last addition to the bank now stands, on Sherman. This building survived the
1889 fire.

        Moulton Elliot Building.

The Moulton-Elliot building was also built in 1885, on the corner of Sherman
and Main streets on the bakery corner. It also survived the fire only to be
destroyed by another fire in 1959. This store had as owners throughout the
years: Messrs. Story, Dale, Kennis, Silverman, Andrew Williams and Lawrence
Heibel. They all had general stores. The building was vacant for a few years,
then in 1939, George Witte opened a bakery, operating this until 1940 when Lee
Crist took over the business. Sid Swanson, Sr. and family purchased the
building in 1942 and continued the bakery business until the building burned in
1959. The Gamble store addition to the building was built in 1907. In 1932 Bob
Mock operated a barber shop and pool hall in this addition, then later E. B.
Rude started a Gamble store which was later sold to Albert Breunig. The second
floor of the Moulton-Elliot store was a meeting place for organizations such as
Masonic Lodge, Order of the Eastern Star, Modern Woodman of America, Odd
Fellows and Rebekah Lodge. It was also the local dance hall and later was
converted into apartments.

The Leola Leader was originally known as the Fox General Store and was located
where the American Legion Hall now stands. The date it was built is unknown,
but it is said to have been moved to a new location, where the city library now
stands, sometime before 1897. This was operated as a general store by Emma
Hickman. There was also a post office located in the southwest corner of the
store. In 1904 she sold out to Johnstone and Sons of Ashley, ND. They continued
in business until May of 1910, when they sold to E. W. Hilgemann.

        Leola Leader.

        Leola Abstract Business.

The McPherson County Abstract business is still in existence in Leola. It was
established in 1885 by L. T. Boucher, John Boucher and H. Sopper. The business
was operated in various buildings in the city until in 1907 when they erected
the Amos Hoffman building that now houses the law office of Floyd Meidinger.
The abstract business is now owned by Lorine Neuharth.

Before 1900 there had been a livery barn behind the hotel now owned by Mary Lou
Lechner. The last person to run this barn was Charley Stone. Another livery
barn owned by C. W. Hawes was located on the present site of Rau's Sinclair.

The building that stood in the parking area of the HiWay Cafe was one of the
older buildings of the community, built before the turn of the century by
George Keisler and Fred Klein. It was originally a wagon and farm supply shop.
Michael Krause, the next owner, carried on the business and in 1911, Ed
Lortscher bought an interest in the firm changing the name to Krause and
Lortscher. Lortscher had been a traveling salesman for J. I. Case Thresher
Company. They handled farm implements, specializing in International, Moline,
and P. & O. line of plows and the Rumley steam tractor. They also sold cream
separators, Lindsey wagons and International tractors. Later Frost and
Lortscher bought out Krause and added a line of furniture. In 1920 E. D.
Berridge bought the business and it became known as Berridge & Son, then he
sold it in 1946 to Emil and Jacob Becker, and they named it Becker's Implement.
They sold home appliances and radios as well as Case machinery. In 1950 Jacob
bought his brother's share and continued the business until 1958 when the last
of the stock was sold at an auction. Later the Paul Henderson family lived on
the second floor of the building. Eleanor Henderson had a beauty parlor on the
first floor.

In the early 1900's there were a variety of businesses in Leola. There were
three banks in operation, Ray Lang had a confectionary parlor (west of Brosz's
hotel), and in 1902, Odenbach built the first saloon in Leola. Leola's fifth
elevator (The Farmers Elevator) was opened in 1901. Later (1907) the Pacific
Elevator was opened by Amos Hoffman, and the Ingold Elevator was operated by
McIntyre. There was an ice cream parlor and millinery owned by Mrs. Eliason in
the building that now is the Harmony of Beauty, owned by Peg Schumack.

        Leola Business section.

In 1906 Peter Schuchardt bought the Clayton Furniture Store, which they named
the Opera House, where all community entertainment took place, including the
lyceum courses and school plays. The second story housed the mortuary and also
a furniture store, until the early 1920's when the front part was rented as an
apartment. With the coming of movies, the Opera House was renovated and renamed
the Royal Theater, which was later sold to Leo Heibel in 1930 and renamed the
Century Theater. The Central Lumber Company, established in 1906 on the site
just north of the present Hoffman's Standard Service, was the first business to
sell lumber as its chief commodity. Dave Owens was the first manager. In 1911
the yards were moved to a site east of the Courthouse. Mr. Grader, the next
manager, was succeeded by Henry Theilen and Schoenfelder. Martin Switzenberg
then took over until 1943, when Henry "Hank" Young, became manager. In 1956,
when Henry retired, Leo Rogers managed the business until December, 1957,
when the yard closed.

        Central Lumber Yard.

A. S. Wattier and Lawrence Heibel bought the City Meat Market from Claude
Chittick in 1908. These partners ran this market, which was located at that
time on a lot just west of the present site of the Equity Filling Station,
until 1919. At this time Heibel bought out Wattier. In l919 Heibel built the
store that is now part of the Leola State Bank. This building had a full
basement and was also built for handling of a full line of meats. In 1946 the
building was enlarged with a locker room added on. In April, 1952, Heibel
passed away and his sons, Clifford and Leo operated the market until January 1,
1956, when Clifford became sole owner. Later operators of the store, before it
permanently closed, were Gary Lapka and Bob Schumacher.

In 1916 Gottlieb Quaschnick built a saloon west of the present bank building.
He sold it to Jacob Heihn, who also operated a saloon, until prohibition, when
the saloon was converted into a pool hall and recreation center. The next
business in this building was a creamery operated by Rod Ronayne until 1939.
Ted Leidle later opened a laundromat there, which was later purchased by Ray
Kappes.

        Gutjahr's Blacksmith Shop.

September 19, 1919, Fred Gutjahr purchased the original Central Lumber Yard
building and converted it to a blacksmith shop. This building was located north
of Walt's Standard Station. His son, Christ, joined him two years later. In
1946 they expanded, buying the McPherson County shed. Fred retired in 1948 and
Christ continued blacksmithing with the help of his grandson, Richard Crist.

The Texaco Service Station was opened in 1937 by Ed Rueb who later sold it to
Milbert Adam. Vince Geffre now owns the building and uses it for storage.

        Koppy's Potato Chip ad.

        1959 fire.

Tony Koppy purchased the Blakeman Pool Hall in 1929 and added a full
block-basement. In the later '30s, Tony's wife, Elizabeth, began her own potato
chip factory housed in this basement. A variety of activities and entertainment
for young and old took place in this building for several years. Leola natives
enjoyed roller skating during the week and dances on Saturday night. They had
an athletic club, barber shop and bowling alley in this building. In the later
'30s, Charlie Pade rented it and ran a pool hall, and Tony Koppy started a
straw-burner factory. In 1959 the building burned down along with the bakery
and the Gamble Store.

                        BUSINESS HISTORY

                American Family Insurance 57 Years of Growth

It was in the spring of 1957 that Calvin Guthmiller became engaged in the
insurance business, which he is still with today.

American Family's forerunner, Farmers Mutual Insurance Company, was founded
October 3, 1927, in Madison, WI.

The Midwestern American family changed drastically during the next 57 years. It
endured the Great Depression, it moved to the cities and became smaller, its
members fought in three wars and entered the atomic and space age. This is how
American Family Insurance grew and changed to meet the family's needs during
this time. It was in 1963 that the name was officially changed to "American
Family Insurance" to better describe the activities.

The Calvin Guthmiller Agency has always been located in his home.

                The Apparel

The Apparel was opened in 1946-47 by Mrs. H. P. Gelling in the building now
owned by DeWayne Lechner. The business was purchased by Calvin Hilgemann. In
March, 1956, Calvin and Martha Gill, partner, moved The Apparel to its present
location, which had formerly been the Red Owl Store which was operated by Dave
and Dorothea Brosz. The building was built in the early thirties as a general
store and was run by Phillip Silverman.

        The Apparel

                ASCS

This Federal Office started out in 1933 as the Agricultural Adjustment Act
(AAA). Henry L. Leonhardt administered the new program with the help of a three
member board elected by the farmers. The first office was located in the
courthouse on the third floor, in the area now occupied by the Soil
Conservation Service (SCS).

Agricultural Conservation Program (ACP) was one of the first programs
administered by this agency. This program is still in existence in our office.
Before World War II the programs were designed to cut production because of an
over supply. Wheat Marketing quotas were in effect. Bins were erected at
different sites around the county to store the oversupply of grain. These bins
were sold during World War II. Federal Crop Insurance (FCIC) was one of the
programs administered by this agency from the later '30s until 1953, when FCIC
was made a separate agency. The programs during World War II were designed to
encourage production to feed a devastated world.

        Left to right: Maude French, Dorothy Miller, Della Guthmiller, Ellen
        Sigler and Leone Thomas.

In 1948 the agency became known as the Production Marketing Administration
(PMA). Programs again were instituted to curb production. Marketing quotas were
again voted in by the farmers. This brought about allotted acres for wheat in
wheat counties and allotted acres for corn in corn counties. Large supplies of
grain again necessitated the establishing of bin storage sites. These were
built in 1953 and 1954. These sites were again dismantled and sold out in the
early '70s. Present storage requirements are met by encouraging on-farm
storage.

In 1954 the internal administration of the office changed with the hiring of an
office manager to oversee the day-to-day functions. Before this time a three
member county committee directed the office operations. James L. Farley was
hired by the county committee as the first office manager in McPherson
County. Mr. Farley served as manager until 1957, when Howard Mettler was hired.

The office has been located in four different locations around town. The
office was located on the third floor of the courthouse until 1950. In 1950 the
office was moved to the basement of the Leola State Bank building. In 1956 the
office was moved to the old Herald office, the "Harmony of Beauty" shop is now
located in this building. In 1963 the office was moved to its present location.
This building was built for ASCS by Albert Breunig.

THE WOOL PROGRAM: started in the '50s by Secretary of Agriculture, Ezra Taft
Benson. This program is still in operation. It is an incentive program designed
to encourage the expansion of the sheep industry.

THE AGRICULTURAL CONSERVATION PROGRAM (ACP): started in the '30s. This program
is still in operation, and is designed to conserve the soil and keep it
productive.

THE WATER BANK PROGRAM: started under Secretary of Agriculture Earl Butz in the
early '70s. This program is designed to enhance wildlife habitat.

COMMODITY LOAN PROGRAM: started in the late '30s under Secretary of Agriculture
Henry Wallace. Commodity loan program is still in operation for both farm
stored and warehouse stored grain. These are all nonrecourse loans.

FACILITY LOAN PROGRAM: started in the late '40s. Under this program money is
borrowed to producers to build or buy new grain storage facilities. This is to
store grain on the farm and help with the orderly marketing of grain.

PRODUCTION ADJUSTMENT: Under this program numerous programs have been used to
adjust production to needs. The first of the programs were allotments and
marketing quotas. This was first used during the latter '30s and '50s. These
were voted down in the early '60s and voluntary programs came into existence.
Cash rental for cropland retirement was started in the late '50s. Conservation
Reserve (Soil Bank) was the first of these programs. The Cropland Adjustment
Program (CAP) was next with some emphasis on wildlife habitat. This has led to
the present Water Bank Program, which is geared primarily to wildlife habitat.

Present adjustment programs require the idling of cropland to earn program
benefits. This cropland must be protected from wind and water erosion. We have
gone from mandatory programs to voluntary programs to adjust production. We
have seen the number of farms drop to 368 from about 1,250 farms in 1950.

The following is a list of individuals who have served on the county committee.
This list is all that are known to the writer from the first committee through
1983. The first committeemen were elected each year. In the '50s the system
went to a three year staggered term with a maximum of nine years of service for
an individual.

Fewings, Albert Bender, Fred Merkel, Albert Hauffe, Donald Warnick, Otto
Hauffe, Julius Reiner, Jacob Becker, Jacob A. Bertsch, Ted Martel, Martin
Grosz, James Farley, Daniel Bieber, Howard Mettler, Adolph Schaible, Daniel J.
Kline, John Weisser, Harold Mohr, William Mehlhaff, Lavern Lapka, Joseph Gab,
Adam Ehley, Rudolph Opp, Rudolph G. Thurn, Reuben Nies, Henry J. Neuharth,
Ernest Jasmer, Orville Knapp, Reinhold Schutz, Willard Goeshel, Emanuel Haupt.

                The Brosz Hotel

The Leola House was built by Moulton in the 1880's. Hawes and Denton purchased
it and added the east wing. It was later sold to Charles Turner, who leased it
to Mr. Wilsey, and then to Dave Ryan. In 1909 Frank McGee took over its
operation until 1915, when Martin and Helena Brosz purchased it.

        Brosz Hotel.

The hotel consisted of 25 beds. Room and board was $5 a week and about 50
people were served at each meal, for 35 cents each. The dining room was closed
in 1921. An interesting service of the hotel was the twice daily meeting of the
train to welcome the guests. The Brosz Hotel, which has apartments for rent as
well as rooms, was also the location of Dave and Dorothea Brosz's cream and
produce station. Mrs. Helena Brosz operated the hotel until 1960 when she
sold the building to Dorothea Brosz. On October 15, 1976, Dorothea Brosz died
and at present Dave and his wife Hulda are living in the Brosz Hotel and still
rent out apartments.

                Lloyd Breitag Construction Company

Lloyd Breitag is a Leola High School graduate who chose to make Leola the site
for his woodworking business. He acquired basic knowledge for his trade in the
high school shop class. After graduating in 1975, Lloyd worked for Schumacher
and Haux Construction Co. until December of 1980. January 1, 1981, he started
his own construction company. In 1982 he attended classes sponsored by Farmland
Industries training him to set up grain bins and steel buildings. Lloyd now
does all kinds of construction and remodeling serving the rural and residential
areas in McPherson County.

Lloyd purchased two lots south of the Methodist Church in April, 1983, where he
has set up a shop. He enjoys doing all kinds of woodworking including cabinets,
furniture and unique picture frames and family signs.

                Curt's Repair Shop

Robert Valentine, assisted by his sons Richard and Albert, in 1910 originally
started business in this building where they sold John Deere and J. I. Case
lines of machinery.

Frank and Joe Kohlhoff purchased the business on March 19, 1918, operating as
Kohlhoff Brothers. They were franchised dealers for International Harvester.

In January 1946, Joe died and Ivan (Bob) Kohlhoff joined his father in the
business, which was then known as Kohlhoffs' Inc.

In January 1952, the company was sold to Calvin Rempher, who with his partner,
Ben Rott, operated the International Harvester business.

In 1959, Mike Schaffner purchased the building. It was then occupied by various
other people. Lowell McIntire operated a mechanic repair shop for a time. Tom
Bell also operated a mechanic repair shop for a short time. Leola Equity used
it as a warehouse and the Leola school used one room for a shop class.

In 1970, Mike Schaffner started operating his own mechanic shop. Mike operated
his business until 1979, when Mr. and Mrs. Curtis Walz purchased the building,
and are now the present owner and operators of Curt's Repair Shop, also a
mechanic repair shop.

        Curt's Repair Shop.

                D & M Cafe

The D & M Cafe, owned by Mary Lou Lechner, stands where Fred Arndt's general
store was in the 1900's. Fred retired in the '20s and his son, Fred Jr.,
managed the store several years before selling to L. Mankoff.

Wm. J. P. Geidt purchased the store in 1928 and operated it under the name of
"Golden Rule Store" until Wm. passed away in 1941. Mrs. Geidt managed it for
over a year and then sold out the stock and the building was torn down.

In 1948, Perry Conahan built a new building on this site and moved his cafe
into the new building as "Perry's Cafe." Perry's Place, on the east side of the
street then became Perry's Shuttleboard Arcade and later a shoe repair shop run
by John Ellis. This building was later torn down and the new post office was
erected.

Perry's Cafe, where the D & M is now, was sold to Keith and Vera Durnill in the
fall of 1955, only one and one-half years after Perry's untimely death.

        D & M Cafe.

Following Durnills there were many different parties who rented the building
and operated the cafe, namely: the Ray Neuharths, Harold Hauxs, Enoch Schafers,
Otto Heupels, Alvin Haucks and Wallace Krackes. The Lechners then bought the
cafe in 1969 and changed the name from the Green Lantern to the D & M. Mary Lou
is presently owner and manager of the cafe.

                Dentists

The first dental office was located over the Bank of Leola. Dr. J. L. Gill
opened his doors in Leola in 1915. Dr. Gill was an active promoter of trap
shooting and baseball and in improving conditions in the city.

Preceding Dr. Gill's death there were several visiting dentists in the 1920's,
a Dr. Sherman and Dr. Fisher and others who came from Ipswich, Eureka and
Aberdeen. Dr. Gillet practiced in Leola in 1923 and a Dr. Martel in the early
'30s. Dr. Hoeven of Aberdeen came several days a week during the late 1930's
and '40s to serve the community's needs.

Dr. F. Otto Schnaidt was warmly welcomed in July of 1954 when he began
practicing in Leola. He served a large surrounding community as well as Leola
proper. A modern dental office was opened in the bank building in July, after
Dr. Schnaidt had completed his dental training at Loyola University in Chicago.
His first patient was Mr. William Job on July 19, 1954.

Dr. Schnaidt was active in Better Leola Club, American Legion, Masonic Lodge,
American Lutheran Church, Explorer Scouts and was an active fireman and member
of the Leola School Board.

In January of 1977 Dr. Schnaidt closed his doors and moved his business to
Aberdeen.

A new building was built where the old Leola Leader stood to provide space for
the Leola City Library and Medical Center. The Aberdeen Dental Associates have
cooperated with the city by providing dental service.

Dr. Brad Marvel, with his assistant Julie Tompkins opened the Leola Dental
Office in December, 1978, with Ruth Geffre as receptionist. Mrs. Sylvia Rott
was their first patient. In August, 1979, Marvel was replaced by Dr. Daniel
Harvey, Mae Click as his assistant, and Donna Krein as receptionist.

Dr. Paul J. Leon carries on the dental practice by coming to Leola from
Aberdeen every Wednesday to serve the community. He is assisted by Crystal Hohn
of Aberdeen.

                Doctors Past and Present

Coming to the Leola area, in the early 1880's a Dr. Stern apparently didn't
care for the pioneer life and stayed only a few days. Dr. Lloyd followed him,
coming to Leola on the stage from Aberdeen. Dr. Lloyd had a drugstore, and his
practice was carried on in the rear of the store, which is the empty building
known as the Pirates' Cove. He added a couple of rooms where he and Mrs. Lloyd
lived until they moved to Rapid City in 1908.

Following Dr. Lloyd came Dr. G. G. Kearns, who arrived in 1909 from Iowa. He
died in 1920.

Dr. Kettner, who came to Leola from Hosmer, confined his work to office
practice. Dr. Kettner came to Leola at the same time Dr. Kearns was practicing
here which meant Leola had two practicing physicians.

Dr. Gilbert Lundquist arrived in Leola in May, 1920, coming from Rapid City.
Dr. Lundquist was quite a sportsman, loving basketball, hunting and fishing. He
loved children. He was a member of the school board when the new school house
was built. One of Dr. Lundquist's projects was a dam for the children to use as
a swimming pool. The dam was built on a site north of Leola. Its real name is
Lundquist Dam and is still a favorite spot for area fishermen and picnickers.
Dr. Lundquist passed away following injury in an automobile accident west of
Leola.

The next doctor to come to Leola was Dr. E. T. Keller, who arrived in October,
1936. He practiced in Leola for about three years.

In 1939, Dr. A. Kositsky came to Leola and remained for several years. After a
span without a doctor, Dr. Erickson practiced here for several months in 1948
and was followed by Dr. J. F. Malloy who came to Leola in 1949.

The Leola Community Hospital was built in 1952 and opened for business in March
of that year. Dr. Malloy and Dr. Karlis Zvejnieks, who set up practice in Leola
in December, 1956, worked in the hospital.

        Dr. J. F. Malloy.

Dr. Malloy left his practice in Leola in December, 1964, because of poor health
and moved to Las Vegas, NV. Finding this did not improve his health he moved
back to Leola and he died on July 29, 1965.

        Dr. Karlis Zvejnieks.

Dr. Zvejnieks continued his practice in Leola until 1966 when he moved to
Aberdeen. He still continued to serve the community by coming to Leola for
office hours once a week until 1970 when he also discontinued his service.

Dr. John McFee started coming to Leola in 1975. He had just moved to Ipswich
and had his offices there but on every Thursday he loads up part of his Ipswich
office and travels to Leola where he often sees patients in the new Clinic
Building until 9-10 o'clock in the evening.

                Farmers Home Administration

Farmers Home Administration has increased its participation ten-fold in
McPherson County rural credit since 1959. Today's present outstanding debt of
nearly $25 million dwarfs the credit needed of 25 years ago. This represents
the largest source of credit for farmers in McPherson County. Poor years for
the area's farmers created by drought in the late '70s and early '80s forced
farmers to ask for emergency aid in record numbers.

Today's Farmers Home Administration handles loans for land, livestock and
machinery. It also loans for houses, community development, recreational
facilities, sewer and water projects, irrigation and grazing associations. This
wide range of assistance varies significantly from the Farmers Home
Administration of 25 years ago when loans were strictly for farmers. Caseload
volume at that time was less than 100 compared to 235 today.

The earlier years of the McPherson County Farmers Home Administration office
was recounted through the assistance of Verna Kulm (Mrs. Allen Kulm), the
County Office Assistant from 1948-1963.

During Mrs. Kulm's tenure as County Office Assistant she helped County
Supervisors E. L. Hague (1947-1956), Maurice McLinn, Acting (1956-1957), Gerald
"Jack" Keehn (1959-1962), Vern Richter (1962) and Harvey Hamman (1962-1967)
administer Farmers Home Administration programs.

Just before the move from the courthouse in 1963 Mrs. Kulm resigned and was
replaced by Margaret Brakhage. She helped Farmers Home Administration move to
its present location on North Sherman into the Valley Telephone Building.

In 1966 Catherine Taylor started her 16 year tenure as County Office Assistant.
During this time Harvey Hamman (1962-1967) completed his stay in Leola. Mrs.
Taylor helped Max Beaver (1967-1970), Hartney Andrisen (1971), Richard Schooley
(1972-1979), Mark Taylor (1979), Lyle Dirks, Acting (1979-1980) and Neal Nelson
(1980-present) assist borrowers with loan programs.

        Farmers Home Administration.

Today's office is staffed by County Supervisor Neal Nelson and Susan Lammle,
who replaced Mrs. Taylor in 1982 after Mrs. Taylor transferred to the Aberdeen
District Farmers Home Administration office.

                Geffre's Produce

Jake Kirschman manages Geffre's Produce station for Vince Geffre. Geffre's
Produce is located along Highway 10, across the street from Hoffman's Standard
Station.

Prior to 1939 this building was owned by Henry Feickert who bought cream and
eggs from the farmers to sell. He then sold the building to Ed Albrecht who
gradually enlarged the station, buying cream and eggs, and feed and seed as
well as other items until it grew to be a grocery market in the '50s. Lloyd
Bain and Ted Leidle purchased the market in 1956 and added a walk-in cooler.

Lloyd bought out Ted in 1960 and then leased the building to Bernard and Janice
Mack.

In 1971, Vince Geffre bought the building and still sells cream, potatoes, and
eggs along with many other items.

Vince also started a junk yard as a hobby on the northwest corner of Leola. He
buys iron, copper, or just about anything you could name.

                Gene's Oil Co.

Gene Rau moved to Leola in 1958 and worked for J. J. Rath who was agent of the
Mobil Oil bulk plant. Gene worked for Mr. Rath until 1963 when Mr. Rath
retired. He then became agent of the bulk plant. In 1979, he bought the bulk
plant from Mobil Oil. In 1969, Gene bought the Schilling Service Station which
his older son, Lee, now manages. Mark, his younger son, helps his father with
the bulk plant.

        Gene's Oil Company.

                Glaesman House Moving

The Reinhold Glaesmans started their business in 1948 when they purchased a
back hoe and did sub-contract work putting in water lines in Ashley, ND.

In 1949-50 they did some water line work for the City of Leola. In 1950 they
moved to Leola where they still reside. In 1951 they built a rock crushing
plant to crush rock for concrete work which now is operated by Arvin Glaesman.
Then in 1957 he built an A-frame trailer to move small buildings but before
long that was not large enough, so they bought timbers and trailers and built a
big truck to move bigger buildings. They kept expanding their moving business.
They bought a big new truck and moved many houses on the reservations.

        Glaesman House Moving

The house moving business is operated by Reinhold and Alvina Glaesman and their
son, Rueben, and Marvin Ketterling.

                Hoffman Parts & Service

Bill and Sheila Hoffman, with the help of Bill's dad, Walter, purchased the
former Leo's Garage September 1, 1981, from Leo and Vi Smolnisky. The business,
known as Hoffman Parts & Service, is an implement and repair shop. While
FARMHAND is the main machinery line the business handles, they have continued
many of the machinery lines Leo carried, while expanding into several newer
lines such as the KRONE round balers and LELY rakes.    The business continues
to operate off Highway 10 in the building previously occupied by Leo's Garage.
Some interior reorganization has been done and a new sign was added to the main
building in March, 1983, when the first open house was held. In July, 1982, the
business added another building, the former Reformed church building, which
Bill and his dad Walter use jointly. The main machinery display lot is at the
west edge of Leola on Highway 10.

        Hoffman Parts and Service.

Gene Weisenburger, employed by the former owners, continues as the diesel
mechanic. Gene also works in the parts department, welds, and does other
repairs. Bill handles parts sales, all machinery sales, and some repairs
including air conditioning and small engine work. Sheila handles the
bookkeeping and accounting work for the business. The business has employed
several others over the past two years, including James Kappes who now farms
near Long Lake.

                Hoffman Oil Co.

        Hoffman Oil Co. and Walt's Standard.

Walter F. Hoffman purchased the Standard bulk plant from Elmer Hoffman on July
1, 1981. Elmer had purchased the plant January 4, 1972, from Vince Geffre, who
had operated it from April, 1951. The business is known as Hoffman Oil Co. and
operates in conjunction with Walt's Standard on Highway 10. Various
improvements have been made in the bulk plant business, including expansion of
tank storage by 40,000 gallons and the addition of business-band-radio for
improved service and efficiency. Walter handles most of the operation of the
bulk business and is assisted by employees who work between the bulk plant and
service station. Marilyn Casey is the bookkeeper.

                Walt's Standard

The Standard service station formerly owned and operated by Vince Geffre was
sold to Walter F. Hoffman in 1980. Vince operated the station from 1963 to
1978; Elmer Hoffman operated the station from 1978 to 1980 when it was sold and
renamed Walt's Standard. The station occupies the same building on Highway 10
that the previous owners had. The building has undergone painting, the office
has been remodeled, and new signs and pumps have been added.

Walter has replaced much of the equipment and added a pipe bender for custom
muffler and tail pipe work. Battery and tire business has been greatly
expanded; and electronic tire balancer was also added. Walter owns and operates
the service station in conjunction with the Standard bulk plant, Hoffman Oil
Co. He is assisted by long-time employees Lloyd Bain and Dave Jacober, and
Elwood Lechner.

        The Honker

"The Honker" as it's now known is located on Lot 19, Block 6 in the City of
Leola and had many owners previously.

On January 5, 1889 this lot was plotted out in Section 20, Township 126, Range
69 and was sold to Edwin D. Haynes.

It is unknown who built the building but prior to 1910 Frank Hooker owned it
and rented it to George Blanchard who had a cafe there. In 1912 Margarretta
Marquardt bought it and also had a cafe and living quarters in it.

                The Honker.

In 1915 Henry Marquardt acquired the property by a Sheriff's Deed. He had a
harness and shoe repair business. Then in 1944 the store was purchased by
Albert Meier. He continued to operate the harness and shoe repair business and
also took over the sale of Municipal Liquor. Later he and his wife Gertrude had
a store there called the Tom Thumb Variety.

In 1959 the store survived the fire that destroyed the north half of the block.

In 1962 Lester A. Bell purchased the building where at different times it
served as a pool hall, beauty shop and barber shop, then later as a home.

In 1980 Ernest Jasmer, Arthur Krein, Byron Kindelspire and John Weisser
purchased it. Today John and Ernest operate it as a recreation parlor. Each
afternoon you may see one of the guys there supervising a card game.

                Law Office


In 1906 Mr. Amos Hoffman of Leola and J. W. Parmley of Ipswich, an experienced
abstractor, became owners of the McPherson County Abstract Company. They
erected the building just east of the courthouse. This building was patterned
after the Ipswich office and was constructed of native fieldstone. They
operated as a partnership for several years when Mr. Hoffman became the sole
owner. The business was operated by Mr. Hoffman until his death and in 1945 was
taken over by his son, Allen Hoffman. It was conducted under this ownership
until August 1, 1949, at which time it was purchased by William D. Hauck and
Raymond E. Neuharth, who operated the business under the original name of
McPherson County Abstract Company. Waneta Geffre was employed as their first
secretary.

        Floyd Meidinger's Law Office.

After the Abstract Company moved to new offices this building housed the
Francis Hohman Law Office. Later it was leased out to the S.C.S. Office and
then to the Senior Citizens. The building was purchased by Floyd Meidinger and
in 1975 he moved his law office into a completely remodeled office. Once
again Waneta is back in the building after an absence of 25 years, working as a
legal secretary.

                The Leola Bakery

The Leola Bakery, owned and operated by Sid Jr. (Tubby) and Agnes Swanson,
stands on the corner of Sherman and Main, where the Moulton-Elliot building was
built in 1885.

The buildings were old landmarks inside whose walls much of Leola's early
history had taken place. There was some point of pride in the owners of the
buildings who felt something tangible and memorable of Leola's founding was
theirs to offer at Leola's 75th Anniversary on June 15 and 16, 1959.

        The Leola Bakery.

However, they were doomed to disappointment, for on February 11, 1959, an early
morning fire originating in the old Moulton-Elliot building completely
destroyed the Bakery, Gamble Store and Pool Hall operated by Tony Koppy.

Sid and Agnes had added new windows and remodeled the apartment one year before
the fire. It was decorated with their first new furniture. Nothing could be
saved from the fire. Albert Breunig bought Tony Koppy's lot for his new Gamble
Store and the Leola Legion bought the extra lot from the Swansons for a new
Legion Bar. Sid and Agnes built a new one-story building to house the new
bakery. It was reopened in August, 1959.

In 1969 disaster struck again. The bakery oven blew up and sent Sid flying
across the bakery table. Luckily he was spared any injuries. The bakery
operated with Agnes in Leola using only a small electric range for kuchen and
the large fryer for the fried goods. Tubby went to Ipswich daily to make bread
and bring it to Leola. It took two months to get another oven set up.

The Leola Bakery has customers from all over the country. These customers, old
and new, come back for the old fashioned German Kuchen (a formula made up from
Agnes' mother's recipe), the same old long-johns, bismarks, and donuts (from
Sid's father's sweet dough), and Tubby's own sugar-free dark breads such as 100
percent whole wheat, rye bread, dark onion rye, cracked wheat, plus many more
products. These products are the secret for a small town bakery to survive for
36 years.

                Leola Equity Exchange

Today's modern service station, as well as the efficient grain-handling
facility had humble beginnings. "A mighty oak from a little acorn grows." The
present organization had its beginnings when a group of our enlightened
pioneers deemed it advisable that they apply the same theory for furthering
their collective business interests in marketing their grains, as they did when
getting together with their neighbors to raise a barn.

In searching the early records of the Leola Equity Exchange, the names
mentioned are early pioneers: Charles Turner, Otto Hauffe, A. Hoffman, Henry
Breunig, D. N. Crouch, Fred Nelson, August Pischke, John Turnwall, S. D. Frost,
C. T. Hill, Ed Joireman, Charles Fosler, N. H. Pierce, Edward Pade, John
Heible, Edward Hickman and Joseph Stephan. The aforementioned, with a few
others, met on an August day in 1912, and subscribed to 46 shares of capital
stock at a value of $25 per share. These people elected the first board of five
directors, namely David H. Crouch, president; Charles T. Hill, vice-president;
A. Hoffman, secretary/treasurer; S. D. Frost and Fred Nelson. A certificate No.
27738 of their Articles of Incorporation were duly issued and signed by Samuel
E. Palley on August 12, 1912.

In early 1913, the directors entered into an agreement with Woodward Commission
Company of Minneapolis, MN, wherewith the commission firm would allow them
$5,000 credit for buying grain. Part of the agreement was that 90 percent of
the grain purchased had to be shipped to their commission firm.

The business of hiring a manager was attended to at the July 5, 1913,
directors' meeting. Mr. Kagle was hired at a salary of $1,120 for one year.

The first directors did not get around to setting director fees until the
December 5, 1914, meeting when they agreed to pay the directors $1 per meeting.

At a special board meeting in the spring of 1914, it was agreed to order a
carload of Marquis seed wheat from McCaul and Densmore at a price of $1.35 per
bushel. At a special meeting in December of 1920, the board accepted the
resignation of Manager J. W. Wallrich and at a meeting in January, 1921, Joe
Kohlhoff was hired. A near financial collapse was averted by a special
reorganization at the March 5, 1921, meeting. It was at this meeting that the
board authorized the issuance of $45,000 in capital stock divided into 1,800
shares at a value of $25 each.

The following directors took over immediately after the reorganization: Fred
Nelson, president; H. H. Yost, secretary; W. G. Schuchardt; Frank Galster; and
Matt Weisser.

From the period following the reorganization, a steady and healthy growth was
experienced by the Leola Equity Exchange. Up to now business had been
exclusively in the grain merchandising area. In the late '20s, it became
apparent that in order to better serve the growing community, it was considered
advisable to expand the organization into the petroleum and service station
field.

An oil station, together with a tank truck and bulk station, was authorized and
began operations in early 1930. At a 1940 board meeting, it was agreed to
expand the filling station and plans were authorized and executed to enlarge
the oil facilities.

The propane bottle gas was purchased from McPherson County Equipment Co. in
1955, at a cost of $8,000. One-hundred pound propane bottles were selling at
that time for $5; presently the price is in the $20 range. Still further
improvement was made in 1958, when the board decided to add a new concrete
elevator. Negotiations were completed with Hogenson Construction of
Minneapolis, MN, to build the elevator with a capacity of 215,000 bushels. Cost
of the unit was $182,000. Grand opening of this new unit was held on November
7, 1959.

        Leola Equity Exchange.

A modern up-to-date service station was built in 1962, at a cost of $45,000 to
its grain merchandising.

Presently the Leola Equity Exchange provides employment to 13 employees, and
generates a payroll of nearly $ 192,000.

Currently this entire unit is under the able management of Terry Heider, who
works with a board of directors consisting of: Denver Guthmiller, president;
Lavern Lapka, vice-president; Wilton Hoffman, secretary/treasurer; LeRoy
Weiszhaar, and Melvin Kessler.

                Leola Insurance Agency

The history of Leola Insurance Agency is rather short. It began on March 8th,
1983, after it was purchased from Leola Insurance & Real Estate. The latter was
formed on January 1, 1972, through a merger of Ed's Insurance Agency, owned by
Ed Hilgemann and Knudson Insurance Agency owned by T. J. Heibel and Clarence

        Leola Insurance and Real Estate Agency.

The insurance agency continues to offer a complete line of insurance and bonds.
It is owned by Financial Transactions Systems, Inc., of Mitchell, SD.

The Real Estate business is still owned and operated by Ed Hilgemann, Reuben
