                Leola Livestock Sale Barn

The Leola Livestock Sale Barn was built on the northeast side of town in 1950.
Clarence Knudson, Roy Stover, and George Geffre, owners, began operating the
barn in the fall of that year.

In 1952, the barn was sold to Alvin Saylor, Floyd C. Ritter, Albert Haefner,
and Ray and Ted Goehring of Herreid, SD. The barn was sold again in October,
1953, to the original owners . They again sold in March, 1954, to Herbert
Weisz, Dean Pade and Donald Mack. Later Pade and Mack bought out Weisz.

        Leola Livestock Sale Barn.

Wayne Scofield bought the barn in 1978 when it was sold after Don Mack's death.
He later sold it to the Scallons of North Dakota and Greg Scallon opened the
barn for business May 30, 1980. The barn is presently owned by Scallons and
managed by Walter C. Wolf.

                The Leola Post Office

An application for a special office to be named Leola, dated June 20, 1883, was
submitted to the First Assistant Postmaster General by John Murrie who had
previously been recommended as postmaster.

The application stated that Leola was not a village and that the office would
serve between 300 and 400 people. Mail would be hauled from Westport until a
regular route would be granted.

The records of the Post Office Department show that an office was established
at Leola, Dakota Territory, on July 2, 1883, with John Murrie as postmaster.

On October 3, 1883, an office was also established at Koto with Julius M. L.
Bergoff as postmaster. Koto was a small village about six miles northeast of
Leola. Bergoff was succeeded by Robert H. Hoag on May 1, 1885. This office was
discontinued on October 23, 1887, and the patrons of this area were then served
from the Leola office.

On February 27, 1885, Edward D. Dunning took over the duties of postmaster at
Leola and held that office until November, 1886, when Paul D. Krobs was
appointed. He was succeeded by John K. Schindler on August 16, 1889.

From the information obtained, it appears that Mr. Schindler operated a general
merchandise store in connection with the post office on the site now occupied
by the Leola State Bank. The building was later moved across the street and was
last known as Tony's Recreational Parlor. It, along with the Bakery,
(originally Moulton's Store) and the Gamble Store were destroyed by fire on
February 11, 1959.

On September 5, 1893, Fred Junge, Jr. was appointed postmaster and he had the
office in the building later known as the Henry B. Hoff residence (which has
now been torn down after being purchased by the Equity). Mr. Junge had charge
of the office until the appointment of Emma Hickman on August 21, 1897.

Miss Hickman had the office in connection with a general store, which was known
as the Post Office Store, later as the Leola Leader and for a short time as the
Gamble Store, before being razed. About 1897 this building was moved from the
location now occupied by the American Legion Hall. Prior to that time it was
known as the Fox Store.

Frank D. Lowry, editor of the McPherson County Herald was appointed to succeed
Miss Hickman on August 26, 1904. Mr. Lowry first had the post office in the
Junge Feed Store, later the Dave Brosz residence. On December 1, 1909, it was
moved to a new brick building that had been put up by him to house the post
office and the McPherson County Herald. The post office remained in this
building until October 1, 1960, when the office with Fred Hepperle as
postmaster moved to its new and present location on the east side of Sherman
Street.

        The Leola Post Office.

Other postmasters serving after Frank Lowry follow with the dates of their
appointments.

Frank Junge,       April 24, 1914, through October 1, 1919.
Phrene June,       October 1, 1919, through May 28, 1920.
William L. Lowry,  May 28, 1920, through August 19, 1920.
Emanuel C. Sigler, August 19, 1920, through February 10, 1922.
Henry W. Knudson,  February 10, 1922, through November 15, 1927.
Theodore B. Reue,  November 15, 1927, through May 10, 1928.
Mrs. Della Reue,   May 10, 1928, through August 17, 1936.
Fred Hepperle,     August 17, 1936, through December 1, 1967.
Delmer Haux,       acting postmaster, December 1, 1967, through March 7, 1970.
Frank Serfoss,     Officer-in-Charge, March 7, 1970, through June 26, 1971.
Frank Serfoss,     Postmaster, June 26, 1971, through June 15, 1979.
Pamela Schaffner,  Officer-in-Charge, June 15, 1979, through February 9, 1980.

Frank was the first postmaster to be appointed under the new merit system.

The present postmaster is VerNiece Haux who received her appointment on
February 9, 1980. She had been a clerk at the office since December 19, 1964,
and also had served as Officer-in-Charge at Wetonka and as a part-time flex at
Aberdeen. Assisting VerNiece at present are Pam Schaffner (Zantow) and Ina
Schock (Albrecht) as parttime flex clerks. At present the rural deliveries are
made by highway contract routes under Jacob Schaible, Star Route 1, and Dean
Schock, Star Route 2.

Until the coming of the M. & St. L. Railroad in 1906, the mail was hauled daily
cross-country from Aberdeen. Usually four teams of horses were used on this
mail run. Each team making a one-way trip every other day. The last contractor
for this route was Henry Young, Sr., who hauled the mail for many years. This
cross-country trail or road over which the mail was transported left Leola
going in a southeasterly direction for about three miles and then went in an
easterly direction for about six miles to the old Soo Railroad Grade. It then
followed the grade in a southeasterly direction to the Delhi post office which
was established on January 7, 1884, several miles north of the present site of
Wetonka. Postmasters at this office were Edward V. Laphan, George W. Wardell,
James W. Tooker, Josephine Tooker and John W. Lebold. That office was
discontinued October 6, 1908. After leaving the Delhi office the trail left
the old Soo grade to miss a grade opening. About one mile farther down the
road, it again followed the Soo grade for a short distance before leaving it to
go south to the Murray Post office which was also known as The Half-Way
Station. From here the trail went east to the neighborhood of Carlyle Hall
where it again went back on the Soo grade following it down near the present
Wylie Park, then angled off to the Milwaukee Depot in Aberdeen.

Several years before the M. & St. L. Railroad came through, the Murray post
office was moved about a halfmile east and was then called the Bern post
office, with Mr. Von Eschen in charge. This office was discontinued soon after
the Wetonka office was established on January 30, 1907, with Edward B. Friel as
postmaster.

For many years, mail was received at Leola via the M. & St. L. Railroad. After
the railroad was abandoned, M. & St. L. continued to truck mail into the area,
later being replaced by a local contract under the Postal Service
Transportation Management office at St. Paul, MN.

                Leola Rexall Drug

In 1919, Mark Holmes established a drugstore in the building that is now empty
but known as Rolly's Pool Hall. Before that, a drugstore had been run by Frank
Billings in the building last known as the Pirates' Cove.

In 1936, the drugstore was moved to its present location. Mark was an active
pharmacist for over 42 years. His son Leslie also worked there as a pharmacist.
In August of 1966, Holmes sold the store to Lila Kramlich of Eureka. Mark
retired and Leslie moved to Arizona. During 40 years of service the Holmeses
had the pleasure of working with the following doctors and dentists: Kearns,
Gillette, Carlson, Gill, Hoeven, Keller, Kositsky, Erickson, Malloy, Schnaidt
and Zvejnieks.

Lila Kramlich employed Kenneth Kraft as a pharmacist for one year when the
local doctor left. The drug department was then discontinued. Now the area once
again is being served by a doctor and prescriptions are filled at the Eureka
Rexall Drug owned by Lila and brought to the Leola Drug.

Katie Lacher was a loyal employee of the Holmes and Lila for many years. Marva
Lou Zelmer is now employed by the drugstore.

                Leola State Bank

The Bank of Leola, also known as Turner's Bank was chartered prior. to 1894,
and was opened by Charles Turner in 1884 as a private bank. Charles N. Herreid
also had his law office in the rear of the bank. In 1907 it became a state
bank which closed in January, 1927, and reopened in April, 1927, after
consolidating with the First State Bank.

In the spring of 1906, Mr. Reagan and Mr. Hooper of Eureka, established the
First State Bank in Leola. John J. Hepperle, J. E. Reagan, and F. H. Hooper
were its officers. This bank was located where the Harmony of Beauty and the
Barber Shop are now located.

In 1927 the Bank of Leola and the First State Bank consolidated. The two were
converted into a national bank when both banks sold their interest to the First
National Bank Corporation of Minneapolis.

Another bank was the Exchange Bank of Leola, chartered on May 12, 1902, and
liquidated October 10, 1903. A McPherson County Bank was chartered on July 1,
1935, but never opened. It was located in the Schindler building with F. A.
Isley, President.

In the dirty '30s, after a time without banking facilities, Leola was served
for a short time by an exchange set up by the First National Bank of Aberdeen.
On about June 15, 1940, a branch office of the Ipswich State Bank was
established in the old First State Bank building. E. W. Hilgemann, Jr. managed
the branch until April, 1942, when Clarence Knudson succeeded him. The branch
was moved to the present bank building. Application for a new charter to open a
new bank at Leola was made on September 24, 1943. On March 10, 1944, the first
stockholders meeting was held at the Leola State Bank, in preparation to
opening the new bank on May 15, 1944. The following officers were elected: J.
F. Holdhusen, Pres.; E. W. Hilgemann, Sr. Vice Pres.; and Clarence E. Knudson,
Cashier. H. S. Crissman and Leo Heibel were elected directors.

The bank opened on May 15, 1944, taking over all deposits of the branch office
of the Ipswich State Bank.

In 1954 J. F. Holdhusen passed away and Clarence Knudson was elected president,
having purchased Mr. Holdhusen's interests in the bank, and David L. Thomas was
elected Cashier.

        Leola State Bank.

J. S. Holdhusen, son of J. F. Holdhusen was elected as director to replace his
father.

D. L. Thomas was elected vice president and cashier, and T. J. Heibel was
elected assistant cashier; also both men were then serving as directors. Thomas
J. Heibel replaced Leo Heibel who passed away.

In 1969 the directors were: C. E. Knudson, D. L. Thomas, T. J. Heibel, J. S.
Holdhusen and H. S. Crissman.

In September, 1982, the board of directors of Leola State Bank were: C. E.
Knudson, J. J. Rath, (who replaced D. L. Thomas), T. J. Heibel, Earle Crissman
(who replaced J. S. Holdhusen). They voted to become a subsidiary of the
Hopkins Financial Corporation, Mitchell, SD, which sale was consummated on
March 7, 1983. The new directors and officers are: T. J. Heibel, Pres.; Doug
Hilmoe, Vice Pres.

The employees are: Angela Schilling, Lila Smalley, Dorothy Daly, Margaret
Heider, Marsha Lapka, Judy Wolff and Kevin Dietz.

                McPherson County Abstract Company

The McPherson County Abstract Company, the oldest business still in existence
in Leola, was organized and established in 1885 by L. T. Boucher, John Boucher,
and H. Sopper. Other Abstractors throughout the years were Chas. Turner, James
Clayton, Arnos Hoffman, F. A. Hoffman, William D. Hauck and Raymond E.
Neuharth. Title work in this office consists of title searching, abstracting,
title reports, title memos, title insurance, etc. The present Abstractor is
Lorine K. Neuharth, President of said Company. She is also an agent for Title
Insurance Company of Minnesota, writing owner's and mortgage policies.

        McPherson County Abstract Company.

                McPherson County Herald

The McPherson County Herald was established in October, 1892, by Andrew
Williams and was later owned by F. D. Lowry in 1905. In 1911 he built the
two-story post office building where the Herald was published for many years.
A. V. Pallviny assumed ownership in 1920. In 1929 Henry Artz bought the Herald
and moved the establishment from the basement of the P.O. building across the
street to the building which is the present municipal liquor store. There was a
rapid turnover of publishers during the war years. Virgil and Norma Smith and
Jack Dorman in 1942 were followed closely by Ralph and Agnes Davidson who also
entered the service. They were succeeded by Frank Cooper who published the
Herald until 1944. Publisher, Edward Walter Bowen purchased the paper in 1944.
Beulah Bowen and Lowell Shannon worked as the staff.

Walter Bowen was born March 23, 1902, at Forman, ND, as he grew up he learned
the printing business from the family business. Mr. Bowen was a member of the
Methodist Church, Leola Lodge No. 154 and the Better Leola Club and was
dedicated to the betterment of the community. He used his pen to focus
attention on community situations.

Beulah Lee Farley was born December 23, 1912, at Wimer, NE, and married E. W.
Bowen August 25, 1941. Beulah took a prominent part in the publication of the
Herald up until her death January 27, 1962.

Walter passed away October 10, 1966. Shirlene and Lowell Shannon took over his
father's business until they moved to California.

Richard and Mabel Morseth served the Leola community well for 10 years as
publisher and editor of the Herald after purchasing it in July, 1969.

        McPherson County Herald.

The Herald has been housed in various buildings including the First State Bank
Building, the present liquor store and is presently located in the Herald
Building.

Monte and Kathy Zimmer are the 1984 publisher and editor of the paper.

                The Leola Municipal Building

For many years the city of Leola did not have a City Municipal Building. All
the city meetings and the bookwork was done in the Leola Fire Hall. The talk of
constructing a Municipal Building had been going on for over a year. The Leola
city council, consisting of Mayor Enoch Schaffer; councilmen, Laverne Skott,
Norbert Steckler, Reuben Kappes, Harvey Schaible, Daryl Thorpe and Marvin Maule
decided to use the $22,000 Revenue Sharing money the city had acquired during
the years 1972-73 and '74 plus further Revenue Sharing monies that the city
would receive to have a City Municipal Building constructed.

At the March 3, 1975, meeting the Council called for bids for the construction
of a 40' x 60' steel building. This was to house the council room, finance
officer's office, public rest rooms and a community room. The bids were to be
let at the April 7th meeting but the Council took the bids under advisement
until April 15. The bid presented by Steel Structures for $37,800 was accepted
by the Council.

This building was built and completely furnished with Revenue Sharing monies
which the city had received from the Federal Government.

        The Leola Municipal Building.

This building is a big asset to the city of Leola because of the many
activities taking place in the community room, such as for family gatherings,
graduation open houses, large rummage sales, bake sales and ice cream socials.
It is also a meeting place for many organizations such as Cub Scouts, Soil
Conservation District, Sportsmans Club and square dancing.

                The Municipal Liquor Store

A vacant lot, where the liquor store now stands, was purchased in 1908 by John
J. Hepperle and was sold to Gottlieb Kammerer in 1910. Before 1913 a meat
market was managed from a building on this lot. In 1913, Jake and Freida Brosz,
brother and sister, operated a cafe for a short time. The building was sold in
1919 to Henry Pruitt and again in 1920 to Jacob Huhm. Rod Ronayne rented the
building during this time for a cream station. In 1929, H. J. Artz bought the
store to use as a print shop.

Henry Hoff bought the shop in 1945 and later sold it to John E. Schock on
January 10, 1946. John did some remodeling by lowering the ceiling and
partitioned it into rooms so it could be lived in.

        The Municipal Liquor Store.

It was then sold to Albert Breitag on June 2, 1958. Albert worked for the city
of Leola and managed the Municipal Liquor Store. The first off-sale municipal
liquor store was established in May, 1935, with Mark L. Holmes as manager. It
was located where the building known as Rollie's Pool Hall is.

Breitag moved the liquor store from what is now known as the Honker, to its
present location. Albert died in 1970 and his wife Esther sold the store to
Clifton Tschappat June 15, 1970.

Clifton and his wife Clara have living quarters in the building and manage the
liquor store for the city of Leola.

                Modern Beauty Shop

Vivian Rueb, presently operates her beauty shop in her home. She began her
career in December of 1941 after she graduated from Remily's Beauty Academy in
Aberdeen. She was employed by Tillie Hoff, who at that time owned the shop. In
1944 she purchased the shop and operated it in the Knudson Hotel until 1947
when she relocated into her home and has operated the shop for 42 years. She
has enjoyed the many years and the many patrons she has served all these years.
During these years she and her husband, Walter, also raised three daughters.

        The Modern Beauty Shop.

                MDU

Very few of the early settlers owned even a kerosene lamp. The typical prairie
lamp was a rag smeared with lard and twisted into a saucer of lard or butter.
Lard in the lamp meant no lard for food. On the other hand, lard for food meant
long winter evenings by stove light or in darkness.

Specific hours for specific districts to run washing machines and use electric
irons (the only "modern" appliances found in most homes when Leola first
started to operate its municipal light plant in the winter of 1911 and 1912)
would definitely be the curtailment of a necessity to us, but to the users of
that first electric power it was the height of utility--and even luxury.

Originally serving only the main business section, the plant was powered by two
Mogul gas engines which, according to old-timers, vibrated enough to shake the
whole town. Located in an older building where the old fire-hall now stands,
the plant was improved in 1915 by adding two International 25 horse power
gasoline engines and two new dynamos for increased power output. A $3,500 bond
issue was passed to finance the purchase of these engines and the wiring of the
balance of the town. Operators were the town marshals; Bill Lortscher was the
first operator. Matt Scherman and Jacob Kiesz both put in long stints at
keeping the lights on.

Leola's street lighting system was started in September, 1922, according to the
city minutes. Montana-Dakota Utilities apparently obtained its first franchise
in Leola in 1926, since they definitely were voted their second franchise on
August 5, 1946. The new street lights were installed by MDU in 1954.

The first mercury vapor street lights were installed in the Leola business
district in 1964. Mercury vapor lights were then installed in the residential
section in 1974.

Cleon Goodrich started with MDU as a salesman in October, 1952, and retired in
February, 1973. LaVerne Challes was a district representative starting in Leola
in 1963 and worked here through 1967. In 1967 Norbert Steckler transferred from
Ipswich to Leola as a district representative. Norbert worked for MDU until his
unexpected death on March 10, 1982. On October 18, 1982, Gerold Weron
transferred from Lemmon, SD, to Leola as district representative.

                Modern Woodmen of America Insurance

        Modern Woodmen Charter.

The Modern Woodmen of America Insurance Company is among the oldest of
organizations in early Leola. A `Leola Camp-No. 2757' was organized by 21
members February 20, 1895. The company, which was 12 years old at the time, had
been forming similar camps throughout the midwest. Eureka's camp was formed in
1894. The company advocated wholesome social activities and character-building
for men along with protection for their widows and orphans. Since there were no
movies or radios to compete with, the camp quickly became one of the social
centers of the town. They held regular meetings and chose delegates to attend
the conventions. The charter members were: James Clayton, Frank X. Junge, Fred
Junge, Jr., Lewis H. Moulton, Albert Junge, Peter LaFontaine, Frank D. Lowry,
F. B. Megarry, E. S. Moulton, Charles W. Murray, Harry Millerueau, Gottlob
Pade, Orvin J. Roe, Charles W. Stone, Charles Turner, Frank L. Warren, Andrew
Williams, John Hickman, Henry Young, Hiram Yost and Emmett L. Yost. The Charter
Document is displayed in Arthur Breitag's office.

The Modern Woodmen Camp remained active for a good many years. They continued
to have members in the Leola area but did not have an area representative until
1971 when Ray Neuharth became a Modern Woodmen Representative. Arthur Breitag
joined him in 1972. The social events had dwindled until 1973 when Ray with the
help of Arthur renewed the social activities by hosting a banquet honoring all
50-year policy holders. Some of the men who were honored were: Albert C.
Hauffe, Earl Heibel, Mark Holmes, and Lester Bell. They were presented with
50-year pins.

The Leola Camp has become a part of the `Aberdeen Camp-No. 2094' and they
continue to sponsor many activities in the area. They all celebrated Modern
Woodmen's Centennial in 1983.

At the present time, Arthur A. Breitag is the Modern Woodmen District
Representative and maintains an office in his home in Leola.

        Art Breitag.

                OK Hardware

Albert Breunig and his wife, Sarah Tribble Breunig, purchased the Gamble Store
from Mr. and Mrs. E. B. Rude in 1947. The Rudes had operated it for many years
before that.

Albert and Sarah often talked of constructing a new building and expanding
their business stock and facilities, but kept putting it off for what they
hoped to be a more opportune time. The plans were shattered on November 1,
1957, when Sarah passed away due to cancer, and Albert consequently abandoned
most thoughts of expansion. In February, 1959, a fire wiped out the Leola
Bakery, the Gamble Store, and the Koppy Recreation Parlor.

        O. K. Hardware.

The bakery owners immediately set out to make plans for a new building. Albert
and the Leola American Legion Post quickly became interested in the project.
The result was the construction of a beautiful 75' x 80' brick and tile
building housing the three enterprises on the ground floor with the Hauck and
Neuharth Insurance Agency occupying the central basement office room under the
American Legion club room. The Gamble portion of the building occupied a space
of 28' x 80'. The Henry Heuther Construction Company were the contractors for
the new structure. In 1981, the Gamble Store name was discontinued. Since that
time, Albert has retained the business in the name of OK Hardware with the help
of his brother, Joe Breunig, Lucille Geffre, and Phyllis Rogers as present
clerks.

                Peavey Lumber

What is now known as Peavey Building Supplies was originally known as the
Mitchell Lumber Company. This was one of two lumberyards established in 1906
following the arrival of the railroad in Leola. The Mitchell yard was managed
by Ray Washburn with Idelette Lundquist as the bookkeeper. The other yard was
the Central. The Central yard originally was located where Hoffman's Standard
is now and was managed by H. Thielen. John V. Hohman followed Washburn as
manager, with Henry Young as assistant of the Mitchell. When the Central was
moved to its permanent site east of the courthouse, Fred Schoenfelder was the
manager. He was succeeded by Martin Switzenberg in 1921. Henry Young was the
next manager until retiring in 1956. Leo Rogers managed the business until
1957, when the store closed.

        Peavey Lumber Company.

In 1948 the Peavey Company of Minneapolis purchased the yard, with Charley
Schmalz remaining as manager, where he remained until 1949, when he was
promoted to a District Superintendent.

At that time, a local man, Ed Hilgemann, took over as manager. Ed managed the
yard for eight years until 1957. From 1957 until 1969 the yard was managed by
several different people.

The present manager, Gary Guthmiller, took over the management in August of
1969.

                Schumacher Construction

Henry Schumacher hailed from the Long Lake area. He started carpentry while
farming. Carpenter work was demanding thus resulting in his quitting farming.

The first home that Henry built was the Robert Opp house north of Long Lake. He
also helped build the church parsonage in Long Lake and Jake Schaible's first
house in Leola. He was hired by Emil Hoffman in the fall of 1958 to build
Emil's house, Enoch Schaffer and Alvin Schilling homes.

He then decided to go into business for himself in 1960 as "Henry
Schumacher--Home Builder and Carpenter."

He built the Parish Education Unit on Salem Emanuel Lutheran Church in Long
Lake and three other houses for himself.

Schumacher Construction.

D. Haux and Henry were together for 12 years until September, 1982, when their
partnership dissolved. Henry bought out Delmer's share and is still known as
"Schumacher Construction."

Part of the building is rented out to the Pre-School Nursery operated by Judy
Weiszhaar, which has been in operation for three years, and part to Jim Evans
where he has operated a Body Shop.

Henry has built some 30 houses and other buildings while in business for
himself and some less while in partnership. Henry's wife Laura helped out
many times also as she did most of the wood finishing.

Henry still enjoys building and remodeling, progress and the end results of a
beautiful home.

                Schumacher's Jack and Jill

When Gerhardt and Mary (Gutjhar) were married they decided to open a creamery
in Leola. They converted the garage building (which housed the car Mary drove
to school) into a cream station. This building stood where the present cooling
car
for the Jack and Jill store stands.

They bought cream from the farmers and sold it to the Sugar Creek Creamery at
Bristol, SD. Eggs, poultry, hides, wool, and turkeys were bought and the
turkeys dressed out in a small building in back of their home. The dressed
turkeys were then marketed in Ellendale, ND, and Aberdeen, SD.

When Gerhardt left for the war, Mary was left to operate the cream station.

In 1943, they built a new store with their living quarters in the back. They
then called the store "Breitag's Market." With volume of cream and eggs being
sold, there was a need for more room and in 1951 a south wing was added.

The Breitag's four sons, Gary, William, Melvin and James helped out in the
store and cream station.

In 1954 another wing was added to the north. Gerhardt bought a truck and hauled
the cream bought from farmers to the Bristol Creamery. Three trips a week were
made and on the return trip he picked up groceries at Aberdeen to stock the
store.

Mary did all the bookkeeping and ordering of groceries besides keeping up the
house, store and cream station.

        Schumacher's Jack & Jill.

In 1958 they sold the business to Wesley and Verna Rueb and in 1960 they
completely remodeled the store and it became known as Rueb's Jack and Jill. It
operated under this name until it was sold to Bob and Marian Schumacher in
1975. Now it is known as Schumacher's Jack and Jill.

                Soil Conservation District

Following years of little moisture and high winds in South Dakota much of the
soil that was farmed was washing or blowing away. As erosion conditions
progressed farmers decided to do something about it and went to Washington to
ask for help and in 1929 the Soil Erosion Service was established to conduct
erosion control investigations on the land.

In 1933, the name was changed to the Soil Conservation Service, and Civilian
Conservation Corp Camps were set up to provide manpower for projects to
demonstrate erosion control practices.

The phasing out of demonstration projects and CCC camps changed some of the
type of assistance the Soil Conservation Service provided to farmers and
ranchers. This change brought about the formation of Soil Conservation
Districts with the aid of the Soil Conservation Service to promote conservation
practices.

State legislation was passed in 1937 and a movement was made to organize local
Soil Conservation Districts providing a statement policy and scope of the law.
The State Soil Conservation Committee was established and the law made to prove
the procedures for setting up a district organization, the duties and
responsibilities of the supervisors.

The McPherson County Conservation District was first organized in 1954 with the
following serving as supervisors: Howard Mettler, Eureka; Lawrence Wachter
Forbes, ND; Walter Strobel, Eureka; Ferdinand Wolff, Eureka; and Harry E.
Hoffman, Leola. Allen Morrison and Dominic Kallas assisted with the
organization of the district.

They named the major problems in McPherson as wind and water erosion and dust
storms; productivity destroyed; too much grass plowed under; too much water
lost by run-off and insufficient livestock water in pastures.

With the assistance of the Soil Conservation Service and other agricultural
agencies, district supervisors applied different conservation practices on the
land to control erosion.

Practices such as: tree planting, terraces, pasture and hayland planting, strip
cropping, pasture and hayland management, developments for livestock water,
crop residue management, grassed waterways, and many others.

        Left to right: Greg Merkel, Robert Gab, Hamey Shafer, Dennis Jahraus,
        John Weisser, Reuben Ehresman, Clifford Wolff and Gordon Rath. Not
        pictured: Frank Geffre.

There are five supervisors who serve on the Conservation Board and are elected
in the general election with assistants that are appointed by the supervisors.
Currently serving on the board are: Robert Gab, Clifford Wolff, Reuben
Ehresman, John Weisser and Frank Geffre, along with their assistants: Reuben
Woehlhoff, Dennis Jahraus, Harvey Shafer and Gordon Rath.

The people behind the scenes are Sylvia Arioso, bookkeeper; Greg Merkel,
district manager; James Schaffer, technician and Yvonne Haefner, soil
conservationist.

                Soil Conservation Service

When homesteaders came to South Dakota and into McPherson County they came from
agricultural communities. They found land that was abundant in variety, from
the lush grasses to the lakes and rivers and creeks for water, and the birds,
fish, and animals. At the time of settlement there was very little information
about the soil and its management and so the settlers looked to their neighbors
from the east for farming methods. But with little rainfall and high winds
crops failed or yields were reduced causing a soil condition that was
susceptible to wind and water erosion. As erosion occurred farmers and ranchers
became concerned and asked the federal government to help. Thus in 1933 the
Soil Erosion Service was established to conduct erosion control investigations.
In 1935 the name was changed to Soil Conservation Service (SCS).

In 1954 when McPherson County Soil and Water Conservation District was
organized the Soil Conservation Service was asked to assist them in
implementing their erosion control practices. The first office being located on
the third floor of the courthouse in Leola, where the judge's office is now.

Charles W. McDaniel, Work Unit Conservationist (WUC) with Floyd Kallenberger,
part-time soil conservation aid, assisted the district in determining which
conservation practice would best control erosion on the land. The office was
later moved to the old McPherson County Abstract building which is now known as
Meidinger's building. In 1964, James Schaffer, of Leola, began working
part-time as a conservation aid and was later promoted to full-time
conservation technician. March 16, 1966, Marva Lou Geffre, of Leola, joined the
staff as an engineering aid and was later promoted to conservation aid. Marva
Lou worked part-time assisting in the field and in doing office work.

The office was then moved back to third floor of the courthouse in 1972. In
1974, the district supervisors asked for a current inventory of the soils in
the county, so an agreement was drawn up and the Soil Conservation Service sent
soil scientists into the area to begin mapping. It took five years to complete
mapping the county and in that time the following soil scientists worked here:
Loren Schultz, party leader; Robert Blank, Tom Martin, Jim Clausen, Dave Bowes,
and Nilo Reber.

The Soil Conservation Service and the district continue to work together in an
endeavor to control the erosion in McPherson County, with SCS providing the
technical assistance needed to implement conservation practices. Currently the
field office is staffed by a soil conservationist and soil conservation
technician, with an acting district conservationist from Edmunds County to
assist.

Following is a list of past work unit conservationists (WUC), district
conservationists (DC), soil conservationists (SC), conservation aids (CA), and
conservation technicians (CT) that have worked or are working in the Leola
field office:

1954-58  Charles W. McDaniel (WUC)
1958-61  Ralph Stensland (WUC)
1962-65  Jim Rezek (DC)
1965-67  Alton Taylor (DC)
1967     Darrel Bentz (SC)
1967-70  Merle Shelbourne (DC)

                The Stitchin' Post

For many years the citizens of Leola depended on the skills of John Voegele for
salvaging worn shoes, repairing tarps, and other leather and canvas needs. In
November, 1983, John retired from his leather shop and sold the business to Jim
Bidwell, who opened The Stitchin' Post downtown the following month. Jim, who
trained with John for several months before purchasing the business, bought and
renovated the old poolhall, which he shares with The Wiser Miser, and he hopes
eventually to expand to include saddle and tack repair, saddlemaking, and
perhaps retail sale of tack and western boots.

        Jim Bidwell.

                The Western Mutual Telephone Company

        Mutual Telephone certificate.

Western Mutual Telephone Company was organized in Leola July 9, 1906. In 1927
Mr. and Mrs. Bill Lindley became the telephone operator and the lineman. At
that time Frances Reible had been the telephone operator for many years. It was
a privately-owned concern and there were at least two country lines that had
their own stockholders and their own lineman to do the work. Koto Township
owned their own lines and Art Mack was their lineman. Hoffman Township also
owned their lines and Fred Feickert was their lineman. (John Hoffman also took
care of one country line.)

The Thomas family had been doing the telephone work when Bill and Leslie
Lindley, were hired. Mr. Thomas was the first lineman that worked here. He and
his family moved from the vicinity when Lindleys were hired. Wages were very
low at that time and many times they had to wait until the next month for their
pay. A monthly paycheck for the two was only $40 per month. Wetonka also had a
small telephone exchange affiliated with Western Mutual. Leonard Von Eschen ran
the switchboard with help from his mother.

Amos Hoffman of Leola and Lou Lorber, and possibly Frank Boyle of Wetonka were
on the Board of Directors. When the dirty '30s hit it was very hard to get the
necessary equipment to keep things going in tip-top shape. All four Lindley
children took their turns running the switchboard. The first board they had was
rung by hand power. After a few years the old switchboard gave out and was
replaced by one run by electricity. It was so much easier to run. In damp
weather the lines would all be grounded and to try to ring by hand was almost
impossible. At first when a fire call came in someone had to run over to the
water tower and ring the fire bell, which still hangs there. Later they put in
a siren which could be operated by the touch of a switch.

        The first switchboard.

Frances Reible had to retire due to poor health. She was succeeded by Virginia
Lindley Schanzenbach who helped a few hours each day. Rosella Gaster worked
parttime but she married and moved to Bismarck, ND. Mildred Schick had moved
into the housing unit in the back part of the office where the Thomas and
Lindley families lived. Meta Bain also was employed as operator for a few
years.

Bill Lindley worked as a lineman for a few years, he was succeeded by Adolph
Bartmus who worked as a lineman for many years. Next linemen in succession
were: Sam Archer, Ben Schaible, Bill Hilgemann and Laverne Skott. Western
Mutual Telephone Co. was already in the transfer of property to Valley
Telephone of Herreid, SD. Bill Schilling of Hosmer helped along with the work
of building the new company.

                Telephone Cooperative--Cable TV

The board of directors of Valley Telephone cooperative, realizing that we must
keep up with current trends, changed the name to Valley Telecommunications
Cooperative and entered the Community Antenna Television business. Franchises
and FCC waivers were obtained in Leola and Herreid in 1979.

A survey was taken and the most interest was shown by the people of Leola.
Construction began in Leola for the Cable TV System in September, 1980 and was
completed in February, 1981.

Valley Telecommunications Cooperative became the first telephone cooperative in
South Dakota to provide Cable TV to a small local community of 800 population.
Leola, SD was one of the first towns in the nation to receive this service by a
telephone cooperative.

                Watkins

The more than one hundred year old J. R. Watkins Company has served this area
since horse and buggy days. Walter Rueb had the dealership of east McPherson
County since May 8, 1938 until his passing November 5, 1981. He devoted full
time to his well-established business for 43 years. During these years he saw
this business grow from a complete household line in the beginning to a
complete farm-line program, dealing in cattle mineral minvite and many other
services for farmers. He enjoyed his many customers and serving them. After his
passing, his wife, Vivian disposed of the farming products, but is still
serving customers with the full household line.

        Wilma's Museum & Rock Shop, Wilma Hilgemann, Proprietor

Wilma's Museum & Rock Shop was officially started in 1973. Wilma's interest in
rocks began while living next door to Wayne and Vina Schuchardts. Vina had a
son-in-law who was a geologist, so Vina had an interest in the hobby. Ed &
Wilma used to bring rocks for Vina whenever they returned from a vacation trip.
Wilma found her first fossil one day and from that time on she became a true
rockhound.

                Wilma's Museum & Rock Shop.

Over the years, the rocks began to pile up in boxes stored in the garage. Ed
came up with the idea of enclosing the screened porch, putting up shelves, and
displaying some of the rocks for people to see. In 1976, Ed and Wilma purchased
their present home which had an old schoolhouse located on the premises, known
as the Krein Ceramic Shop. It was converted into what is now known as "Wilma's
Museum."

Through the years, there have been many visitors; school children, youth
groups, senior citizens' groups, ladies' organizations, and visitors from many
parts of the USA, as well as foreign countries.

Wilma has won many trophies for displaying parts of her collection at Gem &
Mineral Shows. She has won the "Best of Show" in both South and North Dakota,
as well as several local shows.

After a number of years of non-interest, Ed finally decided to join Wilma in
the rock hobby. He became interested in the art of lapidary or jewelry making.
Much of his spare time is consumed in his basement workshop where he turns out
belt buckles, pendants, rings, etc. There is satisfaction in making an old rock
into a shining piece of jewelry.

                The Thrift Car/The Wiser Miser

"Every community needs a re-sale store, is the philosophy of owner Dianne Rood,
who operated The Thrift Car in Leola during 1981-82, and is now proprietor of
The Wiser Miser. "After I bought my first house in Phoenix in 1969, I couldn't
afford to furnish it until I discovered thrift shops, and I've been hooked on
them ever since " It wasn't until 1979, however, that Dianne opened a thrift
shop of her own, The Scavenger Hut, in Rustic, CO.

Dianne and her husband, Jim Bidwell, moved onto Doc and Idelette Lundquist's
place in 1980, and she began immediately planning to convert the stationary
boxcar on the farm into a thrift shop. The Thrift Car opened June 13, 1981. "I
was determined to remain open for at least a year," says Dianne, "to prove to
the people of Leola that I was really serious about being in business here. And
. . . believe me, staying open during the winter of '81-'82 was a challenge:
six major snowstorms, always on weekends, and The Thrift Car was open Thursday,
Friday, and Saturday. Somehow, we survived the winter." After the
first-ever-in- Leola re-sale clothing style show, Spring On A Shoestring, in
March 1982, The Thrift Car flourished and attracted many new customers.
Consigned goods came from as far away as Minneapolis, Sioux Falls, Denver and
"any other place I know someone," says Dianne. The basic principle of both The
Thrift Car and The Wiser Miser is to make clothing and household items
available on a re-sale basis. It provides a service to both the consigner--by
providing an outlet for selling unwanted and unused items, and the buyer--by
providing quality goods at low prices.

        Dianne Rood.

Dianne closed The Thrift Car for the winter in November 1982, fearing a repeat
of the business hardships of the previous winter, and took a job at the OK
Hardware. After working downtown, she decided that Main St. was where she
wanted to re-open. "The Thrift Car is just too far off the beaten path. In our
community where so many people walk downtown to do their business, I wanted
some of that walk-in traffic," Dianne says, "so I started looking for suitable
quarters that would attract the walkers." Thus, The Wiser Miser was conceived,
and after months of planning and building renovation, it opened in the old pool
hall in December 1983.

                Zelmer Electric

Zelmer Electric was established in 1977 by Milbert Zelmer.

Milbert had picked up his training in electrical work while working for Rath
Electric in Long Lake.

Whirlpool appliances could be bought at Zelmer’s Electric in their business
place located in the Heibel Meat Market which is now a part of Leola State
Bank.

Milbert was kept busy when new houses were built doing the electrical wiring.

He sold the business to Ervin Kaul in 1977 and Milbert continued to work for
him until July 1979.

Milbert bought back the business in 19769 and still does electrical wiring in
the Leola area.

                Zulk's Hotel

This hotel was first operated by the McMillin family and then by Mrs. John
Elefson, who sold it in March, 1916 to John Porter, Sr.  This hotel was a very
busy place having a large dining room where they served many people.  It was
named the Gem Restaurant.  After the deaths of Mr. and Mrs. John Porter, Sr.,
the hotel was run by John Porter, Jr., and his sister, Dorothy.

        Zulk Hotel.

On September 24, 1948, the inside of the building was almost entirely burned
out, and during 1949 and 1950 the Porters renovated the building and sold it to
A. J. and Bertha Shafer in 1950.

Leona and Alvin Hauck purchased the Schafer Hotel in October, 1961, and changed
the name to Hauck Hotel. In April, 1966 the Elmer Zulks purchased the hotel and
are still its owners. They rent out rooms and apartments.

                One of the Oldest Buildings in Town

Soon to be torn down is an old one-story building on Sherman St. It has had a
long and varied history, beginning before the turn of the century. In 1897 it
served as a school to house the primary grades. It was later a drugstore owned
by Dr. Lloyd, who had offices and living quarters in the rear. Later Dr. Kerns,
too, had his offices there.

John Hepperle bought the building in 1919. In 1921-23 A. N. Bell was the first
of many Leolans to operate a cafe in this building. Subsequent managers were:
Mr. Rouse, 1924; Mrs. Frohan, 1925; Berle Donald and Charlie Dunn, early '30s.
In 1934 Hepperle renovated the building, at which time W. C. Turner managed the
restaurant. Following him were Walter Hepperle, 1935-37; Gene Kindelspire,
1937-43; Sam Moore was followed by Ken Heibel, 1943-52; Ben Schaible, 1952-59;
Gene Geffre, 1959-61. Hepperle sold to Edwin Diede in 1961, who sold to Ray
Mehlhoff in 1962. Carl Turnwall bought the building in 1965, and he sold it to
the city of Leola in 1968.

The building was known as the Leola Cafe until 1968, when it was taken over by
high school students as a social center and renamed Pirates' Cove, which has
been vacant for a number of years and is to be razed in the spring of 1984.

                An Old Landmark

According to 1892 records, Walter McEowen owned the hotel on the corner of
Moulton and Sherman. In 1908 the owner was listed as R. M. Grimes. In 1909 S.
D. Frost bought the building to house his ranch hands. In the early 1920's A.
Y. Denton owned and operated the hotel. Subsequent owners were Tarquin
Franklin, Charles Hickman, Mrs. Schillingstad, John Hauck, Luella Dunn, Charles
Dunn, Clarence Knudson, Jake Huber and Dewayne Lechner. The hotel, now vacant
in 1984, is owned by Mary Lou Lechner.

                History of Red Angus in McPherson County

Albert Erdmann purchased a Red Angus bull and several female Red Angus in 1967
to start his herd. In 1969 he and Ron Bieber made a trip to Texas to the R. C.
Buckner Dispersion, where they purchased a truck load of Red Angus Cattle.

In 1972 Albert Erdmann dispersed his herd selling the heifer calf crop and a
top herd bull prospect and his dam to Ron Bieber.

        Bieber Red Angus Ranch.

The Bieber Red Angus Ranch had the Grand Champion Bull at the 1982 South Dakota
State Fair. This bull sold at their '83 sale to Canada. At the National Western
in 1983, in Denver, the Biebers showed their bull RAB Abe Lincoln. He was the
Reserve Jr. Champion Bull. (Refer to Ronald Bieber family history.)

                Emil K. Hoffman & Son Registered Herefords

In 1928, Emil K. Hoffman bought six registered Hereford heifers of Fairfax
breeding and a Domino herd bull, purchased in partnership with Pete Sherman for
$750 from Mrs. Reed, who lived northeast of Watertown. This was the start of
the herd that is known today as the Emil K. Hoffman and Son Ranch.

Emil started with his brothers Fred and Dan on the home farm. In 1932, with the
encouragement of his brother Carl, Emil purchased the Evans-Frost Ranch.

In the drought years of 1933-'34, when they didn't get "a forkful of hay," Emil
was forced to sell part of his herd of cattle and part of the cow herd was sent
down to C. C. Collins Brothers Farm, Ramson, IA, on the train, to be wintered.
An eight-month-old calf was furnished for each cow wintered.

Emil and his brother Fred accompanied these cows and milked them twice a day
during the trip to Iowa and sold the milk to restaurants along the way, earning
a little spending money.

In the spring of 1935, when these cows came back home, a good share of them had
Bangs disease.

As Emil's small herd grew he recalls his first two bull buyers, Fred Gischer
and Henry Schmidt, who paid "very high prices" for their bulls--$15 and $12.

In the 1950s, Gerald, Emil's son, became an active partner in building the
breeding herd. With the aid of Walton W. Thorpe, Britton, SD, a number of
Hazelett-bred females from C. H. Hall, Leedy, OK, were added to the herd.
During this same time, three herd bulls were added that were vital building
blocks in this herd. They were Pioneer 22d, TH Lodge Advance 3 and TH Beau
Modest 10. All of the present herd of 300 cows trace to these three herd bulls.

In 1959, the first annual production sale was held. Over the years cattle have
been sold to 11 states. The 25th annual sale was held in 1984.

One of Hoffman's Registered Herefords.

In 1966 a large barn was built in which the annual sales were held. It is
equipped with a calving area and cattle-working chutes.

The present herd bulls consist of Mr. Incredible, considered one of the top
bulls in the Hereford breed.

The cow herd has been enrolled in the American Hereford Association's Total
Performance Records since 1965. Each year the American Hereford Association
lists the most efficient cows on the TPR that meet certain high standards. This
herd has the honor of being within the top five herds in the nation with the
most number of cows on the list.

From a small beginning the Ranch now consists of 2,500 acres with 1,000
additional leased acres. Two thousand acres are grass.

With Gerald's two sons, Jerome and Colin, the third generation is taking an
active part in keeping the ranch going.

                Luther and Brian Hoffman Registered Herefords

Luther Hoffman took over his father's Hereford herd, which he started in the
1930's. The Hoffmans sold their registered bulls at the Bowdle and Aberdeen
sale barns. In 1977 they remodeled a dairy barn and started having their own
sales on the farm in February of that same year. They enlarged their sale to
include heifers. Brian joined his father in 1983.

                        ORGANIZATIONS

                Introduction

Organizations have been an integral part of the growth of any community, from
its basic beginning up to the present time.

Early assemblies of persons in the Leola area promoted the gathering of
settlers to organize and set up rule for law and order in the area. From this
evolved various organizations for city betterment; church, school, social,
political and fraternal organizations.

Following is a list of some of the earliest groups to organize.

July 1889--     GAR Boys organize Simon Cameron Post (Civil War Veterans)
June 1890--     Willow Township Trotting Association (Horse Racing)
February 1896-- Woodman Camp
March 1898--    Royal Neighbors
May 1908--      Leola Commercial
Club May 1908-- Leola Cornet Band

                Better Leola Club

According to records located, the first Commercial Club of Leola was organized
August 25, 1908. It was entitled Leola Commercial Club, with John J. Hepperle
as president and C. S. Acker, secretary. How long this club was active is
unknown. There was no similar organization in existence in 1952 when the
present "Better Leola Club" was formulated by William L. Hilgemann and Ed
Hilgemann. William was the first president, and Ed the first secretary.

The Club has been striving through the years to make Leola and the surrounding
community a better place to live and work. They have done this by promoting
ideas and projects to the betterment of the people. Just a few examples are:
building a hospital, doctor and dentist obtained, Santa Claus Day, Customer
Appreciation Day, Awards Night, highway improvements, Snow Queen Contest,
All-School Reunion, low rent housing, Senior Citizens Center, lighted ball
park, celebrations including the Rhubarb Festival and the Diamond Jubilee, a
well at Leola Dam, and cooperation with city and school and county on many
joint projects.

There have been many people who pitched in to help with all these projects
through the years, but it is not possible to name them all. The Presidents
since 1952 are as follows:

                EMT Association

The Leola Medical Technician Association (EMTs) was organized in 1978.  EMTs
spent 81 hours in extensive medical training and many hours are spent in
learning CPR and practical applications of bandages and splints.  EMTs provide
emergency medical care to the sick and the injured patient, before and during
transport to a medical facility.

                Leola's Ambulance Corporation

These dedicated persons are well trained and are doing an excellent service to
the community in an emergency. The vehicle is equipped for carrying injured or
sick persons to a medical facility.

Leola's first ambulance was purchased by the Leola Fire Department in 1955. It
has been replaced with a new and modern vehicle, fully equipped to meet federal
regulations. In 1971, two ambulances were purchased by the county commissioners
for McPherson County. The Leola ambulance is being operated by the Leola
Firemen. The second is housed at Eureka and is operated by a volunteer
ambulance service.

                Leola Public Library

The desire to have a library in Leola, was much in the minds of several caring
persons as early as 1901, according to news stories reported in early
newspapers. Books were donated, read and reread until the 1920's when a group
of local ladies formed a Civic League. The project was to improve the library
by purchasing and renting books from a rental library. In the '30s and '40s
amateur shows were held each summer, with each organization providing one or
more acts. All of the "frustrated" musicians and actors, men and women,
willingly contributed their time to make these programs the entertainment treat
of the year. This was the main source of income for the library.

Early day librarians included: Mrs. Minnie Yost, Mrs. Ida Lowry, Pearl
McElhone, Elda Gill, Martha Gill, Blanche Frost, Phrene Junge, Helen Ferkin,
Mabel Odle, Vina Schuchardt, and Jessie Goeshel.

The library has been housed in various locations, at the Stanley McElhone
residence, basement of the old post office, sheriff's office and basement of
the courthouse in 1940.

In 1950 Perry Conahan, city mayor decided to get financial assistance from the
city and a library fund was set up. Library board members at the time were:
Margaret Holmes, Bonnie Gill and Thelma Rempfer.

In 1966 board members Delmar Haux, Betty Lou Heibel, Gail Hammon, Lillian
Kindelspire and Arlene Schemp met with Pierre officials and declared the Leola
Library a legal library in 1968, as it had been established for 18 years.

Sarah Mehlhoff was head librarian with Jessie Goeschel as her assistant. Later,
Mona Swanson was hired and with the help of Sarah Mehlhoff processed the books
and set up the library. Annie Shelbourne was hired following Mona Swanson's
resignation. Librarians since that time have been: Thelma Opp, Rosalie Larson,
Virginia Schanzenbach and the present librarian Adeline Grabowska.

        Adeline Grabowska.

In December 1978, the library was moved to the south half of the new City
Building. In September 1979 an open house was held.

The present trustees are Thelma Opp, Mrs. Nicki Steckler, Angela Schilling and
Virginia Schanzenbach.

                Leola's Volunteer Fire Department

Up until 1889 Fire Department records are not available. During that time every
able bodied man was a fire fighter, but no registered fire calls were found. In
1909 the Board of Trustees acquired fire fighting apparatus, most of the fires
were fought with chemicals. Chemicals were effective only in the early stages
of a fire.

Leola's railroad depot burned to the ground on Christmas Day, 1925. A fire
department was organized on December 26, 1925, by a group of citizens at the
meeting called for that purpose. Charter members were: C. L. Berridge, Clifford
Heibel, Theo Kapp, T. B. Reue, A. N. Bell, Lester Bell, C. F. Bertz, Leo
Heibel, Irvin Kraus›, M. Scharping, F. G. Smith, H. R. LaFontaine, Clayton
Lang, H. Hoff, Rod Ronayne, A. W. Giedt, W. P. Thomas, Ed Clifford, L. L.
Durnil, R. Yost, Albert Reiner, Jno Marzolf, and Jake Kiesz.

In July of 1929, a Model-A truck and fire fighting equipment was acquired by
the Fire Department.

The Fire Department has functioned continuously since its creation, first under
the bucket brigade system, when everybody brought his own pail and did
commendable fire fighting at the sound of the bell. The old fire bell which
summoned fire fighters has been replaced with a siren.

In 1955 an ambulance was secured and in 1958 it was felt that rural fire
fighting equipment was needed and a truck was purchased.

The Fire Department had in addition to numerous small fires, had to fight
several conflagrations, such as the Century Theater fire in 1947 and the Porter
Hotel fire in 1948. The fire that took the Leola Bakery, the Gamble Store and
Tony's Pool Hall in 1959 was one of the most spectacular blazes the department
has been called to quell. The prairie fires west of Leola in November 1958 and
April 1959 were brought under control by the farm fire truck, towns-people and
area farmers.

Honorary members are: Christ Gutjahr, C. C. Hilgemann, Ed Hilgemann, Carl Pade,
J. J. Rath, Enoch E. Schaffer, Oscar Schilling, Leo Smolnisky, and Sid Swanson,
Jr.

        Back row: Ed Hilgemann, Enoch Schaffer, Oscar Shilling, Laverne Skott,
        Eugene Rau, Curt Walz, Charles Hoffman, Jack Geffre, Greg Scallon,
        Terry Heider, Ron Kappes, Neal Nelson, Dean Schock and DeuWayne Pudwill.
        Front row: Jim Schaffer, Pat Schaffner, Jerry Weron, Lee Rau, Norman
        Tschappat, and Lloyd Breitag.

Active firemen are. DuWayne Pudwill, Chief; Roy Meyer, Vice Chief; Dean Schock,
Secretary; Neal Nelson, Treasurer, present officers. Lloyd Breitag, Jack
Geffre, Arlen Guthmiller, Gary Guthmiller, Terry Heider, Charles Hoffman, Ron

Norman Tschappat, Curt Walz, Gerald Weron, Milbert Zelmer and Elmer Zulk.
Standby members: Clint Blumhardt, Eugene Rau and Laverne Skott.

New fire trucks and modern equipment have replaced the old in recent years.

In summation, the Fire Department has not only kept a fine fire fighting
record, but has developed into a highly trained body of volunteers which
respond immediately to ambulance, fire and other emergency calls.

The annual firemen's fishing trip has become a tradition to the community whose
citizens enjoy the annual firemen's ball. The family picnic is especially
enjoyed by the children for getting rides on the fire truck. Santa Claus and
his helpers (the Leola Volunteer Fire Department) come via the traditional fire
truck, for Santa Clause Day at Christmas time with bags of nuts and candy for
the children.

                History of Leola Senior Citizens' Center

In the early 1960's, a local club, the L & S (Leola & Spring) Extension Club
decided to do something entertaining for the older citizens of the community.
So once a month a social meeting was held in the club room of the Courthouse.
Entertainment and lunch was provided by the club. Attendance and interest grew
in the project. Then the Better Leola Club with Clarence Knudson and Rev.
Brinkman as their leaders started planning to finance and house the growing
senior organization.

The Senior Citizen Club still met in the club room of the courthouse, but were
more or less on their own. They decided to organize. On July 20, 1972 the first
officers were elected--Mrs. Christ (Ann) Rath, President; Mrs. Walter
(Elizabeth) Kline, Vice President; Jessie Goeshel, Secretary; and Irene Lapka,
Treasurer. Board of Directors were Frieda Schell, Esther Brietag, Mrs. Jacob
(Elizabeth) Jakober, Mrs. Ed (Martha) Zenker and Lola Christian. There were 30
charter members.

Various committees were chosen for the activities which were: recreation, arts
and crafts; health, birthdays, potlucks, speakers, holiday parties and so on.

As the attendance and interest grew, ways to finance the organization were
looked into. With the Better Leola Club as the sponsors, federal money was
available for a three-year span with matching funds provided by the club. Some
county finances were also available. With the funds supplies were bought. These
were tables, chairs, cupboards, dishes, song books, pool table and many other
necessary supplies. The labor was all donated which was an (in kind) share.

Many long hours and out of town trips were made to bring back good ideas for
making the center a success. With Ann Rath as a very interested and efficient
leader, the interest and membership grew. Soon they outgrew the room in the
courthouse basement, so a building across the street (east) of the courthouse,
owned by Floyd Meidinger, was rented and became the Leola senior citizens'
first home. That was March 1973.

A used piano was donated by the Lutheran Church and the singing group was
started. English and German hymn books were printed and weekly practice was
started. This is still a very active group that meets on Tuesday evenings to
enjoy themselves. They also sing for senior homes, church gatherings and
funerals.

        Choir. Back row: Carl Hoffman, Carl Wahl, Edwin Loebs, Christ
        Schanzenbach, John Bendewald, Christ Schock, Dave Jacober, Jacob
        Jakober, Emil Albrecht, Bill Job, and Christ Jakober. Middle row:
        Eldora Morrison, Emma Heupel, Emgard Loebs, Freida Schell, Hulda Brosz,

        Jundt, LaVina Albrecht, Anna Jakober, Anna Schock, Othilda Weisser,
        Bertha Job and Elizabeth Jakober.

As the membership and interest grew, the building was getting too crowded, so
on December 11, 1974 the Masonic Temple was offered to the Leola senior
citizens for their use. So work began--cleaning, painting, roof repair, rest
rooms put in, ceiling lowered in small room, shelves added. It is now a very
interesting place where the get togethers can be enjoyed.

The senior citizens started serving lunches October 20, 1981 on Tuesday and
Thursday. The lunch costs a dollar for anyone over 60 years of age and
ministers and their wives. The cook is Olivia Kaul. She is under the Green
Thumb program. Ladies volunteer to help each week. Mrs. Kaul generally needs
two helpers and they get their meals free. All help with cleanup.

After lunch, members may play Bingo or cards. The last Tuesday of the month, a
nurse takes blood pressures. This service is paid by the Center. The group does
not get federal help on meals, but still comes out ahead. They have purchased
some needed appliances, such as a deep freeze and a second refrigerator. There
is good attendance at the meals and the last Tuesday of the month is a special
meal for birthdays and anniversaries. More people come to this.

Senior citizens have homemade and purchased crafts which are sold to anyone who
comes to the Center. Don't forget to join when you reach 60 years of age!
