                Cooperative Extension Service

The Extension Service began its first service to McPherson County in 1920 when
County Agent Walter Broich of Eureka was appointed. His duties, including
managing the McPherson-Campbell County Fair, were livestock disease control and
starting new varieties of grain.

After Mr. Broich resigned, McPherson County did not have an agent until August
of 1933, when Henry L. Leonhardt was installed as an emergency agent for the
wheat acreage reduction program.

During 1934, five extension homemaker clubs were organized with a total
membership of 90; 20 youth from Stickel Township formed two 4-H clubs, one
boys' handicraft club and one girls' clothing club.

In 1935, the first extension board was appointed to help develop a program of
work and administer the $500 budget. Members of the board were: Mrs. E. B.
Rude, Leola, Chairman; John F. Walth, Hosmer, Secretary-Treasurer; George
Lapka, Leola, Vice Chairman; Jakob J. Spitzer, Long Lake; and Fred Odenbach,
Greenway.

The first 4-Hers to journey to the South Dakota State Fair were: Myron Lapka,
Jerome Ganser, Gerald Lapka, and Erwin Martel, who formed the livestock judging
team. Myron and Jerome also showed their pigs. The first 4-H Recognition Night
was hosted by the Star Extension Club to recognize parents, leaders and guests.

Mr. Leonhardt served as county agent until 1937 when he was succeeded by John
E. Welch. Also in 1937, Mary Bodwell was appointed as the first home extension
agent, followed by Laurena Isaksen in 1938. In 1940, Walter Lassen became the
county agent followed by Vern Baer in 1941 and Vernon Johnson from 1942 to
1948.

Research on grain varieties, sorghums, soybeans, turkeys and sheep was
conducted during the 1940's at the Eureka Experiment Farm. Other work conducted
by the extension included: conservation programs, seed testing, livestock
disease control, small grain test plots, mattress making, farm and home
accounting, food preservation, and grasshopper control.

Ralph Sorenson became county agent in 1948 and was followed by Carroll P . Ness
from 1951 to 1956. Alan Wilcox served for a short time until being drafted at
which time Pat Moriarity was appointed Ag agent. He was followed in 1959 by
Wayne Nesby.

Eleanore Krokosh became the area extension home economist in 1971. She was
followed by Karen Zilverberg from 1972 to 1976.

County agents since Wayne Nesby's move to Hand County have been Leonard Nelson
in 1980 and Rory Metz from 1980-83.

The present extension agents are Carole Sweeter, who assumed her duties as
extension home economist in 1976 and Sheri Thoreson, county agricultural agent,
who began her employment in June of 1983. Their duties include serving as
advisors to the 82 members in seven 4-H clubs. Other organizations with which
they work include: Extension Homemakers, Crop Improvement Association,
Livestock Improvement Association and the County Weed Board, as well as
numerous individuals on a day to day basis.

The roots of the extension service have remained with the people of the county
due to the service of many dedicated extension board members over the years. At
present the members of the board are: Harry Mehlhaff, June Shafer, Viola
Woehlhaff, Dawn Bornemann, Lee Kindelspire and Eugene Kurle.

                Country Club Organization

The Country Club was organized in September 1921 with the following 12 country
women making up its charter: May Christensen, who was the organizer and also
became the first president; Kitty Bell; Mary Ann Colberg; Caroline Fewings;
Myrtle Gatrell; Ellen Hauffe; Adalaid Hickman; Blanche Hickman; Floy Hickman;
Anna Jones; and Gladys Morrison. The club organized for the purpose of
furthering friendship in the community and sociability among the members and
their friends. They had club every two weeks and election of officers every six
months. The Country Club had yearly events such as the June picnic, watermelon
picnic, Halloween party, oyster stew supper and all-day meeting in February.
The club gave bridal showers; Ethel Woodall Yost being the first one. The first
baby shower was for Chester Berlin. The first Halloween party was held at the
Evan Jones' home on October 29, 1921. During the depression many barn dances
were enjoyed at the Ed Hickman barn. One year the ladies even put on a
three-act play titled, "The Old Maids' Convention.

In September 1925 the club met at the home of Etta Serdahl for the purpose of
organizing the first extension club in McPherson County through the Brown
County chapter for demonstration lessons. County agent Dittmore and Home
Economics leader Nellie McLaughlin gave demonstration lessons to 12 clubs.
McPherson County did not have a county agent for some time so the club attended
these lessons for ten years.

Over the period of 60 years the membership has varied from its original 12 to
32 members at one time. Club is held the second Thursday of every month except
July and August and election of officers once a year. The club motto is "United
We Stand, Divided We Fall" and the colors are purple and gold. Bridal showers
are still presented to our young people as well as baby showers to the members.
In times of bereavement the ladies help in any way possible. Members draw names
for secret sisters and get them a gift for their birthday and the last few
years also Valentine's Day. We have helped many members celebrate
anniversaries. The ladies go on a yearly skip day. The card committee sends
cards to the members in the hospital, sympathy cards and anniversary greetings.
The club also takes part of worthy cause. During the past Rhubarb Days they
have entered floats and served pie and coffee with the proceeds going to the
Rhubarb committee. They also purchased items for the new doctors' office
building. They have continued taking the extension lessons, many which were fun
and interesting.

        Back row: June Schafer, Brenda Kolb, Carol Kindelspire, Mary Ann Mack,
        Margaret Kindelspire, Alice Bonnet, Irene Schumack, Dianna Shafer,
        Olive Lapka, Virginia Kindelspire, Betty Geffre, Nadine Hatlewick and
        Betty Mack.

Present and past members of the County Club celebrated their 30th anniversary
on August 31, 1951 at the Carl Rogers barn. The loft was nicely decorated for
the banquet and dance. The 40th anniversary was held at the Leola Legion Hall
in October 1961. A banquet supper was served and a program provided
entertainment for all the guests. The 50th anniversary was held at the Catholic
Parish Center in September 1971. With the banquet there was a program, letters
from former members, display of pictures, scrapbook and other memorabilia.

The County Club still tries to follow the goals of its beginning. They still
have their showers, parties, picnic and suppers for all the members and their
families to enjoy.

The County Club celebrated its 60th anniversary September 20, 1981. They had
open house at the Catholic Parish Center. A program was presented and
refreshments were served.

At that time the club had ten active members and seven honorary. Officers were:
Virginia Kindelspire, president; Nadine Hatlewick, vice president; Olive Lapka,
secretary; and Betty Geffre, treasurer. Other members were: Alice Bonnet,
Margaret Kindelspire, Betty Mack, Mary Ann Mack, Irene Schumack, and June
Shafer. Betty Mack was the McPherson County Home Extension Council president.
Honorary members of the club are: Eldora Fewings, Adeline Grabowska, Laura
Kindelspire, Myrtle Kindelspire, Annie Lapka, Irene Mack and Ethel Yost.

                L & S Extension Club

The Leola and Spring Township Extension Club was organized October 25, 1957.
The charter members were: Violet Hoffman, Thelma Opp, Marcella Job, Bertha Job,
Ann Stoecker, Esther Maisch and Anna Rath.

The first officers were: Chairman, Violet Hoffman; Secretary, Esther Maisch;
Treasurer, Thelma Opp.

Some activities were participating in Boy Scout Talent Show, the milk program,
and yearly family picnics.

Our club adopted a young Indian boy at the Redfield State School. His name is
Arthur Antelope. We adopted him in 1960. We remember him with cards, letters
and gifts. We receive letters and gifts from him. We have been to Redfield and
have taken cake and ice cream to his dorm and celebrated his birthday with him.
Arthur was transferred from the state school to the Live Center at Lemmon, SD
in 1982. Our hostess remembers him with a gift and card every month.

In 1963 we started entertaining the Senior Citizens once a month, in the
community room at the courthouse. We continued this until the Senior Citizens
organized their own.

We were active in district and state extension meetings. In 1982 Anna Rath and
Thelma Opp received their 25 year pins.

The L & S Club had many ladies enrolled during our 25 years. Our members in
1982 were Lila Rau, Arlene Job, Thelma Opp, Kay Henderson, Ann Rath, Emma
Jacober, Mildred McIntire, and Lillian Voegele.

We have decided to discontinue as an extension club, due to the fact that many
of our members are unable to be active in extension work, but in order to keep
up with our commitment to Arthur Antelope, we have decided to remain a social
club, meeting the second Thursday of the month as usual.

Activities that the club feels are worthwhile mentioning are listed below. We
entered a float in the Leola 75th Jubilee. Our float was antique containing an
old fashioned sod stove that really worked (Mrs. Ludwig Job showed us how to
make it. We used cow-chips and had a fire in the stove during the parade), an
antique meat cutting table and meat stuffer, and a homemade pig which was
butchered several times throughout the parade. Three ladies rode on the float,
with sun bonnets and matching dresses. We won first prize for organizational
floats ($10) and first prize in historical floats (a trophy). Our trophy is on
display at the Leola City Library.

The L & S Extension Club purchased a radio, a magazine table and a Harvey Dunn
painting for the doctor's office when the city built the new professional
building.

                Leola Homemakers Extension Club

The Homemakers Extension Club was organized July 11, 1938, at the home of
Christina Kiesz, under the supervision of the county chairman Mrs. E. B. Rude.

The purpose of the organization was to foster improved homemaking methods,
including sewing, cooking, money management, raising children, use of time and
talent and to help those less fortunate.

The first elected officers were: Mrs. Pat Brown, chairman; Mrs. John Welch,
vice chairman; Mrs. Emil Stoebner, secretary; Mrs. Herbert Hoff, treasurer.

Brown and yellow were chosen to be the club colors. The yellow rose is the club
flower.

Regular annual charitable donations were made. Nearly $1,000 was raised and
donated to the Leola Community Hospital through a dance, a play, an auction and
galloping breakfasts in 1950.

The past 25 years have seen many changes in programs and membership. The club
has conducted several open house invitations for an elderly gentleman or a
retiring teacher. Every year or two we hold a special open house for all
newcomers in the community to get acquainted with the "natives." The club
members furnish the bars and coffee for these events plus a door prize.

It was this club that was instrumental in initiating the first Rhubarb Festival
for 1972 which was a huge success. The first Rhubarb Queen, Mrs. Art (Myrtle)
Kindelspire, was crowned the night before the festivities. In 1973 one of our
members, Mrs. Sid Swanson, Sr. (Irene) was selected queen.

        Back row: Yvonne Haefner, Virginia Breitag, Helen Steiger, Bormie Gill,
        Adeline Ehley, Leone Thomas, and Lois Bieber. Front row: Olivia Kaul,
        Delores Wahl, Nicki Stekler, and Freda Kappes.

In 1976 our town celebrated the nation's Bicentennial along with the all-school
reunion and the Rhubarb Festival. It was for this event we compiled a Rhubarb
cookbook which was a sell-out with many orders from far and wide.

For the Leola Centennial in 1984 we prepared a general cookbook containing all
types of cooking and baking as well as portions of our original rhubarb
cookbook. Recipes are from all facets in the community as well as from state
and national dignitaries.

The 1983-84 officers are: President, Yvonne Haefner; Vice President, Virginia
Breitag; Secretary, Lois Bieber; Treasurer, Helen Steiger. The balance of the
membership consists of Adeline Ehley, Bonnie Gill, Freda Kappes, Olivia Kaul,
Nicki Steckler, Leone Thomas, Helen Thompson, and
Delores Wahl.

                Little Women Extension Club

The Little Women Extension Club was organized on February 10, 1971 at 8:00 P.M.
at the Community Room of the Leola Courthouse, with Eleanor Krokosh conducting
the meeting. Election of officers was held, and it was decided the club members
would meet the second Wednesday of each month (presently the second Thursday of
each month) at the homes of the members. On March 10, 1971, at the home of
Nancy Crist, the name of the club was chosen, installation of officers was held
by Home Economist Krokosh, and by-laws were proposed. It was decided that 12
members would be allowed in the club and meeting months would be September
through May. First year officers and members were Pam Schaffner, president;
Jeannie Feickert, vice president; Kathy Zantow, secretary; JoAnn Sanborn,
treasurer; Nancy Crist, reporter; Valerie Rath, historian; Betty Hoffman, song
leader; and Janet Noble.

Some of the activities and projects of the club through the years have been:
Participation in the annual Holiday Fairs of the McPherson County Extension
Clubs, County, district and state extension meetings; Leola Rhubarb Days
(sponsored queen), Bicentennial Year Celebration, entered float; Leola Farmers
Appreciation Day, set up booth; In 1980 participated in Leola Health Fair for
Adults. For 4-H McPherson County Achievement Days presented plaques for various
projects. Assisted JW Club of Leola with basketball tournaments; sold community
and anniversary calendars; maintained rural cemetery northeast of Leola;
answered letters to Santa Claus and donated candy for sacks for the children
for Santa Claus day. Delivered fruit baskets to elderly shut-ins and sent gifts
to the children at the Redfield State Hospital. Donated to Susan Wilder Student
Loan & Scholarship Fund, International Fund, Pennies for Friendship, 1971
McPherson County Book Fair, new Doctor-Dentist Office in Leola, Leola Library
and 1984 Leola Centennial Fund. The club was largely responsible for the
Community Health Nurse coming to McPherson County (sponsored meeting and
circulated petition). Throughout the years the club has presented skits,
donated door prizes, helped with horse shows, craft and bake sales, served at
auction sales, mother-daughter tea; served lunch for picnics, holiday parties,
baby showers, housewarmings and farewell parties for members and their
families.

Past members of the club were Alberta Grabowska, Sheila Fauth, Susan Hoffman,
Susan Kolb, Judi Rauscher, Karen Reis, Lena Cox and Marilyn Casey.

Nineteen eighty-three officers and members: Sharon Hoffman, president; Kristy
Zandstra, vice president; Nancy Kallas, secretary; Elaine Geffre, treasurer;
Peg Schumack, historian; Kathy DeYoung, Carol Geffre, Betty Hoffman, Joyce
Kohlhoff, Kay Lapka, Mary Schaunaman, and Pat Schaible.

                Mothers and Others Extension Club

The Mothers and Others Club was organized in the fall of 1979 by a group of
mothers who wanted to join an extension club, but felt they could not spend
another night away from their families.

The club members decided to meet in the morning and take their children with
them. Those who attended the meetings were able to return to their homes by
lunch time.

The original members of the club were: Susan Bultsma; Kathy Munson, one child;
Sheila Metz, one child; Vicky Sieh, two children; Colleen Wangsness, two
children; and Jeanette Glaesman, two children.

                The Star Extension Club

In April of 1934 the Star Extension Club was organized. Officers were:
chairman, Mrs. Ed Pade; vice chairman, Mrs. E. R. Rude; secretary, Mrs. Felix
Ronayne; treasurer, Mrs. Adam Heupel; 4-H club leader, Mrs. H. Turnwall. They
chose for their club colors, sky-blue and silver. The members kept themselves
busy by making tea towels, linen handkerchiefs and aprons. There were 24
members the first year.

In 1935 the State Extension Club Agent met with all the area extension members
and organized Achievement Days. This was held in the courthouse on June 15,
1935. In October of 1934, the county commissioners appointed an Extension Board
with Mrs. Minna Rude of the Star Extension Club being appointed a member. She
served as chairman for nine years.

Throughout the years the membership roll has seen many new faces. Emma Pade was
a charter member and was still a member at the time of her death in 1978. Kate
Opp is another member of long standing. She joined the club in 1945. At present
she is an honorary member. Many new babies of members were welcomed into the
community by gifts from the club.

The club has continued playing an active roll in the community by helping with
many causes during the war and supporting 4-H club members. Members still enjoy
a Christmas party, Valentine party, many interesting and informative
demonstrations and an annual skip day.

Present members of the club are: Lucille Geffre, Viola Geffre, Waneta Geffre,
Alverde Daniel, Lorraine Schaible, Delores Bain, Leone Hoffman, Vivian Mack,
Vivian Rueb, Ella Krein, Della Schaffner, Betty Porter and Ruth
Hoffman.

                Washington Agricola Club

The Washington Agricola Club was organized in September 1926 by ten neighbor
ladies (who wanted to get together socially) at the home of Freda Maas.
Officers elected were: president, Bertha Witte; vice president, Bertha Pade;
and secretary-treasurer, Viola Nelson. Members were Freda Maas, Grace Rouse,
Elizabeth Kindelspire, Emma Pade, Estella Nelson, Mary Nelson, Elizabeth Young,
Bertha Pade, and Viola Nelson.

Only one charter member, Viola Nelson, is still living. She resides at the
Bethesda Nursing Home in Aberdeen.

Meetings were held every Wednesday, at 2:00 P.M. Dues were ten cents a meeting
(present or not). One penny was collected from each member to be used for
buying flowers, when a member was ill.

During the winter months they met before noon to help each other with quilting.
The hostess would then prepare a noon meal. Sometimes the men would come along
to visit or to help. In later years the club served at farm sales to raise
money for the club.

One Agricola Club tradition was to present each member with a quilt. Each
member made a block and then they would put them together at their meetings.
Meetings were held and the hostess received a helping hand many times when
there was mending to be done, shucking peas, fancy work or whatever there was
that had to be done.

The club now meets once a month, on the fourth Thursday from October through
June. In July, the family picnic is held. Skip day is taken once a year. At
Christmas time, they have a family supper and party.

A quilt, Raggedy Ann and Andy doll were made by the members, for raising money
to help support the centennial.

The present membership is ten and the officers are: president, Lorraine Krein;
vice president, Lois Merkel; and secretary-treasurer, Virginia Kessler. Other
members are Viola Nelson, Lola Christian, Fern Kline, Edith Rath, Sylvia Rott,
Valerie Rath and Marlene Kessler. The club is 57 years
old.

                Prairie Rustlers 4-H Club

The Sodbusters 4-H Club (all boys) had its beginning in 1953 and the Prairie
Priscillas 4-H Club (all girls) was started in 1958.

The Prairie Rustlers 4-H Club was organized in 1971 when the two clubs
combined. The club had 16 members participating at that time. Their leader was
Mrs. Gordon Mack. The club met once each month in the home of a member.

The Prairie Rustlers 4-H Club now has ten members and meet in the community
room at the courthouse. Their leader is Mrs. Lee Kindelspire.

                Willing Workers 4-H Club

The Willing Workers 4-H Club was organized in 1959 with Mr. and Mrs. Albert
Feickert and Mrs. Clifford Durheim as leaders. At that time a group of 14
children participated in the club.

Mr. and Mrs. Walter Hoffman, Mrs. Gordon Rath and Mrs. Erwin Rau, were given
the reins of leadership during the years 1965 to 1974.

Beginning 1974, Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Lapka and Mr. and Mrs. Gerald Hoffman,
guided the young people in 4-H projects. Activities for the year included
making nut cups for the senior citizens, Christmas caroling, planting flowers
in the Leola Park, and making a "Rhubarb Day" float.

The Willing Workers 4-H Club has participated in many community projects as
well as county and state programs. Three club members have participated in
judging at the State Fair.

In '79-'80 the members put on a skit for the senior citizens. Since then skit
books have been donated to the Leola Library.

Nineteen eighty, '81-'82 included a paper drive, setting up a promotion booth,
selling community calendars, making leather goods and judging food.

Leaders for 1982-'83 were: Lois Bieber, Mary Zantow and Sylvia Regnier.
Activities included having a Halloween party, and making centerpieces.

Many of the club's members have served as president, vice president, secretary,
historian and reporters. Present officers are: Patricia Lapka, president; Joel
Weig, vice president; Sandy Bieber, secretary; Sheila Kallas, historian;
Melissa Kallas, treasurer; Troy Sandmeier; and Kristi
Bieber, reporters.

                Leola Legion

On December 16, 1919, the following veterans held the first meeting of Roy S.
Hickman Post 78 of the American Legion: William Lowry, N. J. Kramer, Joseph
Lapka, A. L. LaFontaine, H. O. Arndt, George Hickman, Harold Yost, Julius Reue,
Fred Hepperle, O. H. Potratz, L. E. Turner, A. O. Hildreth, and Ralph Farnum.
Their charter was officially received from the South Dakota department
headquarters on August 10, 1920. The post received its name from Roy S.
Hickman, son of Mr. and Mrs. Samuel Hickman, the first Leola serviceman killed
on the battlefield of France, on July 17, 1918. His brother George enlisted the
same day as Roy, and was one of the charter members of the post named in Roy's
honor.

Charter members of Roy S. Hickman Post 78 were: Idelette Reue, Burl Blanchard,
Wm. L. Lowry, Joseph McLaughlin, Freeman Nelson, Frank G. Smith, Don Anderson,
Oliver Berlin, Peter R. Geffre, Robert Schoenfelder, Joseph Koppy, Enos
Peterman, Carl Isaacson, Mark L. Holmes, Charles Broadbent and Joseph Sherman.
The first officers were: Wm. L. Lowry, post commander; George Hickman, vice
commander; N. J. Kramer, post-adjutant; L. E. Turner, finance officer; H. O.
Arndt, historian; A. O. Hildreth, chaplain; and Joseph Lapka, sergeant-at-arms.

Idelette Lundquist, nee Reue, who saw a lot of WWI as an army nurse in France,
had the distinction of being elected the first woman commander of an American
Legion Post in South Dakota in 1939. She had also served several years as post
adjutant. At the time of her election she was also a member of the city council
and managed a private hospital and a dairy farm.

The post had several meeting places before making the present Legion Hall their
permanent headquarters. The first meeting was held in the basement of the Bank
of Leola. Subsequent meetings were held in the old Blanchard garage, the Farmer
Room in the courthouse, and in the old jail house.

Several attempts had been made to construct a permanent Legion Hall in Leola.
Finally, on June 15, 1948, plans were formulated for the Leola American Legion
building, which was to be 48' x 110'. After 29 years it would have its first
permanent, official post. Melvin Grabowska was post commander at the time, and
Allen Hoffman, Walter Sherman, and Leo Smolnisky were appointed to the building
committee.

        Back row: Gerhardt Breitag, Gorton Rath, Derald Mack, Ed Hilgemann,
        Alvin Zandstra, Elmer Schock, Art Breitag and Darrel Yost. Front
        row: Denver Guthmiller, Calvin Guthmiller, Luther Hoffman, Ray Kappes,
        Adolph Schaible, Walter Hoffman and Delmer Wahl.

Ivan (Bob) Kohlhoff was post commander when the footing for the basement was
laid in September, 1949. The first meeting was held in the new hall on October
11, 1949. In 1951, when Francis Lapka was commander, the hall was completed by
volunteer help.

In 1959, the Leola American Legion acquired a license from the city of Leola,
and designed, built, and in the fall opened the L & L Bar. The profits from
this business help the Legion to support and contribute to various community
activities.

        Legion Hall.

High on the list of the Leola Legion is the concern for the young people of the
community. In enriching the mind as well as the spirit, the Legion sponsors
delegates to attend Boys' and Girls' State. Here, these delegates obtain first
hand knowledge of how the American Government works. The Legion also makes
contributions to the Leola High School for purchasing equipment or facility
improvement. The Legion also has a very active student loan fund. This fund is
available to students who have graduated from Leola High School and wish to
continue their education.

When the city built the Municipal Swimming Pool, the Legion was involved. A
summer baseball program is supported by the Legion, in which Legion teams have
been very successful.

Having a membership of approximately 175 year after year, in 1981 the Leola
Legion took on the task of supporting a candidate for the State Commander's
job. After the roll call vote was counted, Leola's candidate fell short by a
slim margin. But the following year fortune smiled on Leola's Legion, and Roy
S. Hickman Post No. 78 became the home post of the 1982 State Commander, Wayne
Nesby, who as, post adjutant for many years, held this
position for one year.

        Wayne Nesby.

The Legion is an active organization involved in community, state, and national

                American Legion Auxiliary Has Second Charter

Records show that the first charter was granted to Leola Chapter of the
American Legion Auxiliary on March 25, 1922. No records of meetings or when the
organization disbanded are to be found. The charter members were: Mrs. Sam
Hickman, Edna Hickman, Mrs. George Blanchard, Mrs. F. C. Shoenfelder, Mrs.
Theo. B. Reue, Ruth Reue, Mrs. F. D. Lowry, Mrs. A. H. McMillin, Dorothy
Porter, Jesse Porter, Mrs. H. H. Yost, Mrs. Mark L. Holmes and Mrs. A. L.
Bartlett.

The second charter was granted in December 1931. Mrs. Alice Van Kuren of
Aberdeen, president of the 14th district, met with a group of the Leola women
in the old schoolhouse for the purpose of organizing the local unit.

The Gold Star Mother, Mrs. Mary Hickman (Mary Catherine Friend) was born April
3, 1851, at Elkhart, IN, where she spent her early childhood. Her parents moved
to Lexington, IA in 1859. Her father, the Rev. Friend, was a Methodist
minister. On December 25, 1871 she was married to Samuel Hickman in Grand View,
IA. To this union four children were born: three sons and one daughter, namely,
Edward, Samuel, Roy and Edna.

Mrs. Hickman and family moved to South Dakota in 1884 and lived on their
homestead until the spring of 1920, when they moved to the city of Leola, where
she resided until her death.

Roy Hickman was killed in action in France during WWI. It is from this son that
our post got its name, Roy S. Hickman Post No. 78.

The American Legion Auxiliary is a non-profit organization to help the veteran,
his family and the community. The Leola unit has two classes of membership,
senior and junior, with a total of 189. At present, Gold Star Mothers are: Emma
Adam, Lola Christian, Nellie Ganser, Alvina Glaesman, Esther Jung, Elizabeth
Opp and Christina Wolff.

Several times the unit has received first prize from the department in the
history competition.

The Auxiliary acts in conjunction with the Legion in such activities as the
annual turkey raffle, Memorial Day Services and district conventions.

The Auxiliary has been sponsoring the Girls' Staters and a girl to Journalism
City when one is eligible. They also host an annual scholarship Spring Salad
Luncheon. For Halloween, the Auxiliary and the J. W. Club have movies for the
children of the community.

A day of pillow cleaning has been held annually by the organization for the
past several years.

        Myrna Zandstra and Leone Thomas.

Althea Lapka from 1968 to 1972 and from 1980 to 1982, and Myrna Zandstra from
1982 to 1984.

                Leola Masonic Lodge No. 154 A.F. & A.M.

Leola Masonic Lodge No . 154, AF & AM was organized by virtue of a dispensation
granted by the Most Worshipful Grand Master Jas. J. Davenport of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge AF & AM of South Dakota. The first meeting was held
August 3, 1908 with the following officers present: James Clayton, W. M.; F. M.
Billings, S. W.; A. Williams, J. W.; P. H. Carlsgaard, treasurer, and Charles
Turner, secretary. Fred Nelson, Guy Fox, Ralph Lynn and Ray Washburn were all
charter members.

Regular and special meetings were held until June 9, 1909 when a charter was
granted by the Grand Lodge.

The meetings were held upstairs over what was the Leola Bakery, which burned
February 11, 1959. They were then held in the basement of the Temple for about
two years until the Temple was completed. It was dedicated June 6, 1929 at
which time Charley Schmalz was Worshipful Master.

E. W. Hilgemann, Sr., received his 50-year medal in 1955 and Guy Fox received
his in 1956. Clarence Knudson received a 50-year medal, also, Mark Holmes was
awarded his 60-year medal.

The lodge closed in 1974 and members affiliated with other lodges.

                Leola Chapter No. 124, O.E.S.

Leola Chapter No. 124, Order of the Eastern Star, was instituted May 8, 1916 by
A. N. Axford, Worthy Grand Patron.

The following is a list of the charter members: Myrtle M. Clayton, Blanche
Bartlett, Emma C. Knutson, Johanna Turner, Lorraine Kerns, Clara DeWitte, Ella
Hilgemann, Lena Bishop, Minnie Hoffman, George L. Blanchard, A. L. Bartlett, G.
G. Kerns, H. W. Knutson, Guy Fox, James S. Clayton, E. W. Hilgemann, W. B.
DeWitte, and G. H. Turner.

The first regular meetings were held on the first and third Wednesdays of each
month. The first meeting place was on the second floor of the Moulton-Elliot
building, the first floor being a general store. This was at the site of the
now Leola Bakery.

The constitution and by-laws were adopted on May 20, 1916. Leola Chapter was
granted a charter by the Grand Chapter on June 8, 1916. On September 26, 1916
Worthy Grand Patron B. M. Hart presided during the Constitution ceremonies and
11 new members were initiated.

At a special meeting held on November 8, 1916 the first initiation was held and
the following received the degrees of the Order; Rena Parkhurst, I. T.
Parkhurst, Mary Nelson, Fred Nelson, and Amos Hoffman.

The first official visit took place on October 26, 1917 when Worthy Grand
Matron Florence Hoon visited the Chapter.

The first demit was granted to Clara DeWitte on February 25, 1919, one of the
charter members, who had moved to Wolf Point, MT. G. G. Kerns, the first Worthy
Patron. died on April 19, 1920 after a long illness. Dr. Kerns was an
enthusiastic and untiring worker in the Chapter.

On September 2, 1925 the Chapter held its first meeting in the new Masonic
Temple.

The Order of the Eastern Star is a world-wide organization to which both men
and women can belong. It is a charitable organization giving financial aid not
only to its own members, but also other charities. Among those that have
received support from Leola Chapter is the Children's Home in Sioux Falls, the
Red Cross, Abbot House, the Crippled Children's Hospital, and the Leola
Community Hospital.

The Grand Chapter of South Dakota funded and built an Eastern Star Home for
aged members in Redfield, SD. This new facility is completely supported by
Eastern Star members through their dues and various donations from the members.

Leola Chapter has been honored over the years by appointments as Grand Officers
the following members: Emma Knutson, Grand Electa, 1923; Augusta Merkle, Grand
Warder, 1928; Gertrud Becker, Grand Ruth, 1955; Elsie Kohlhoff, Grand Marshal,
1969; Elsie Kohlhoff, Worthy Grand Matron, 1973.

On October 15, 1974 it was voted to close Leola Chapter and consolidate with
Naomi Chapter at Frederick. The last meeting of the Chapter was held on this
date. The last corps of officers to serve Leola Chapter was: Betty Nesby, Wayne
Nesby, Phyllis Young, Sid Swanson, Jr., Lucy Bell, Florence Krein, Betty Maule,
Evelyn Rogers, Vera Kohlhoff, Bonnie Gill, Agnes Swanson, Virginia
Schanzenbach, Wilma Hilgemann, Elsie Kohlhoff, Darlene Schmidt, Marian
Schumacher, Berniece Pade, and Alma Hauffe.

                Leola Golf Club

The Leola Golf Club, located 3 1/2 miles west of Leola, dates back to 1957, but
an earlier golf course, north of the Catholic Cemetery, was laid out in 1926.
Early members of that club included Orrin Berridge, Chris Merkel, Emil
Smolnisky, Judge Acker, Leslie Turner, Mark Holmes and Martin Switzenberg.

        Leola Golf Club.

The present club, whose earliest officers were Tom Heibel, Keith Durnil, Leslie
Holmes, Ted Liedle, Loren Gill, Adam Ehley, and Pat Moriarty, had 39 members
who purchased 40 acres south of Highway 10. The west 20 acres were bought by
the State Game and Fish Department as a game refuge and roadside
park.

Over the years many people have worked at clearing and improving the course. In
1970-71 a basement was dug and finished, and a schoolhouse was moved onto the
property for a Club House. Many improvements have been added.

The Club House, with its kitchen, attached garage and sun deck, is completely
furnished and is the center of many activities. All during the year the men
meet there weekly for steaks and cards, and the women sponsor potlucks and golf
events for couples.

The women sponsor an Invitational Ladies' Golf Tournament during the summer,
with guests from 14 nearby clubs, and a Kids' Night, complete with golf events,
prizes and food. They meet regularly during June, July and August for golf,
supper and cards.

At present the membership varies from 60 to 80 families.

                Leola Sportsman Club

On March 3, 1964 a group of interested sports minded citizens met in the Leola
Legion Hall to organize a club. A secretary was selected to conduct the
election of officers. Elected were: Harold Haux, president; Mike Schaffner Sr.,
vice president; Gordon Schanzenbach, secretary; and Duane
Bain, treasurer.

The first board of directors consisted of Bob Schumacher, Ernest Jasmer, Byron
Kindelspire, Bill Lapka and Milbert Dockter.

The name Leola Sportsman Club was adopted. Fifteen members participated. That
same year the club joined the South Dakota Wildlife Federation. Several
projects have been completed by the club and the Wildlife Federation. It has
set aside acres of land for wildlife habitat, has supported Pheasants
Unlimited. Took part in the South Dakota Sportsman Council operation. Bought
and raised young pheasants. A fishing derby is held once a year. In the ensuing
years, rabbit drives, trap shoots, and work at the Leola Park was done. Large
round bales of flax straw have been placed in lake areas for waterfowl nesting,
especially the Canadian geese.

The Sportsman Club received the South Dakota Wildlife banner and pin in 1975,
for having over 160 members. In 1976 it received the pin for the second highest
membership. Presently 80 members participate in the club. The club holds a
family steak fry annually. Present officers are: Ron Kappes, president; Glenn
Fischer, vice president; Mike Rath, treasurer; and
Jack Geffre, secretary.

                Leola Trail Riders

Herbert Ketterling, Lee Kindelspire and Marvin Hoffman, had set up a rodeo on
the west side of Leola during the 1972 "Rhubarb Festival" celebration. It was
such a great success that it inspired a group of men to form a horse
club.

The first meeting to organize a club was held on July 15, 1973. The first
officers of the club were: LeRoy Weiszhaar, president; Jim Goebel, vice
president; Bill Waddell, secretary; and Lee Kindelspire, treasurer. The name
Leola Trail Riders was adopted by the club. Senior directors were Gerald
Hoffman, Herbert Ketterling and Byron Kindelspire. Junior directors were Leo
Kindelspire and David Yost. Thirty-nine members participated in the club the
first year.

An arena was built one mile west of Leola. Each year the club has a rodeo,
paint shows, trail rides, and a kids' fun day. The arena is also being used by
the county 4-H horse shows and by the Jaycees for their demolition
derbies.

The first Rodeo Queen and Rodeo Princess contest was held in 1975. Wanita
Hoffman was selected as queen and Debbie Goebel as the first princess.

The club membership presently is 31. Officers are: Darrel Yost, president; Wade
Weiszhaar, vice president; Alvin Kallas, secretary and Julius Bonnet,
treasurer.

                Town and Country Twirlers

Ron and Nadine Hatlewick, who had square danced for several years in the
Jamestown area; invited Ruth and Joseph Lapka to the Aberdeen Belles and Beaux
square dance lessons "just to watch." Seeing that square dancing was wholesome
entertainment and "friendship set to music" as the saying goes, the two couples
decided to see if there would be enough interest to start a club in the Leola
area.

Eighteen interested couples met at the Leola Municipal Building. Dale and Ella
Maye Bengston from Aberdeen were caller and teacher. Lessons began September of
1978.

After practicing the challenging steps for 22 weeks, the group decided to form
a local club. On March 9, 1979 an organization meeting was held. Albert and
Viola Feickert were elected to serve as president. Ron and Nadine Hatlewick
were chosen vice president, Ruth and Joseph Lapka continued duties as
secretary-treasurer and Harold and Luella Shafer were given duties to record
the club's history. Other charter members were Luther and Delores Hoffman,
Gerald and Dorothy Hoffman, Reuben and Ada Wagemann, Arnold and Carol Becker,
Ervin and Lila Rau, Curtis and Leona Hoffman, James and Betty Evans, Gerhardt
and Ella Hoffman, Alvin and Nancy Kallas, Dominic and Dorothy Kallas, Denver
and Mary Ann Guthmiller, James and Eileen Goebel, Douglas and Lena Cox, Laverne
and Donna Skott.

The name Town and Country Twirlers was chosen because it fit the makeup of the
club's membership.

The club designed a badge in the shape of the state of South Dakota with a city
scene and a barn and silo on it, along with the club name and address. Each
member then got a badge with their name on it.

The members completed the Basic and Mainstream lessons and June 3, 1979, was
chosen as graduation day. This was held in the Legion Hall, where ladies in
their graduation dresses and can-cans and men with matching shirts and ties
received their graduation certificates. Graduations were held in 1980 and 1982
also.

In August, 1979, the Twirlers became members of the South Dakota Square, Folk
and Round Dance Association, Inc.

On June 7, 1981 the club hosted the State Knot Head Dance. This is a dance for
"Knot Heads" or square dancers who have earned a Knot Head Badge. To qualify as
a "Knot Head," three couples from the same club must travel 100 miles or more
to attend a square dance.

Viola Feickert, the first twirler to hold office in the State Square, Folk and
Round Dance Association was installed historian at this Knot Head dance.

A large variety of fun badges can be earned by members. The twirlers have had
two special badge dances where dancers show off the badges earned during their
dancing career and earn new badges.

The Harold Shafers attended a national convention in Seattle in 1980 and the
Albert Feickerts earned a badge for square dancing in five countries, in a
guided square dance tour to Switzerland in 1980.

Square dancing is fun to watch, too. Club members entertained by dancing at the
Rhubarb Festival at Leola and the Golden Jubilee in Long Lake, SD in 1979, the
Diamond Jubilee in Forbes, ND in 1980, and the Centennial in Leola in 1984.
Residents of the nursing homes in Ipswich and Eureka also enjoyed being
entertained by the square dancers.

The Twirlers dance the second and fourth Friday nights of each month in the
Legion Hall in Leola. Leola is a popular place for area dancers because of the
wood floor in the hall. Popular callers from North Dakota and South Dakota are
booked to call square and round dances, line dances, folk
dances, and mixers.

The Town and Country Twirlers are noted for their friendliness and good
food.

                Disco Club

On February 23, 1912, a group of ladies of Leola, SD formed a club for the
purpose of sewing and sociability. Later that year, Palma Goebels, one of the
new members, suggested calling it Disco, meaning learn and connection with.
Later the motto, "I would study, I would learn," was selected by Jennie Turner
and Minnie Yost. The club flower is the red carnation and the colors are red
and green.

        Fiftieth Anniversary Picture, February 1962. Fourth row: Louise Reimer,
Leone Hohman, Wilma Hilgemann, Vi. Smolnisky, Betty Lou Heibel, Harriet
Turnwall, Leone Thomas, Lorene Neuharth, Biruta Zvejnieks and Esther Knudson.
Third row: Leona Kulm, Jan Kraft, Marian Schumacher, Margaret Holmes. Second
row: Lillian Kindelspire, Agnes Swanson and Jessie Pade. First row: Bonnie Gill
and Martha Rath.

Disco has always taken an active part m any movement which was for the good of
the community, such as the city library and music recitals. They were sponsors
of the March of Dimes fund campaign for the east half of our
county also.

The program committee, which is appointed by the president each year, arranges
a program, appoints the leaders for each month and presents its topic to the
group. Also one outing is planned for the group each year. For many years the
club held an annual party for the teachers in September and an annual spring
tea for the senior girls and their mothers.

At the present time we have 22 members, including honorary members. They are as
follows: Dorothy Daly, Alverde Daniel, Mabel Freitag, Waneta Geffre, Grace
Giesecke, Bonnie Gill, Jean Guffy, Della Guthmiller, Elma Hepperle, Wilma

Betty Maule, Jessie Pade, Martha Rath, Violet Schaffer, Marion Schumacher,
Leone Thomas, Helen Thompson and Colleen Wangsness. Disco Club is 72 years old.

                        CHURCHES

                Baptist Church

Reaching all the way back to South Russia, the land from which its founders
migrated, the Leola First Baptist Church has its roots in the early years of
McPherson County. The Frederich Rueb and Adam Hauck families had settled in
Arena Township and were attending Long Lake Baptist Church services as often as
possible. In 1901, the Nicolas Lechner family also settled in the Arena Valley,
and the three families began to hold services in their own homes, inviting
neighbors and friends to join them. John Lechner was one of the old pioneer
members of the group and as the church grew, services were held in the Arena
Valley schoolhouse.

With Rev. B. Hilzinger of Eureka as officiating pastor, the group was known as
the Arena Valley Station of the First Baptist Church of Eureka. Rev. B.
Hilzinger held services at least once a month, conducting weddings and funeral
services when called upon. In 1918 the congregation built its first church,
dedicating in August of that year.

In November, 1931, a decision was made to purchase two acres of land in
Highland Township and the Arena Valley Church was moved to the new location 21
miles east of Eureka on the Long Lake road, where it continued to serve as a
worship center known as the Hoffnungsfeld Baptist Church, served by the Eureka
pastor. In the fall of 1954 it was decided to relocate in the city of Leola,
where a building site was purchased and building began immediately. Walter Rueb
served as building chairman of the group. A contractor was hired. The basement
was completed so that worship services could be conducted, and the shell of the
superstructure, complete with tower and roof were erected. Rev. A. Krombein was
pastor at that time. In October of 1955 under Rev. A. H. Reeh as pastor, plans
were formulated and projected into the future to complete the interior and
install furniture. The work was completed in April of 1960 and dedication was
held on May 29, 1960. The membership at that time was 56. On December 10, 1958
the church separated from the First Baptist Church of Eureka and became a
self-governing organization known as First Baptist Church of Leola and since
then have had their own pastor, which in previous time they shared a pastor
with Eureka. In 1963 the church felt the need of a new parsonage which a site
was purchased and a parsonage was constructed one half of a block south and two
blocks west of the church.

On June 3, 1979 the members were able to hold mortgage burning service as the
church was completely debtfree, and for this the group rejoiced, for only
through the grace of God that this became reality.

The first deacon of the Arena Valley was John Lechner; trustee, Frederich Rueb.
Present officers include: deacons, Eugene Weisenburger, Chr., Ed. Head; and
Edwin Loebs. The trustees are Emil Albrecht, Gordon Hauck and Albert Loebs.
Church treasurer, Jake Kirschman; clerk, Vivian Rueb; S.S. superintendent,
Eugene Wiesenburger.

        Leola First Baptist Church.

Pastors who have served since the church is in Leola:
Rev. Edward Oster
Rev. Lorimer Potratz (part time)
Rev. Arthur J. Fischer
Ray Lick, served as student pastor for one summer
Duane Owens, served as student pastor for one summer
Rev. Arnold Friez, present pastor

American Indians and Spanish-Americans in Texas and Colorado as well as the
people of Japan and the Cameroons (Africa) and Brazil in South America have
benefited from the formation of the Mary Martha Mission Society by the ladies
of the First Baptist Church in May, 1956. Organized to promote missionary
interest among members and to support the missionary projects of their church
in the fields mentioned, the group's first officers were LaVina Albrecht,
president; Emma Heupel, vice president; Florence McDaniel, secretary; and Vivan
Rueb, treasurer

        Back Row, L to R: Jewel Head, Emgard Loebs, Vivian Rueb, Ella Loebs
        and Anges Weisenberger. Front Row: Grace Frissz, Emma Heupel, Amy
        Heageley, LaVina Albrecht.

Although, a ladies' mission band had been formed in earlier years, it had
ceased to function when the present group united. Besides supporting missions,
they also furnish White Cross material including baby layettes to the hospitals

        Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church

When the first Catholic families came to the Leola Community there was no
Catholic church here so those living northeast of Leola went to Frederick and
those living south of Leola went to Ipswich.

Sometimes Holy Mass was said in some of the homes.

John Mack purchased a store building at Koto for a house which he sold again.
This in time became their church.

John Fritza donated some land about six miles northeast of Leola so the
pioneers living near decided to move their building there.

John Lapka and John Fritza drove to Aberdeen by team to get some timbers to
move it. After it was moved they remodeled it by contributing their time, labor
and whatever money it took to build the little church which became known as St.
Hyacinths, in 1891.

        St. Hyacinths.

Some of the pioneer families at that time were: John and Joe Mack, Jake and
George Reible, Rochus Sr., Peter Sr., and Joseph Geffre, John Kraft, Julius and
John Kallas, August Grabowska, John Lapka, Benedict Robert and Thomas Mastel,
Henry Speth, John Fritza, Henry Breunig, John and Bela Dexter, Frank Pietz,
Paul Wenda, John, Maggie and Will Lebold, Igness Lapka, Fr. Dahlmans, Ernest
Schuchardt, Mrs. William Rapp and family, Andrew Geffre,
and John Taylor.

Most of these were German or Polish, some came directly from Russia and others
came from other states, such as Wisconsin, Ohio and New York.

By 1891 they had a church but no pastor. Priests came from other places now and
then, among them were Fr. John Lomesh, the first priest, Fr. Dahlmans, Fr. F.
X. Feldmeier, and others.

August Grabowska and Rochus Geffre Sr., were the first trustees of St.
Hyacinths. Carl Mack was the first infant baptized in the new church. A
Catholic Rectory was built in 1908 at the east end of Leola and in 1916 was
moved to the present location. Services were held in the rectory part of the
time to accommodate people in town or south of town who were too far from that
little country church.

Fr. Edward Fierek, who was the first resident priest, came in 1907 and remained
here until 1910.

Fr. John Donley came in 1910, he was succeeded in 1912 by Fr. Albert
Wallock.

In the spring of 1916, under the leadership of Fr. Wallock, the present church
was built.

On September 17, 1916, Holy Mass was celebrated in it for the first time. It
was dedicated on September 28, 1916 to Our Lady of Perpetual Help.

Frank and Martha (Geffre) Grabowska were the first couple to be married in the
new church on September 26, 1916.

Fr. Wallock was succeeded by Fr. George Heinen in September 1924.

Fr. John Prytarski came in November 1937 and served until 1955, when Fr. Marvin
J. McMahon came. Next priests in succession were: Fr. John Kash, Fr. Vincent
Healy, Fr. Gary Nolt, Fr. Anthony Imberi, Fr. Norbert Rader, Fr. William Osborn
and the present Fr. Bob Krantz.

                Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church.

A parish center was built in 1966, while Fr. Gary Nolt and Fr. Anthony Imberi
served the parish. The parish center consists of classrooms, auditorium,
kitchen and other facilities useful to the church and the
community.

The Parish Hall was dedicated by Bishop Lambert Hock, Bishop of the Diocese of
Sioux Falls, in 1967.

Recent improvements include lowering the ceiling, installing ceiling fans,
decorating the church, a new organ, building a ramp for the handicapped, and a
new basement under the rectory.

Two Masses are said on weekends. One on Saturday evening at 8:00 and one at
11:00 on Sunday morning, to accommodate the increasing membership.

                United Methodist Church, Leola, South Dakota

In 1887, the Rev. G. W. Hickman, the first resident methodist minister came to
Leola and organized the church.  It was on December 15, 1888 that the church
was incorporated and plans were made to erect a house of worship in 1889.
Lumber had been stacked on the site by the new foundation for construction, but
was burned in the April 2, 1889 fire.  Services were held in a schoolhouse
until the congregation could buy more lumber and continue with the building of
the church as the town was rebuilt.  The same year, a new church which still
stands called the First Methodist Episcopal Church, was built at a cost of
$5,000.  In December 1908 the church acquired a bell which served to call
worshipers on Sunday and was also dedicated to the city as a fire alarm.  In
1924 an annex was added to the south side of the
church.

In 1907, a house was moved to the lot south of the church for a parsonage. In
August 1966, an 8-year-old house 2 1/2 blocks W and 1/2 block S of the church
became the parsonage.  In the spring or 1981 the old parsonage south of the
church was torn down.

The Methodist Episcopal Church led the community in supporting many education
functions.  June 1, 1901, a library benefit program was hosted at the church.
The first commencement exercises for the village school was held at the church
in June of 1903.

In 1939 when the three major branches of the church: Methodist Episcopal,
Methodist Episcopal South, and Methodist Protestant Churches were united, the
name was then changed to the Methodist Church.  By a conference action in 1968
the Evangelical United Brethren Church and Methodist Church were joined to form
the United Methodist Church.

Present membership numbers 98 with Sunday School enrollment at 25. Maryette
Sears is the oldest living full member in the congregation.  She was received
into the church on March 24, 1913.

The following pastors served the church since 1888.

                United Methodist Women, Leola, South Dakota

Although there are no records available prior to 1909, the Methodist Ladies Aid
Society has definitely been in existence for 75 years, since there are records
of its existence in August, 1909. Rev. Redmayne was pastor of the church at
that time.

First officers were Mrs. Helen Redding, president; Mrs. Delphy Turner,
secretary; and Mrs. Aleatha Junge, treasurer. Meetings of the 24 members were
held every two weeks, usually in the homes.

In 1940 all women's societies of the Methodist church were reorganized into the
Women's Society of Christian Service (WSCS) with 32 charter members when Rev.
Omstead was pastor. In 1955 the local society celebrated its fiftieth
anniversary by inviting the Frederick WSCS as guests for a program
and lunch.

In 1959 when Leola celebrated its 75th jubilee members at that time were
Florence Krein, Virginia Schanzenbach, Mildred Henderson, Louise Bain, Leslie
Lindley, Emma Pade, Esther Knudson, Ethel Yost, Mabel Odel, Ann Rath, Berneice
Pade, Edith Davis, Caroline Fewings, Viola Nelson, Bertha Shafer, Lola
Christian, Lucy Bell, Pearl LaFontaine, Edna Cowherd, Grace Rogers, Edith
Holmes, and Gladys Morrison.

                Leola Methodist Church.

In January of 1972 the Women's Society of Christian Service changed its name to
the United Methodist Women (UMW).

Two circles, Eve and Julia are active in the church. Eve Circle organized on
February 1, 1961 at a meeting in Esther Knudson's home with Lorretta Huber as
president. Julia Circle's 16 members held an organizational meeting at Emma
Pade's home on June 7, 1962.

The Methodist women of the Leola church, although formally not organized, were
very active as the following articles appeared in our local McPherson County
Herald. On May 30, 1907 this article was printed. "Paper Methodist Church:
Several of the prominent young ladies of the Methodist Episcopal Church
solicited sufficient funds to pay for papering the walls of the interior of the
church. The work was completed last week and is a great improvement and all
concerned are proud of the appearance of the room."

Reported on December 10, 1908: "Methodist Bazaar is Outstanding Success: The
Bazaar conducted at Pierce's Hall last Saturday afternoon and evening by the
ladies of the Methodist Church, was a decided success both socially and
financially. Booths were very attractively arranged around the hall from which
were sold the numerous articles prepared by the ladies for the occasion. A
lunch booth from which hot lunches were served and sumptuous supper in the
evening was the big attraction for the gentlemen and proved a source of
considerable revenue. The literary program in the evening was very good and
greatly enjoyed by all who were there."

Then, as now our, United Methodist Women's Unit is still very active in our
congregation with 15 members. The summer and fall of 1982 the women aided in
helping to paint the interior of the church. Our fall bazaar is still one of
our main events to plan for each year.

Present officers are Hazel Zetterlund, president; Deloris Bain, vice president;
Kay Henderson, secretary; Viola Geffre, treasurer. Besides executive officers,
the group has various committees each year. They are: Rhea Smith, Christian
personhood; Alverde Daniel, social involvement; June Shafer, Delores Rath, and
Evelyn Rogers, supportive community; Mabel Freitag, Eldora Fewings, and Alverde
Daniel, nominating committee. Other present members are: Ethel Yost, Jessie
Pade, Virginia Schanzenbach, Lola Christian, Monica Meyer, and Teresa
Zetterlund.

                Reformed Church

The Leola Reformed Church was organized by Rev. Ulrich Reue. D. D. Opp, J. P.
Guthmiller, Valentine Lehr, Melcher Bonnet were some of the members. The church
had D. D. Opp as elder and J. P. Guthmiller as deacon as its first
officers.

The first Reformed minister in McPherson County was Rev. Edward Scheidt, who
preached the first sermon at the Daniel Opp home on April 12, 1886 in Odessa
Township about 15 miles northeast of Eureka.

Rev. Ulrich Reue was born in Evenhausen, Germany. He came to America in his
younger years. In 1887 while living in Indiana, he received a call from the
Reformed Church to come to Dakotas to do missionary work. He accepted the call
and came to Eureka. In 1900 he moved with his family to Leola where he presided
as Clerk of Courts for 22 years and where he preached the Gospel
until 1925.

Rev. Peter Bauer was pastor from 1926 to 1936. The Leola Reformed Church had
been a Free Reformed Church until 1926, when they affiliated with the Dakota
Synod of the Reformed Church in the U.S.A. and the Eureka Classis of the
Reformed Church in the U.S.A. Ministers were:

Rev. George E. Wolfe, 1937 to 1942
Rev. Kasper Krueger, 1944 to 1949
Rev. Fred Hersog, 1950 to 1953
Rev. Herman Mensch, 1955 to 1956

In 1957 Leola and Aberdeen Reformed Churches organized as one charge. They
called Rev. Calvin Stuebbe from Sutton, NE. Rev. Stuebbe served Aberdeen and
Leola from 1958 to 1966. Rev. Donald Treick from 1966 to 1974. Rev. Neale R.
Riffert from 1974 to 1982. Whenever the Leola Church was without a pastor the
Eureka Classis would supply pastors to fill the pulpit.

The first Reformed services in Leola were started in 1900 by Rev. Reue. The
Leola Township schoolhouse was sold to the German Oranian Reformed Church on
August 19, 1909 and was used to worship until April 8, 1918. The congregation
bought the church in the west part of town from the Baptist Congregation, who
on June 22, 1916 had bought it from the Presbyterian Church, who bought the lot
in 1889. The church was built by Presbyterian congregation. In 1957 the church
was remodeled and used by the Reformed Congregation from 1918 until March 1974.

        Leola Reformed Church.

In 1974 the building was sold to Schaible's Trucking. They bought the Christian
Alliance Church on the east end of Leola along Highway 10, where the Reformed
Congregation is now worshipping. The present officers are: Dr. Rev. Doug
Erlandson, elders Milbert Kappas and Rudolph Opp. Deacons are Gottlieb Sperle
and Milbert Bender.

                St. James Lutheran Church

As we in the year 1984 look back over the history of St. James, we also observe
the beginning and growth of the Lutheran Church in northern South Dakota,
McPherson County.

Mission pastors of the Iowa Synod had been sent to the borders of North and
South Dakota to contact scattered Lutherans and gather them into congregations.

Most of the travel was with horses, occasionally there was an ox in use.
Churches, towns, all needed to be close together; close enough that the trip to
and from could be made within one day of travel. With the coming of the auto
the pastor was able to go to as many as three places each Sunday and the people
could come to these locations where worship services were
held.

When the missionary pastors, Prue and LeBahn of the old Iowa Synod came through
Leola, they conducted services and baptized children, but more often than not
reading services had to suffice.

The courage and determination of these Lutheran pioneers and their counselors
prepared the way for the organization of a Lutheran church in Leola. Pastor
Andreas Hahn, who arrived in Leola in the summer of 1887 founded the Leola
congregation two weeks later.

Early church records show that after a worship service conducted by Pastor Hahn
in the schoolhouse on July 10, 1887, a group of pioneers met with the pastor to
organize a congregation. The name St. James was agreed upon for this first
Lutheran congregation organized in McPherson County, Dakota
Territory.

On July 24, 1887, under the leadership of Pastor Hahn the permanent
organization took place. Charter members instrumental in organizing the
congregation were: Fredrich Arndt, Philip Becker, Karl A. Breitag, Frederick
Glaseman, Karl Glaseman, Carl Granmann, Otto Hauffe, Frederick Jasmer, Andreas
Jung, Heinrich Jung, Gottlob Pade, August Pischke, Ferdinand Pose, Ferdinand
Potratz, Gustav Tonn, Robert Valentine, and
Andreas Zapf.

Andreas Hahn was the first resident pastor to serve this congregation. However,
as the membership grew it became evident that a more adequate house of worship
was necessary. It became known that a former saloon was available for the price
of the mortgage against it. It was moved to the east end of the town to several
acres already donated to the congregation. A three room addition was built on
for a parsonage. This house of worship was destroyed in the great Leola Fire of
April 2, 1889.

Pastor Hahn, his wife, and a confirmation class of five students, Louisa Pose,
Marie Pade, Emelia Jasmer, Alvina Milbrandt, and Marie Jung just barely escaped
with their lives.

But undaunted, the pioneers stood together. Another parsonage and barn were
built. Church services were held in the schoolhouse, courthouse, and the
Reformed Church.

During the ministry of Pastor A. Haag a new church 28' by 40' was built on a
tract of land donated by F. Arndt, at the east edge of Leola. The cornerstone
was laid July 20, 1902; items placed in the corner stone were a list of its
church members, names of the council, the Kirschenblatt, three small coins and
Sunday school tickets. The church was dedicated on October 14, 1902. This
church served the congregation until the present one was dedicated in 1951. (It
was sold to the Evangelical congregation, it now is
the Reformed Church.)

Pastor Reischauer, who organized the Hope and Salem Congregations was followed
in 1894 by N. Brunn, who served the three congregations of the parish. Salary
stipulated in his call was $350 per year. Dues were set at $4 per member per
year. Salem church was founded in May 1891 and discontinued after the last
service held December 26, 1954. Hope Lutheran Church was organized on January
8, 1894, and held their final church service on December 26, 1960. Most of the
members of the two congregations joined St.
James of Leola.

On April 18, 1915, the first service in the English language and Sunday school
was started, held in an effort to serve Norwegian Lutherans in Leola. This
created a hardship for the early settlers who had always worshipped in the
German language.

        St. James Lutheran Church.

The history of the congregation shows that there was not always progress and
growth. The crop failures of the 1890's and the 1930's, and the language
controversy in the congregation from l919 to 1921 resulted in the loss of
members.

For the celebration of the 30th and 40th anniversaries of the congregation,
Pastor Hahn, the organizing pastor, was able to be present and deliver the
festival sermon. Also, present were charter members Carl Breitag, Fred
Glaseman, Otto Hauffe and Fred Potratz. During the ministry of Rev. Wm.
Reinecke the 40th and 50th anniversaries of the church were celebrated. Only
Carl Breitag was able to be present.

The present buff-colored brick church with a seating capacity of 300 was built
near the center of town under the leadership of Pastor H. Haase. The
cornerstone was laid November 5, 1950. The church was built and furnished at a
total cost of about $50,000. Dedication services were held September
23, 1951.

A Wurlitzer electric organ purchased in 1948, was replaced with a concert type
Hammond organ in 1955.

The old parsonage served until 1958, when it was sold and a new ranch style
structure measuring 32 by 50 feet without the garage, was built on the same
site. The building cost about $24,000 plus many hours of contributed labor.
Dedication services were held on June 28, 1959. A new furnace and
air-conditioning was added in 1983, at a cost of $4,344.

A new parish education unit was built on to the east side of the present church
by National Bldgs. Co., of Fargo, ND. The cost of this buff-colored brick
addition was $41,000. It was dedicated on October 4, 1964.

Throughout the years a number of additions and improvements have been made. The
ceiling in the church was refinished in the early '70's, carpeting in the
church proper was replaced in '74. A new furnace and ceiling fans have been
installed. A new piano for the Sunday school was purchased. In 1978 the new
"Lutheran Book of Worship" hymnal was accepted.

The following pastors served the congregation since its founding in 1887: A.
Hahn, 1887-90; M. Reischauer, 1890-94; N. Brunn, 1895-97; A. Haag, 1898-1904;
F. Walther, 1904-05; C. Taubert, 1906-10; J. O. Staehling, 1910-12; C. Taubert,
1912-19; Wm. Reinecke, 1919-41; H. H. Haase, 1942-54; J. Schmierer, 1954-58; K.
J. Reimer, 1958-70; A. R. Borchardt, 1971-77; M. Wangsness, since January 2,
1978.

Active in the ministry at the present time are Pastor Martin Haase and Pastor
Robert Reimer, sons of former pastors of St. James.

CONGREGATIONAL LEADERS: Many have served in its various offices throughout
these many years.

LUTHERAN BROTHERHOOD: Was founded during the time Rev. Schmierer served as
pastor, in 1955. It disbanded in 1979, due to membership loss.

ST. JAMES LADIES AID: There had been a ladies aid before Rev. Taubert came to
Leola, but it had disbanded. The present St. James Aid, known as the "Frauen
Verein," was organized January 7, 1919. Christina Steiger is the only living
member of the early aid. In 1947, the aid consisted of 27 members, they met in
the members' homes. On October 5, 1951, they began meeting in the church
basement. The group meets the first Thursday in the after-noon, Bible Study is
led by the pastor. A Food and Fancy Work sale is held by the members in
December, each year. Proceeds are used for different church projects. The Aid
started in 1983 with 37 members, of which four are officers.

        St. James Ladies Aid.

LADIES AID CIRCLE II: On April 6, 1950 at the home of Eva Balliet, it was
decided to organize a new circle of younger church members, since the
membership was getting too large to meet in the homes. The first meeting to
organize was held at the home of Priscilla Hilgemann, on April 21, 1950.

Circle II which affiliated with the Women's Missionary Federation in 1957, is
now known as the American Lutheran Church Women, (ALCW). St. James ALCW holds
their regular meeting on the first Thursday evening of each month. Presently it
consists of 43 members, six of whom are officers. A Fall Festival (food and
white elephant sale) is sponsored annually. The group continues to contribute
much to the congregation and various charities and missions.

        Ladies Aid Circle II.

LUTHER LEAGUE: Facts about early youth organizations are missing. The present
was organized on October 19, 1943. The Luther League consists of young
confirmed high school youth. The young people enjoy and participate in league
sponsored activities, and serve as ushers at Sunday morning church services.

OUR CHOIRS: Consists of a Men's choir, a Senior, and a Sunday school children's
choir.

ORGANISTS: Are a valuable part of our congregation, a complete list was not
available.

SUNDAY SCHOOL: Enrollment at the beginning of the year is 69. St. James
Congregation has a baptized membership of 444, and confirmed, 370 as of January
1, 1984.

                St. Paul's Lutheran Church

St. Paul's Lutheran Church, one of the later organizations of Leola will be in
its 62nd year as the city is celebrating its 100th. The process of becoming
organized began in 1921. Peter Schuchardt offered his theater building and by
request of 11 families from the Leola area, the first worship service was held
on July 17, 1921, by the Rev. P. L. Kluender. At that time the Rev. Kluender
was pastor of Christ Lutheran Church of the Missouri Synod, located nine miles
west of Ellendale, ND. He was serving five other congregations besides the one
in Leola, and could not take over permanent ministry of this church. They found
the vacant Immanuel Congregation in Long Lake, SD which Rev. Kluender was
serving as vacancy pastor, to be willing to join with them in forming a dual
parish and calling a pastor.

The Mission Festival worship service on November 6, 1921 can be considered the
first important event of the early church. Rev. Theodore Klatt was the guest
speaker for the morning service. Rev. John Dewald conducted the German service
and Pastor Kluender, the English service in the afternoon. The offering in the
morning service was $44.70 and the afternoon $26.66, certainly a substantial
amount for an unorganized congregation.

Sunday School was organized on December 21, 1921. At that time classes and
worship services were held in the evening.

At a regular meeting held on January 25, 1922, the Rev. A. Merkens of Scobey,
MT was called as pastor. He was installed on Sunday May 21, 1922 at Long Lake
in the forenoon and at Leola in the afternoon by the Rev. Kluenger conducting
the services.

Worship services were still being held in the local theater where Rev. Merkens
delivered his first sermon in Leola the following Sunday.

Shortly after his arrival there was a strong desire among the people to have
their own house of worship.

On June 5, 1922 the decision was made to build a new church. On July 2, four
lots were purchased (the present site) for $364. By July 27, excavation of the
basement measuring 30' by 50' was begun. Cornerstone laying ceremonies were
held August 5, 1922. Rev. Kluender was the speaker for the German service and
Rev. A. G. Merkens for the English.

The following membership list was placed inside the cornerstone:

There were many volunteers who helped faithfully in the building of the church.
The cost of the building was approximately $10,000. The new church was
completed and dedicated on November 19, 1922. Speakers for the services were
Rev. E. A. Klaus of Addison, IL and Rev. Victor Bartling of Bismarck, ND.

        St. Paul's Lutheran Church.

In April 1932 the congregation purchased the house directly east of the church
for a parsonage at the cost of $2,620. Securing of the house was looked upon by
the congregation as a "Tenth Anniversary Memorial."

The tenth anniversary worship was conducted by Rev. G. Bauer in the German and
Pastor F. Graiber of Aberdeen, guest speaker for the English.

The 25th anniversary of the congregation was celebrated on August 3, 1947. The
speaker was a former pastor of the congregation, the Rev. H. Bauer.

During the ministry of Rev. E. Boniek a Hammond organ replaced the reed organ
which had been in use since 1922.

A new garage and driveway as well as a new A. B. Dick mimeograph were added
during the ministry of Rev. Hellman.

Good Shepherd Lutheran Church of Ipswich was aligned with the Leola
congregation during the ministry of Rev. Nordquist.

Rev. Robert A. Kriger was instrumental in getting the bell which now resides in
the tower.

On June 25, 1972, the congregation looked back at 50 years of service to its
Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. In honor of the occasion a new entry to the
church was added at a cost of $10,000, same amount as the cost of the church
building 50 years previous.

The parsonage was given an extensive remodeling in 1980. Through the generosity
of many people's time, talent and gifts; new windows, new carpeting, paneling
and a new paint job inside and out, gave new life and vitality to the parsonage.

60 YEARS: In honor of this special occasion, the congregation completed
rejuvenating the outside and inside of the church building.

        LWML (St. Paul's Ladies Aid).
