                Seventh Day Adventist Church

The Seventh Day Adventist Church of Leola, SD was organized on April 6, 1891. A
small group of believers under the leadership of its first pastor, Eldor
Valentine Lehr, met and organized a Seventh Day Adventist Church body, 13 miles
west of Leola, SD, in the home of Michael Binder.

Charter members instrumental in organizing the congregation were the families
of Andreas Fetz; Michael Binder; Phillip Reiling; Henry Renschler; Wilhelm
Tabert; Henry Kindopp; Christoph Maisch; and Mr. Henry Human. The first
officers were Andreas Fetz, Elder; Michael Binder, Deacon and Phillip Reiling,
Clerk. They met in the Michael Binder home for several years.

The congregation continued to progress; it soon was in need of a church
building and also make provisions for a cemetery.

A building 22 feet by 30 feet was constructed of homemade clay bricks, on two
acres of land which was donated by Phillip Reiling, located 12 1/2 miles west
of Leola on old Highway 10. The cemetery is located at this site.

In 1907, the sod building was abandoned and a new frame building was erected at
the same site. Pastor Valentine Lehr organized this assembly known as the Long
Lake Seventh Day Adventist Church, until June 7, 1922, when it was changed to
Leola Seventh Day Adventist Church.

During the years it became more evident that the congregation should have a
larger house of worship. In 1925 a new church was built. This frame building
26' by 54' was erected one-half mile east and one-half mile south of the first
site. The church was dedicated on October 25, 1925, by Pastors Julius
Boettchers and Emil Oswald.

        Seventh Day Adventist Church.

On November 1, 1956, the country church was moved into Leola, on to a full
basement. The basement provides several accommodations, one of which is a room
for Dorcas Welfare Work. At this time a new entrance was added and remodeling
was done. The church was dedicated on November 29, 1958 by Pastors R. H.
Nightingale, of Minneapolis, Minnesota and O. J. Garner of Watertown, SD.

The congregation has within the years given a number of its sons into the
ministry; Clarence Renschler, Myron Voegele, Leverne Krenzler.

The pastors who have served the church are as follows: Valentine Lehr; Conrad
Reising; D. N. Wall; E. N. Oswald; Elder Fritz; M. Weutland; F. F. Schwindt; C.
Hein; C. Beck; S. Reile; C. A. Renschler; Adam Rudy; John Herr, Elder Goede;
Don Copsey, Allen Bidwell; Robert Kurth; J. C. Parmele; Henry Preston; George
Whitsett; Alfred Bernhardt; Everett Calkins; Weldon Treat and James Neergard.
Pastor Dennis Shafter is serving the congregation at this time.

The oldest living member of the church in 1983 is Christoph Rueb, age 97.

                Leola Dorcas Society

The first Dorcas Society was organized at Battle Creek, MI, in 1872. The
special mission of the society was to minister to the needs of the poor.
Wartime and post-war needs encouraged development on the community level.
Knowing the need for emergency facilities and workers trained in disaster
relief, each church's society tries to be prepared to meet these needs to the
best of their ability in their local community. In recent years, the Dorcas
Society has come to be known as Adventist Community Services.

Realizing that the physical, mental, social and spiritual aspects of each
person are closely related, the Leola Adventist Community Services, though
small, tries to be of service to the community in a variety of ways. Food
baskets at Christmas and at times of need, quilts, bedding and money given when
disaster strikes, 5-Day Stop Smoking Clinics and blood pressure screening,
financing camp vacations for disadvantaged children, personal visits, and
collecting and processing clothing for international shipment, are among the
services offered. "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these
my brethren, Ye have done it unto me." Matthew 25:40.

                        SCHOOLS

                A Brief History of Leola Elementary and
                McPherson County Rural Schools

In the late 1880's and early 1900's there was very little difference between
the McPherson County rural schools and the Leola village school. Each was
housed in a one-room building furnished with a teacher's desk, a recitation
bench, pupils' double desks with inkwells, a blackboard, a washstand holding a
basin and water pail with a common drinking-dipper; and a pot-bellied stove
centered in the room to somewhat equalize the distribution of heat. Even so,
those sitting near the stove complained of being too warm, while those on the
fringes were shivering. Books were few and assorted.

Common Problems: Each school had one teacher who was responsible for teaching
and maintaining discipline (the hickory stick was not uncommon) and janitorial
duties. Wages reflected the economy, usually $25 a month. The school term
lasted from two to four months. The teacher sometimes had 40 or more pupils of
all ages with varying abilities--some grasping the material readily, others
struggling to learn and, of course, some indifferent. Despite the teacher's
limited scholastic qualifications, most of them were dedicated and did their
best to teach the basics, as records of well-educated people who were their
former students testify.

Many immigrant children had never attended any school; some could not talk
English, which made the school work doubly hard for them and for the teacher.
However, not all immigrants were foreign born; some came from other states, and
their children helped Americanize their schoolmates, who in turn helped
Americanize their parents. All pupils, regardless of age, were grouped
according to their ability to read and to do simple arithmetic.

Some of the early county school officers were unable to read English, so, in
1899, the county commissioners had school laws printed in English and German.
According to County Superintendent of Schools C. B. Foncannon, "Regardless of
which language the reports were in, the fact remains that financial matters of
these districts were handled honestly and efficiently by the school officers,
who deserve much from the present generation who inherited no debts from that
source."

Rural Schools: Excerpts taken from Homesteaders of McPherson County state: "In
the fall of 1884 the school was opened in Weber Township with Irene Brewer as
teacher.... At the time Minnie Slye taught, it was the largest school in
McPherson County.... Children of the Webers, the Harts, the Habermans, the
Scots, the Howells, the Peppers, the Bardens, Floy Hickman and Maria Ayleworth
attended five months of school a year, some driving four or five miles....
Excellent teachers, and, later many of the first pupils taught there, as Fred
and Mayme Weber, Helen Howell, Anna Haberman and Johnnie Hickman."

The first Third Grade certificate in the county was granted to Mrs. J. G.
Oulson in 1884. She taught the Leola school in 1885. The first Second Grade
certificate issued in the county was granted to Miss Emma Hickman in 1885 and
the first First Grade certificate, also to Miss Hickman in 1886. According to
official records in 1885, the following township schools were in session: Koto,
Weber, Leola, Willow, Washington, Carl, Gluckthan, Hillsview, Spring and
Howard.

The county superintendent's records do not support the assertion that all rural
schools measured up to the standards of the village school. Some had such
equipment as described earlier, while others had only make-shift furnishings:
no blackboards, a table instead of a teacher's desk, and benches instead of
desks for the children. In fact, a backward look shows that the 1909 elementary
school in Leola had a few advantages over the rural schools: generally, the
town schoolteachers were better qualified; the town school was supplied with
better equipment, both in the classroom and out on the playground; and the town
school with its larger enrollment gave the children a greater opportunity to
increase their circle of friends and consequent social skills. All the schools
were concerned primarily with basic skills and had few, if any, extracurricular
activities.

Village School: The Leola Blade, August 27, 1891 reported that the school board
had hired D. B. Strait as the teacher of the village school for a term of six
months. Mr. Strait had been identified with school work ever since the
organization of the county in 1884.

At a special meeting in 1897 the village school board decided to divide the
school and engage another teacher, as Miss Bertha Gottwald had 70 pupils of
various ages. Miss Anna Haberman was hired to teach the primary grades. To
alleviate crowded conditions at the school, the board moved 32 of the younger
children to the vacant Billings building on Sherman Street. Having the two
school buildings separated apparently was inconvenient, so in 1890 a
schoolhouse was moved adjacent to the original school on Main Street; the
larger building housing the intermediate and upper grades, the other, the
primary. Crowded conditions and building problems continued to be a recurrent
theme in the history of the Leola school.

        Souvenirs, 1897-1898

The first commencement exercises of the village school were held at the M. E.
Church. The church was filled to capacity with people from all parts of the
county to honor the eighth grade graduating class of 1903. Members of the class
were Ida Arndt, Ree Ronayne, Leslie Moulton, Mabel Hurst, Mark Spencer, Iva
Broadbent, Martha Kallas and Clara Grabowska.

German School: Although German was not being taught in the village school, it
was not neglected, according to a McPherson County Herald notice:

"Reverend Taubert will open the annual German school in the Lutheran church,
June 2, 1906. Everyone who wishes his children to learn German is invited to
send his boys and girls. The school will continue for two months until the
public school commences. School fees for nonmembers of the Lutheran
congregation are $ 1.00 per month."

Obviously the German school was popular, and as long as it was held in the
church building, Rev. Taubert was able to handle large classes. However, when
the congregation purchased a small schoolhouse and moved it on the church
premises in early 1908, the following item was published: "The German school
opened with an enrollment of 50 pupils. Rev. Taubert is the instructor and
states that the little schoolhouse is not large enough to accommodate all the
pupils, and we have been informed that only those preparing for the
confirmation will be admitted to the school." German school continued to
convene every summer for Lutherans until war was declared with Germany in 1917.
The study of German was then discontinued in the Lutheran school and in the
local high school.

Cramped Quarters: Having the two public school buildings together on Main
Street was satisfactory for a time, but the continual increase in enrollment
forced finding additional quarters in 1908, when the upper grades had to be
moved to the vacant German schoolhouse. The voters overwhelmingly approved an
$8,000 bond issue to build a school large enough for all time. When the new
two-story brick building was completed in 1909, it had almost everything
desired in a school plant at that time, and would accommodate the new high
school as well as the elementary.

The Leola Public School opened in September 1909 with Mr. W. K. Bishop as
principal, who taught the eighth grade and was the sole teacher of the two-year
high school. Three other teachers completed the faculty: Rena Busch, fifth,
sixth and seventh grades; Laura Harrison, third and fourth grades; and Sarah
Redding, primary grades. The entire enrollment totaled 75 pupils. By the
opening of school in the fall of 1910 the enrollment had increased to 137.

On August 12, 1915 the board of education held a special meeting and elected
five of the six teachers to be hired for the ensuing year. The twelfth grade
had now been added and pupil enrollment was 167.... Graduation exercises and a
class play were presented at the M. E. Church in 1915 by the seventh and eighth
grade pupils with a program under the direction of Miss Luvicey Hill. Mr. A.
Hoffman, on behalf of the school board, presented the diplomas.

Influenza Epidemic: Owing to the rapid progress and spread of influenza over
the whole county and the seriousness of the situation, it is ordered that from
this date and until further notice, all public sales, all public and private
meetings are forbidden. It is further ordered: that all schools and churches,
all theaters and pool halls, be and remain closed. By order of the County Board
of Health, October 18, 1918.

The siege of influenza hit nearly every family in the area; oftentimes there
was no well member to care for the stricken. The school, having been closed,
offered the only haven and was thereupon converted into a hospital. Rural
schoolteachers were recruited as nurses, serving under the supervision of Mrs.
Emmaline Wheeler, R.N. and Dr. G. G. Kerns.

After an unusually long school year, the Leola Public Schools closed with a
picnic out at Cochran's grove, the last gathering of the school year. The
school had operated under unusual difficulties, owing to the 'flu epidemic,
which forced the school to lose nearly two months. Part of the time was made up
by holding Saturday classes and the remainder, by extending the school year.

World War I recruitment exposed the need for a better educated citizenry. In
response, a drive for better schools in South Dakota and McPherson County was
launched in Leola November 3, 1919 at the Royal Theater. The movement involved
both city and rural schools. Hiring better qualified teachers at increased
salaries, and encouraging more parental concern over the education of their
children should produce improvement.

YCL: About this time Mr. M. M. Guhin, Director of Americanization of the State
Dept. of Public Instruction, proposed a Young Citizens League as accompaniment
to the 1919 plan for bettering the schools. This league would engage the
children themselves in the quest for a better education. The Young Citizens
League (YCL), a statewide project to be divided along county lines, would be
the common bond to give the children a sense of belonging to a larger group
than only to the one-room school. Through YCL they could participate in music
festivals, speaking contests, spelling bees, essay contests and handicrafts
throughout the school year, emphasizing athletic events during the pleasant
autumn and spring days. Learning could be exciting. Through these activities
YCL would provide opportunities for pupils throughout the county to become
acquainted with each other, to perform in the various events and to acquire
growth as contributing young citizens. YCL was the best thing that ever
happened to the rural schools. Although there were winners of events each year,
the first complete record available reports that Leona Kallas represented the
Leola elementary school and Adeline Pade represented the McPherson County rural
schools in 1930. The girls won their respective divisions and were awarded the
honor of being delegates to the State YCL Convention at Pierre.

Miss Ruth Reue, elected in 1921, was the only woman to hold the office of
county superintendent of schools in this county, until Miss Rose Gab was
elected in 1947. Miss Reue's term was marked by the construction of many new
rural schools and the enforcement of the truancy laws that went into effect at
that time. In 1923, County Superintendent Ruth Reue received notice that the
first McPherson County school to receive state aid was the "Grant Tooker
School" in Willow Township. State aid of $500 was given to any rural school
complying with regulations and specifications laid down by the state department
of public instruction.

New Schools: Twice during the decade of the 1920's the Leola school faced space
problems. A special election, held April 21, 1921 approved a $6,500 bond issue
for an additional school building. Plans were submitted, bids accepted, and a
one-story wooden structure, 30 by 66 feet, was erected in the summer of 1921 to
handle the first two grades. This building, located south of the old school,
was separated into two classrooms by folding doors, which when opened provided
one spacious room for PTA meetings and other school affairs. The increased
enrollment of the Leola School made it necessary in 1927 to move the eighth
grade to the German school, the same building that housed the overflow in 1908.
A special election in 1929 approved a bond issue of $50,000 for the building of
a new school. The new high school building measured 81 by 84 feet with a tunnel
connecting the old grade school to the new building.

First P.E.: Non-academic activities (which had heretofore been pretty much
limited to the primary grades performing in the annual operettas) began to
emerge. The first physical education program in the elementary school consisted
of calisthenics, directed by classroom teachers and track events, directed by
high school students who received their instructions from A. V. Pallviny
(Editor of the Herald). The athletic program for the entire school culminated
in a Play Festival, in which everyone participated, held May 5, 1921. Judges
were Idelette Reue, R.N., Dr. C. G. Lundquist and Lon McMillin, and the
proceeds of the day were to be used for athletic equipment.

Music: The first records available indicate that instrumental music was
introduced by Mr. David Fischer, who directed a junior high orchestra in 1929,
which played for PTA and other school functions. In 1934-35 Mr. Ted Trautman,
directed a junior high orchestra and chorus. Then in 1937, the Junior High Glee
Club, under the direction of Mr. Dan K. Jones and Miss Ann Marek broadcast over
KABR in Aberdeen, with the Glee Club, Girls' Sextet, Warren Giedt and Wallace
Giedt on the program. Despite incomplete records, it is known that in the
1950's the first graders were enjoying rhythm band, flutophones, and tonettes.
Throughout the lower grades, students were learning to count and to read notes
under the direction of Mr. Marvin Maule, Music Instructor, in 1956. In 1957
three superiors and five excellents were awarded Leola at the grade school
contest at Redfield.

Instrumental instruction after the 1950's was consistent and effective
throughout the elementary grades in generating interest in both Beginners' and
the B bands. In 1964-65 Mr. Maule worked with 50 tonette players, the largest
single group of beginners. By the time the children reached the fifth grade,
some were candidates for the Beginners' band, directed by Mr. Don Wade in the
late 1960's. Mr. Mick Guffey joined the faculty in 1968 as the first full time
music instructor. In 1978 he organized the Junior High State Band and the B
Band. Both groups performed at the annual Elementary Awards Day program and the
annual Christmas Concert. As the students improved, they auditioned for the
high school band. Each spring instrumentalists from grades five through eight
entered the Grade School Music Contest at Selby and captured numerous superior
and excellent ratings.

Vocal music had not been neglected during this time. In addition to chorus
work, some participated in the newly formed double quintet and the triple trio
ensembles under the direction of Mrs. Yvonne Huber, Elementary Music
Instructor, K-6. Mr. Jim Ochsner joined the Leola staff in 1973 as the vocal
instructor. Under his direction vocal music was taught twice a week in the
elementary grades, with public presentations at the Christmas program and the
elementary Awards Day program. The Junior High Choir and Junior High Band,
beginning in 1968 have entered the Music Festival at Aberdeen, where all
entries practice during the day in preparation for the Grand Concert, an
evening performance for the public.

Athletics: Despite the popularity of athletics in Leola, there was no organized
athletic program until 1921, when local health conscious individuals were
instrumental in setting up the program for grades 1-12. Later, exercises to
develop coordination, such as baton twirling, marching, square dancing and
relays were part of the primary physical education program. The boys looked
forward to entering the fifth grade, as that seemed to be their passport to
basketball practice with a real coach. Until then their basketball activities
had been limited to shooting baskets on an outdoor court. Mr. Mayo, the eighth
grade teacher coached seventh and eighth grade boys' basketball in 1945-47. LHS
Coach Turnwall recruited two sixth graders in 1947 to practice with the high
school B team. In the ensuing years this practice was repeated with seventh and
eighth graders who demonstrated natural ability for basketball. During the
1960's the Leola grade school team entered the annual YMCA basketball
tournaments at Aberdeen. In 1961 an athletic program offering football,
basketball and track was open to the seventh and eighth grade boys.

Beginning in 1964, under the direction of Coach Hepperle, a full physical
education program was offered in grades K-8; the K-6 grades met twice a week,
and the seventh and eighth grades met daily. In 1967 an all-school recreation
program with extensive equipment and games for grades 1-12 was initiated in the
Leola school by coaches Greeno and Hepperle. During the school year the program
was active only on Saturdays, with boys and girls alternating. In June,
activity was in full swing five days a week. In 1969-70, wrestling was added to
the eighth grade athletic program, and basketball and track were offered to
seventh and eighth grade girls in 1970.

In 1979 Coach Gary Kast introduced the first Field Day, involving K-8. There
were five events per grade and ribbons were awarded for first, second and third
places. In 1983 Coach Ron Struck set up a P.E. program for the fifth and sixth
grades and scheduled athletics and P.E. for junior high during the school day.
At this time, both boys' and girls' teams are involved in interschool games and
tournaments.

                McPherson County

        Leola No. 44-2.

Decline of Rural Schools: While this growth and enrichment was being
experienced by the town school, rural schools were suffering decline. County
Superintendent Rose Gab estimated that the rural schools of this county needed
50 new teachers for the 1947-48 term, as 50 emergency licenses had been issued
for the 1946-47 term. This represents an alarming decline in rural teacher
training since 1941.

County Superintendent Otto Strobel reported that seven rural schools, which
were in operation a year ago, were not opened for the 1958-59 term. The six
units were: Bauer Nos. II, III, IV; Bergdorf No. III; Spring No. I; Moscow No.
III; and Wachter No. I.

Twenty-nine rural graduates from McPherson County schools were awarded eighth
grade diplomas at commencement exercises held at Long Lake May 29, 1965.

Another School: The Leola Elementary School was housed in the brick building
ever since it was constructed in 1909, although it had been inadequate for
years. A special election was held in 1961 in which the Leola Independent
School District approved overwhelmingly the proposed bond issue of $250,000 for
the construction of a new building. Under the supervision of Superintendent B.
J. Hilsendeger construction of the north addition to the high school was begun,
housing a grade building and an auditorium, remodeling the high school
gymnasium to provide classrooms, and remodeling the first floor of the old
grade building for a lunchroom and kitchen. The new building was planned not
only to take care of the present needs, but to be so arranged that additions
could be added.

Reorganization: Because of the influx of children from neighboring school
districts, it was evident that reorganization would soon be a reality. More
additional space would be needed, as all school districts were required by 1971
to become part of an independent district offering a 12-year school program and
meeting the standards adopted by the state board of education.

A special election in 1965 indicated an overwhelming majority in favor of
reorganization of school districts. In early 1968 under the supervision of
Superintendent Clark Schemp and the school board, construction began on the
$345,000 addition, which included several grade and high school classrooms, a
shop, a home economics department and a central library. With the addition of
the school lunch program and the fleet of busses added in 1965, the school
became a well-rounded establishment. The only rural schools still active at
this time are the Hutterite Colony schools: Spring Creek near Forbes, ND and
Long Lake near Wetonka. Both are two-room schools, K-4 and 5-8, with two
certified teachers in each colony. The schools are under the supervision of
Superintendent Durell Thompson. In the fall of 1978 the Long Lake school was
closed and the students are now bussed to Leola.

There has traditionally been great concern for upgrading academic areas in the
Leola school curriculum, and several programs deserve mention. During National
Library Week in 1958 the grade school joined the Library Club of America, a
nationwide, non-profit organization whose purpose it was to encourage children
to read good books. All organizations in Leola financially supported this
"Readers Are Leaders" program. This activity is still part of the program and
ribbons are presented to participants on elementary Awards Day.

A developmental reading program under Mrs. Berniece Pade was added to the
curriculum in 1967. The following year Marvin Maule, elementary principal
introduced the departmental reading plan under Title I. Teachers involved were:
Mrs. Phyl Young, grades one and two; Mrs. Lois Merkel, grades three and four;
Mrs. Berniece Pade, grades five and six.

Special Education: In the spring of 1972, Mrs. Jean Guffey, who was employed as
the English teacher for grades eight, nine and ten, recognized a need for a
speech therapy program in the school, as there was no special education program
for the handicapped children in the district. Mrs. Guffey wrote a project
prospectus which was accepted by the State Superintendent of Public
Instruction, Don Barnhart, and by the South Dakota Office for Exceptional
Children. The project proposal generated funding for the school year 1972-73
and the speech therapy program was under way. It was called the McPherson
County Communication Disorders Program, and Mrs. Guffey provided speech therapy
at both Leola and Eureka schools for three years. The program continued in the
Leola school system and expanded to include services for language delayed
students. In compliance with the law, speech and language services are
available to any child between the ages of 0-21.

        Left to Right: Jean Guffey, Marlys Thurow, Lois Merkel. Seated: Diane
        Tschappat.

In the spring of 1981, Mrs. Guffey, with the help of Superintendent Clark
Schemp, encouraged the school board to offer services for learning disabled and
gifted students. Mr. Schemp secured funding and Mrs. Marlys Thurow, the Title I
reading teacher began testing students during the school year 1981-82. The
following year Mrs. Thurow was employed as a part-time Special Education
teacher, serving children with learning difficulties as well as those with
exceptional abilities. Because of the broad spectrum and need of the program,
as well as its success, she was employed in 1983-84 as a full-time Special
Education teacher.

        Back row: Dorothy Kolb and Candice Hilmoe. Front row: Julia Opitz and
        Arnie Schock.

        Back row: Betty Maule, Bernice Turnwall, Janice Jasmer, Yvonne
        Morrison. Front row: Sue Ackerson, Brenda White, Betty Hemen and
        Richard Jasmer.

In 1983 Superintendent Durell Thompson instituted beginning courses in typing,
computer, home economics and shop for seventh and eighth grade students. The
program is operating on a nine-weeks rotation basis in the high school
classrooms with high school instructors. It is but the latest in a long history
of progressive developments that have marked the traditions of the Leola
schools, and a trend that is certain to continue as long as the citizens of
McPherson County value and give priority to the education of our young people.

        Leola High School: A Centennial History

From 1909, when the board of education voted to extend the course of study
available to its students through the ninth and tenth grades, to the present,
the community of Leola has demonstrated over and over again a strong commitment
to the education of its young people.

In 1909, after the history-making decision, Principal W. K. Bishop was handed
responsibility for organizing and teaching the ninth and tenth classes being
newly incorporated into the school curriculum. In time he was aided by
elementary teacher Ruth Reue, who agreed to teach a class in high school German
each day after she had finished her regular duties. In 1909, the ninth and
tenth grade curriculum was brought into compliance with state guidelines, and
three years later, eleventh and twelfth grade courses of study were added to
the curriculum.

In 1916, Herbert O. Arndt became the first student to complete the four-year
course of study at Leola High School under Principal L. F. Slocum and Assistant
Lillian Streit. Arndt took an additional year of post-graduate study and took
part in LHS's first commencement exercises in 1917, along with graduates Esther
Arndt, Lyle Clayton and Fred Hepperle.

Class Motto: Green, but growing.

Class Colors: Purple and Gold.

Class Flower: Lily of the Valley.

Class Roll:

Esther P. Arndt
Lyle G. Clayton
Fred J. Hepperle

Post-Graduate
Herbert O. Arndt

Assistant, Lillian Streit.

From these humble beginnings, Leola High School has grown into a modern
institution with well-equipped classrooms and laboratories, a staff of 15 men
and women who work with Leola's high school students on either a full-time or
part-time basis and a wide-ranging curriculum of academic, vocational and
interest courses from which students can choose.

The basic curriculum has changed relatively little over the past 70 years. Now,
as then, students are required to take four years of English in order to be
eligible for graduation. Other staples of the academic curriculum include math
courses such as Algebra I, geometry, Algebra II and advanced math; science
courses such as general science, biology, chemistry and physics; and social
science courses such as world history, U.S. history and U.S. government.

The major changes in curriculum that have evolved over the past 70 years have
been in the area of vocational training. A vocational agriculture lab was a
feature of the first permanent school structure built in 1909 and vocational
agriculture courses continued to be taught until climbing enrollments and a
need for space caused them to be dropped from the curriculum. Agriculture
returned briefly during the 1940's and again from 1959 until 1970, under Mr.
Loren Gill, but they are no longer being taught at LHS. Instead, their place
has been taken by industrial arts courses. When the north wing was added to the
existing structure in 1963, it included a well-equipped shop area. The
industrial arts department, currently headed by John Daly, offers courses in
mechanical drawing, welding, mechanics and wood-working to the students of LHS.

Home economics was also a part of the early LHS curriculum, until it, like
vocational agriculture, was dropped in 1924 because of lack of space. The 1963
addition, however, also included space for a home economics department, and
courses in home ec are again in the curriculum, under the direction of Alverde
Daniel.

Probably no area of the high school curriculum has grown and changed to the
extent that the business department has. While typing was offered to LHS
students as far back as the 1940's, students were required to furnish their own
typewriters. By 1940, however, the school had committed itself to the support
of a modern business program, which now offers courses in typing, advanced
typing, shorthand, office practice, business math, accounting and computers.

In 1969, LHS's office education program, under Doris Hepperle, became
vocationally certified. This certification allows the school to be reimbursed
for 50 percent of the cost of all new equipment purchased and has resulted in
LHS's business students being given the opportunity to train on the latest
office equipment.

Hepperle was also responsible for the 1973 organization of a local chapter of
the Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA). FBLA is an organization open to
any high school student currently enrolled in a business course; its purpose is
to promote the American free enterprise system through community service and
various business-related activities. Since its inception the local group has
been among the most active FBLA organizations in the state. Each year it has
sent delegates to both the state and national conventions, including Susie
Zulk, who placed ninth in business math competition at the 1979 national
convention in New Orleans. The 1983-84 chapter boasts 35 members, including
Michelle Brandner, State President, and Cindi Schmidt, State Secretary.

In 1982, LHS made the leap into the Computer Age when the School Board
authorized the purchase of six Commodore PET computers and an Apple II. These
purchases made it possible for LHS juniors to begin learning the fundamentals
of computer programming in a course taught by Principal Marvin Maule. In 1983
Miss Brenda Steiger joined the staff of LHS as a full-time computer teacher.

Available to LHS freshmen is a course in driver education, under Duane Daniel.
Daniel also serves as LHS's guidance counselor, with responsibilities in the
areas of testing, career planning and personal counseling.

Besides the services of a high school counselor, LHS students also have access
to a well-stocked library and media center. Prior to 1957 library facilities
were relatively primitive. Shelving was provided to house the books the school
had accumulated. But since the school had no qualified librarian, the books
remained unclassified on the shelves and finding specific volumes could be
quite time consuming. In 1957 Lillian Kindelspire became the school's first
librarian, setting up both elementary and high school libraries with the aid of
the loyal members of the LHS Library Club. In 1968 the library was moved to its
present quarters in the new south wing. Throughout the years the library grew
from a collection of books to also include an audio-visual center equipped with
opaque projector, over-head projectors, record players, tape recorders,
filmstrip projectors, a movie projector, and video cassette recorder. Today the
combined elementary and secondary library houses nearly 8,000 volumes and
operates on an annual budget of more than $4,000, all of which are the
responsibility of librarian Virginia Becktold.

In addition to academic and vocational courses, a variety of special interest
courses are available to Leola high school students. These courses, which were
once available only on an extra-curricular basis, have now made their way into
the high school curriculum. Among them are such recent additions as journalism
and drama, both of which are currently under the direction of Julie George.
Although both courses have appeared briefly in the curriculum in the past, they
have been considered primarily extra-curricular activities . Beginning in 1981,
however, organized classes took over responsibility for publication of both the
LHS yearbook, the Buccaneer, and the school newspaper, LHS Live. The Buccaneer,
first published in 1938 and published consecutively each year except 1939-1944,
has won All-State ratings in competition sponsored by the South Dakota High
School Press Association six of the past nine years. LHS Live made its first
appearance in 1981, taking over from the Pirate Chatter, which had been
published by the students of LHS since 1928.

Dramatics and oral interpretation (declam), which were both extra-curricular
staples in the past, have been missing at LHS since 1976. School records show
that as early as the 1920's drama was an important activity at LHS, with
students producing as many as three plays and an operetta each year, even
though the school had no stage facilities and students were required to make
use of Schuchardt's Royal Theatre for their productions. As the number of
activities on the school calendar increased and the number of students
available for participation in dramatic presentations declined, drama
disappeared from the scene. The spring of 1984 should bring about a return that
is long overdue.

Another activity that has grown widely both in size and scope is the music
program. Information on the music program at LHS before the 1970's is scattered
and limited; however, records go back as far as 1935, when a number of LHS
students participated in a South Dakota music contest. Since LHS had no formal
music program at the time, these students were probably being taught outside
the school by teachers giving lessons in their homes.

There is no information about directors until 1941 when R. Olmsted and C. P.
Sandeen served as directors of vocal and instrumental music. In 1956 Marvin
Maule joined the school faculty to direct the music department. In that year
there were 18 members in the band, five of whom were drummers and none of whom
were beginners. Perhaps the most important accomplishment of Maule's tenure was
the organization of a beginner's program down through the fifth grade. After
that the music program at LHS started to take off.

        Leola High School Band--Back row: Martin Haase, Vance Durnil, Orvin
        Hieb, Marion Heupel, Evelyn Geffre, James Weisser and Melvin Tuscher.
        Front row: Leo Geffre, Allen Kulm, Stanley Kein, Harry Linder, Alma
        Eichelberg, Doryce Koerner, Luella Maier and Joyce Brosz.

In 1966, Don Wade became the new music director and organized the first
magazine drive to raise funds for the music program. In 1967, LHS singers took
first place in the Snow Queen Talent Contest. In 1968, Mick Guffey took over as
band and chorus director, and in 1969, new band uniforms were purchased. In
1970, Julie Hilgemann made LHS history when she was selected as the first
student to represent the school in All-State Band. The music department also
performed its first musical, "Oklahoma." In 1971, the music department split,
with Guffey taking the instrumental section and Susan Wolf the vocal. In 1972,
LHS musicians broke a contest record with 12 superior ratings at the regional
music contest.

In 1973, Vocal Director Jim Ochsner organized the first LHS Swing Choir; he
also began giving vocal lessons during the school day. Another musical, "South
Pacific," was performed in 1973, followed by "Lil Abner" in 1974, "Oliver" in
1975, and "You're A Good Man, Charlie Brown" in 1976. In 1975, Mike Maule was
selected as the first LHS student to perform with the South Dakota Honors
Choir. In 1977, the Swing Choir bought uniforms and went on their first tour,
to Sioux Falls, where they performed at the American Family Insurance
Convention. In 1978, the Stage Band joined the Swing Choir on tour. In 1980,
the Swing Choir won the South Dakota Snow Queen Talent Contest, toured Pierre
and sang at the State Capitol for Governor William Janklow.

High school athletics have always been a cornerstone of American small town
life. Athletic contests continue to be major social events, and local athletic
achievements are a source of pride for the entire community. It would be
impossible to summarize all the athletic achievements of Leola High School
students, but to state that LHS athletes have been successful overall would be
essentially correct.

Leola High School's history has also been studded with many exceptional
achievements. One such achievement was Miles Blumhardt's five-touchdown night
against Tripp in the Dakota Dome in 1978. Blumhardt's performance won for LHS a
No. 1 ranking in the state football poll and for Blumhardt the Hertz Number One
Award for best athletic performance in South Dakota for that year. In 1979 the
Pirates dropped from 11 to nine man football ranks but once again made it
through the season undefeated to retain their No. 1 state rating for a second
consecutive year.

Other outstanding years are recalled also, such as the 1937-38 season when LHS
went 6-0 and won the North Central Conference in football and went 16-4 in
basketball.

The 1959-60 season also stands out as one of Leola's finest. The football team
went 6-0. The basketball team went 26-1, losing only to Selby in the Region.
The track team won the NCC championship and the Region II crown, while tying
for fourth at the State Meet.

The 1973-74 season was also a standout for the Bucs, with a 9-0, No. l-rated
football team and a region championship in basketball. In all, Pirate
basketball teams have won 17 district championships and have gone to the state
tournament three times.

The Pirate "cinder-pounders" have also won numerous track titles and have fared
well at the State Track Meets.

LHS has always been a contender for championships, and its athletes have
represented the community well at both the local and the state level, a source
of continuing pride for the city of Leola.

Perhaps the biggest day of the school year at LHS is Homecoming Day--or "Pirate
Day," as it has always been called. The first Pirate Day was held in 1926, and
there has been one annually ever since, although some aspects of the
celebration have changed. Today only the elementary students dress in
costume--and few of the costumes represent pirates. Homecoming festivities are
kicked off on Friday morning with the coronation of a king and queen (Mark
Maule and Leisha Fauth reigned over the 1983 festivities), the various classes
and organizations present humorous skits to entertain the community, and the
entire student body repairs downtown to watch a "real" parade. The day ends
with the traditional homecoming football game, and, in most years, a homecoming
dance.

The second biggest event of the year is the juniorsenior banquet. Early
banquets were held in private homes, but by 1926 class size mandated that the
festivities be held in a more spacious area. The 1926 banquet was held in the
Methodist Church parlors, while in 1927 the Masonic Temple played host to the
event. Decorations were limited to nut cups, place cards and a few crepe paper
streamers, and no dance was held. In later years the event was moved to the
school gym, decorations became far more lavish and bands were hired to provide
music for a prom. Although the junior-senior banquet continues to be the most
important social event of the school year, the prom was discontinued once again
in 1981 due to poor attendance. One last attempt will be made in 1984 to bring
it back.

What lies ahead for LHS? The current enrollment at Leola High School stands at
98, approximately where it was before consolidation. Enrollment peaked at 222
during the period between 1963 and 1975 when the school was feeling the effects
of the post-war baby boom. Declining enrollment will certainly affect the
future of LHS, but in what ways and to what extent only tomorrow can tell.
