                        TOWNSHIPS

                Arena Township

Homesteaders, arriving in 1884 in Arena Township, found a hunter's paradise
called Arena Valley. (The bulk of the Ordway Conservancy acreage lie in Arena
Township.) Some of the earlier settlers were: Reuben and Samuel Daugherty,
Henry and Johanna Renschler, Philipp Reiling, Samuel M. Brachway, Heinrich
Goehring, Ebenezer and Rueben Craig, Frederich Rueb, George Heupel, J. M.
Brickney and Nickolas Lechner.

The first school in Arena Township was organized in 1891 with the following
officers: Philip Reiling, chairman; Reuben Craig, clerk and J. M. Brickney,
treasurer. As Arena prospered, three more schools were added, Kurle No. 1,
Renschler No. 2, and Rueb No. 3.

A post office was started in Arena on Section 30, August 8, 1917 with Fred A.
Rueb as Postmaster. It was moved to Leola in 1922.

In describing family life in 1884, Fred A. Rueb recalls that his father worked
during the summer of that year for an Edmund's County farmer for 25 cents per
day. The family continuing to live on the homestead, added to the income by
gathering and selling buffalo bones. The following year, 1885, brought an
excellent grain crop and the elder Rueb was able to earn four times as much or
$1.00 per day, which was comparable to others in 1885. Recalling the storm of
1888, Fred related: the storm raged throughout the night and when the family
awoke at noon the next day, they found their house pitch dark covered with
snow. The shanty doors, hung to open outward, were banked shut with heavy snow.
The only exit was the man-sized chimney. His father climbed up through this,
returning with straw to burn and hay for the oxen, which were in a partition
next to the shanty. This chimney served as a doorway until the storm subsided.

        Back row--left to right: Alma Hoffman, Leo Hoffman, Della Neuharth
        Irene Binder, Theo Neuharth, Otellia Heupel, Ella Feiock, Melvin
        Morrison, Regina Heupel, Elmer Feiock, Albena Hoffman, Allen Morrison,
        Lillian Heupel. Front row: Ephriam Nies, Otto Heupel, Harold Heupel,
        and Harry Hoffman.

Many of the early settlers left Arena Township but three generations of the
George Heupel family remained in the area, where grandson Harold continued
farming until 1969 when the family sold their farm and moved to Aberdeen.

                Carl Township

In 1884 when the surveyors moved into Carl Township they found 15 squatters;
Simon Olson, George Riley, Hans Nelson, Annie and M. D. Haugestal, Carl
Schuchardt, Harvey Brown, J. H. Parke, Wm. McGraham, Dewey R. Burke, David A.
Kingsley, August Grabowska, Julius Kesser, Howard Warren and John Murdoch .

Carl Township was named in honor of Carl Schuchardt, one of the earlier
settlers. Carl Schuchardt won local recognition as a thresher. His first steam
engine was a Huber portable that was pulled about the county by four oxen.
Schuchardt and Bela Dexter teamed up and went about the area threshing for
others for many years. His next power unit was a Huber traction steam engine,
said to be the first traction steamer in the county.

March 12, 1885, County Supt. D. B. Strait met with the county commissioners and
recommended the organizing of Carl Township as a school district, and on April
18, 1885 at an election held in the home of Carl Schuchardt, the following
officers were elected: J. W. Mansfield, director; David Kingsley, clerk; and P.
H. Carlsgard, treasurer.

There were two schools, with 34 children ranging from seven to 20 years of age,
in the year of 1885. School was held May, June, July and August during that
year. Mr. James Evins and Miss Addie Reeves were the first teachers. They each
received a wage of $25.00 per month. Tuition charged for scholars coming in
from Willow Township was 50 cents per week. As the township population
increased, two more schools were added. The four schools were located in
sections 7. 14, 30, and 34.

        Back row--left to right: Allan Liedle, Eugene Kline, Elmer Liedle,
        Alice Liedle. Third row: Harold Haux, Caroline Haux, Gloria Lapka,
        Violet Haux. Second row: Arlene Liedle, Eldon Haux, Orville Liedle,
        Dorothy Kline. Front row: Merlin Fauth and Norma Haux.

Carl Township was organized as a civil township in 1913. They elected a
three-man council consisting of Edward D. Olson, George Lapka and Frank O.
Schuchardt; a clerk, Hans Carlsgard; and a treasurer, Edward J. Meyer. It is
unusual for one man to hold the same office for many years, but Carl Township
had such a man. Edward J. Meyer, treasurer, held that office until 1949 when
his son, Gilbert, was chosen to continue on in his place. The combined total of
the years the Meyers have served Carl Township is 71 years.

Carl remains an organized township in order to maintain its roads. The present
day officers are: Gilbert Meyer, treasurer; Dominic Kallas, clerk; and Jim
Zandstra, supervisor.

                Dewey Township

Dewey Township was not settled until 1886. Perhaps the fact that Dewey is a
ranching area accounts for the reason the surrounding townships were
homesteaded first. Some of Dewey's early settlers were Johann Neifer, Johannes
Kranzler, Sr., John Reynold, William M. Morris, Jacob Jundt and the Eva Adam
family.

One of the first ranches in Dewey Township was the Morris and Davis Ranch,
situated 16 miles southwest of Leola. This ranch was later known as the Matt
Kindelspire ranch. The Kindelspire ranch covered from 2,500 to 3,000 acres of
land, and was known as one of the larger ranches in the area. The Kindelspires
ran about 100 head of horses and 700 head of cattle. Matt Kindelspire employed
at least three ranch hands year-round, and during haying season he employed
between 15 and 20 men. Many times they camped out on the prairie and cooked
over the campfires during the haying season. Matt's son, Gene, was included in
the group often. Gene was between six and eight years old at the time.

The first school of the township was organized in 1912 at the request of Matt
Kindelspire, who was one of the first officers. One of the houses on the ranch
was converted to a schoolhouse. Mrs. P. E. Ehrenfeldt was the first teacher at
this school. Three of the first pupils are still living in the vicinity. They
are: Fred Jundt and Gene Kindelspire, Leola; and Viola Nelson, Aberdeen.

It was most unusual to have running water in rural areas in 1917, but the
Kindelspires accomplished this feat. They had a cement reservoir built on a
hill (at the ranch) which provided water for the household and the livestock.
Windmills pumped the water uphill and gravity flow brought it down through
pipes to the desired points at the house and the barns.

Not far from the Kindelspire ranch lived another of the earlier homesteaders,
Jacob Jundt, Sr., who settled in Dewey in 1892. Jacob's son, Fred, was born in
1899, and lived there all his life until moving into Leola. Fred attended
school on the Kindelspire ranch. As a youngster he helped his father thresh
with a family rig. Fred married a neighboring township girl, Rose Mayer, and
moved to a farm near his parents. Fred and Rose built a large barn on their
farm and this was used for many barn dances, including wedding celebrations.
They charged 50 cents per person, but if the neighbor was really down and out,
they let him in out of the goodness of their hearts. Fred remembers, "One night
a man threw a match into the hay below the loft." With over 300 people in the
barn, Fred had to act quickly. Jumping from the loft into the burning area, he
extinguished the fire himself.

All was not pleasure though, for in 1926, the Jundts recall a terrible blizzard
that came up suddenly and sent Fred out looking for 200 head of livestock. He
and his brother rode on horses, looking for their cattle and sheep in the
ferocious storm. Rose spent some anxious hours waiting for them to return. They
had to give up until morning, when they found that their cattle and sheep had
wandered quite a few miles away.

        Dewey No. 1 school pupils.

As Dewey Township grew, another school was added in 1934, but by the early
'70's they were closed. Even though farms and ranches change ownership, Dewey
Township continues to thrive, with six family farms at the present time.

                Harrison Township

Harrison Township was an unorganized township governed by the board of county
commissioners. The first school was organized in 1892 with the following
officers: John Heidt, chairman; John Lammle, clerk; and Christian D. Rath,
treasurer.

Some of the early settlers homesteading in 1886 were Amalia Stuber, Konrad
Feickert, Jr., Mahund Sweiden, Konrad Feickert, Sr., Phillip Ehresman, Johann
Spitzer, Christina Spitzer, Jacob Sandmaier, Sam Sweiden, Bertram H. Bundy,
Joseph Beshara, Elias Shama, Jacob Forsch, Heinrich Gimbel and George Shama.

Settlers Bundy, Beshara and the Shamas were of Syrian descent. They homesteaded
in groups, later selling to other settlers. The Syrians were not farmers at
heart. They were known to farm only the low ground, leaving the higher ground
intact. It was rumored that they took life a little easier than their
Anglo-Saxon and Germanic neighbors. Housekeeping was kept on the lighter side.
A good example is the method of making pancakes. They did not bother with using
a pan; the batter was poured on the range to bake. This group of people usually
dressed more shabbily than the other settlers, although they owned finer
clothing.

Johann Spitzer's daughter, Elisabeth (Hoffman), narrated in later years as to
how the brick houses were built. A mixture of clay, straw and water (the brick
batter)


        A Sod house.

was put into a frame about 14x6x6 inches in size and left to dry until it held
its shape. Then it was taken out of the frame and another batch was poured.
After the bricks were dry, another clay mixture was made and used as mortar to
cement the bricks together. On the roof of the house, a little lumber was used
and covered with this clay mixture. These materials prevailed until hit by hard
rain or hail storms, after which another layer of clay was added. Floors were
made of clay also. Instead of scrubbing the floor, a little clay was mixed with
water and spread on the floor with a rag and then sprinkled with a little sand
to give it a shine. The stove for cooking and heating in these houses was built
in. It was constructed of clay brick with an oven large enough to hold from ten
to 12 loaves of bread at one time. The oven had to be heated long enough to
accumulate enough heat for the entire baking. Ashes had to be removed and all
the bread put in at once.

A house of that type of construction was erected on the Johann Spitzer
homestead around 1900 and was in use until about 1952.

Travel was a slow process for the pioneers. Oxen were used in many cases to
transport the families to town or to church. No one got anywhere in a hurry.

The power furnished by the oxen enabled the farmer to plow his ground, later
sowing the seed by hand. The animals were unpredictable. If they were well
broken and the weather was cool, they would plow steadily, but if the weather
was warm, it was hard to predict when they would lie down. If a lake was close
by, they might head for the lake to stand in water to cool off. Perhaps if the
operator had followed the oxen into the lake he would have had the same
necessary cooling effects on his hard-tried patience.

Many stories are told by the homesteaders of the wandering bands of gypsies
traveling through the territory shortly after WWI. The gypsies had a devious
technique of begging. The gypsy menfolk would stay out in the yard keeping the
farmer occupied while the gypsy womenfolk would enter the house, plying their
trade. It was related by one housewife that during one of those missions, after
the gypsies left, she started looking around, and to her amazement realized she
had given away all of the food in the house, leaving an empty larder for her
and her family. This all-out generosity was not uncommon, for many of the
homesteaders held the firm belief that if they didn't give all they asked, the
gypsies would put a curse on them. The gypsies traveled in groups, and nearly
every week a new clan would travel through.

Progress has left its mark on the township, for many of the farms are either
gone or combined into larger farming operations. The official 1982 farm
directory lists ten family farms in Harrison Township.

                Highland Township

Highland Township contains an abundance of high rises and low lands,
consequently the name, Highland, applies very well.

The northern part of the township was settled as early as 1885. Some of the
energetic men were: Karl Zenker, John and Jacob Maier, John Jesser, John J.
Rath, Christ Gugel, Christ Voegele, Carl Schock, George Schott, Gottlieb Wolff,
the Magdalina Kiesz family, Fred Lahman, Charlie Gray, Jacob Hohnecker and John
Goeschel, Sr. The southern part was settled a few years later by John Fred
Junge, Jacob Schlenker, O. C. Gibson, F. Schumack, Christ Frieh, Reuben
Daughtery, Fred and Tracy Meidinger.

Fred and Tracy were a brother-sister team. Fred homesteaded on Section 20 and
Tracy proved up a homestead about two miles east of Fred's. Tracy lived in a
little shack and had her own well on the homestead. Smoke had to be seen coming
out of her chimney every day to prove to all that she was unwavering. Herbert
Meidinger lives on the land homesteaded by Fred.

Harold Weisser, who came to Highland in 1906, remembers the Rueben Daughtery
Shorthorn ranch that Rueben and his sister operated. Rueben plowed a wide fire
guard all around his ranch, so when the fires raged, his land and cattle were
well protected.

Harold told of the hardships of the industrious, religious settlers. Many times
the homesteaders had to walk to town for flour and supplies, carrying them home
many miles. The more fortunate ones used oxen for transportation. Sometimes the
homesteaders formed partnerships and bought headers to harvest their grain.

John Goeshel, Sr. settled in Highland Township around 1890. John left his
homeland (Austria-Hungary) to avoid military service. He traveled throughout
Europe, finally working his way to London, England, where he took a job in the
shipyards. While they were loading a ship bound for the U.S., he hid on board.
After two days at sea, the Captain discovered him. Unable to return the fellow,
he put him to work in the kitchen. When the ship approached Ellis Island, John,
knowing he would be sent back, jumped overboard and swam to shore. He stayed
undercover until he could dry his clothes. John found work in Philadelphia, PA
and through this opportunity he went to Wisconsin working as a lumberjack.
While in Wisconsin he heard about South Dakota. He caught a ride to Aberdeen,
then Eureka, and from there to the township. After homesteading he sent for the
girlfriend he had left in Wisconsin. John spent the rest of his years in
Highland, apparently finding a land that suited him. He served his township
well, for he was Justice of Peace and a school board member.

        Highland No. 3 schoolhouse (1927).

Schools were organized a little later than most, since the township was more
sparsely settled than the neighboring townships. Records disclose that a school
was operating in the township in 1891. By 1906 there were two schools in the
northern part, located in Section 8 and Section 11. Two more were added in the
southern part in approximately 1911, one in Section 26 and one in Section 29.

One of the first teachers was Mrs. John Goeschel, Sr. The 1906-1915 records
show that John Hohman, Mrs. Gugel, Mrs. Botton, C. B. Clark, Josie V. Bryan,
Mrs. M. Weisser, and Phrene Junge taught in Highland schools.

        1922-1923 school boys. Back row--left to right: Herbert Meidinger, Ted
        Heupel, Erwin Loebs, Fred Benter, and Art Loebs. Middle row: Fred
        Meidinger, Art Kolb, Julius Heupel, Reinhold Frieh. Front row: Emil
        Kolb, Leo Kolb and Gust Kolb.

Some of the homesteaders' descendants are still living on the farms in
Highland, and they continue to practice conservation and improve farming
conditions. There are 13 farms left in Highland Township.

                Hoffman Township

Near springs and potholes along creeks and runs in various parts of the county,
and especially noticeable in Hoffman Township, is evidence of camps where
Indians pitched their tents. Particularly noticed, due to the great numbers,
are the teepee rings found on hilltops. The summer landscape, with abundance of
prairie grasses, was the great Sioux hunting ground where herds of buffalo,
deer and antelope roamed. There were many kinds of waterfowl populating the
sloughs.

There were three prominent Indian tribes that passed through on their hunting
trips. They were the Sioux or Dakota, the Cheyenne, and the Mandan, although
only a small fraction of the Mandan were here.

The Indians depended greatly on the wildlife to provide them with food,
clothing, shelter and fuel. Numerous plants were for medicine. Many of the
plants found in Hoffman Township were: Leadplant leaves (crushed for tea); the
Pasque flower which they used for rheumatism; Black Samson roots for a
toothache cure; dotted gay feather roots for starch, and American plum and
chokecherry berries for fruit.

In 1889 settlers came, and one of the first to appear was Fred Hoffman. Fred
homesteaded and shortly after, he helped his four younger brothers, Christoph,
Phillip, Carl, and Christian settle in the area. Since there were so many of
them homesteading in this area, it seemed appropriate to name the township
"Hoffman."

Hoffman Township citizens, like all the early people in the county, desired
churches and schools. Hope Lutheran Church was organized January 8, 1894 under
the leadership of Pastor Martin Reischauer. There were nine charter members.

Hoffman had two schools, one along the section line (north of 24-127-68, south
of 13-127-68) and another in Section 5-127-68. The school in Section 5 was
called Hilltop school, due to the fact that it was built on a high hill and the
school-age youngsters romped and sledded down it in the wintertime. It not only
attracted the youngsters, but many adults likewise. A controversy developed
over the location of this school among the settlers. Some wanted it moved to
another place and others wanted it to stay. The school mysteriously burned down
at one time, only to be rebuilt at the very same site. This school closed in
1966.

        Last pupils to attend Hoffman Hilltop school (1966). Back row--left to
        right: Dennis Ottenbacher, Vickie Lechner, Arlen Gehring, Valerie
        Lechner, Roger Feickert, and Pattie Hoffman. Middle row: Polly
        Ottenbacher, Nancy Ottenbacher, Wade Lechner, Jim Hoffman, Randy
        Lechner, Peter Feickert. Front row: Charlotte Hoffman, Marsha Lechner,
        Clyde Ottenbacher, Brenda Hoffman and Karley Hoffman.

Hoffman citizens voted to become an organized township in 1953. The main
purpose for organizing was to gain better roads. The first officers were: Leo
Hoffman, Jacob Gehring, and Elvin Feickert, supervisors; Gottlieb, Gienger,
clerk; and Dan Hoffman, treasurer. Hoffman is still an organized township at
the present time. Present officers are: chairman, Doug Cox; clerk, Curtis
Hoffman; and treasurer, Wilton Hoffman; supervisors, Gary Hoffman, and Doug
Cox.

In 1984 there are 11 occupied farms.

                Howard Township

The first record of homesteaders in Howard Township is found in McPherson
County's 1884 real estate tax list. Some of the early pioneers were: Frank A.
Child, George J. Potter, Prescott B. Potter, Frank Slocum, Wallace McMaster,
Daniel McGrady, Mrs. J. E. Norton, Frederick Norton, M. B. Wynn, and Etta M.
Strait. There were ten people listed as personal property owners. All but one
paid their taxes in full. By 1886, there were 21 taxpayers listed in Howard.

The first school in Howard Township was organized in 1885 by an election held
March 31, 1885. Elected officers were George Finical, director; George Bingham,
clerk; William Conn, treasurer. The school was located in Section 26. Some of
the early teachers were: Marion B. Hall, Ida H. Calkins, Emma Huntly, Maud
Lucy, Florence Hall, and Pearl Magee.

        1900 memento from schoolteacher with list of pupils.

November 22, 1906, a post office was established in Onange Slocum's home
(Section 25). It was there a short time, for in December of 1907, it was moved
to Leola.

Howard Township was organized as a civil township in 1918, remaining so until
1966.

Many of the early pioneers became discouraged and sold their land, moving to
other greener (?) areas. Some remained and raised their families on the
homesteads. Joe Stephan decided to continue on. He homesteaded around 1888.
Later he took a wife and the two of them lived on his homestead. After his
marriage, the need for money forced Joe to go to North Dakota to work with a
threshing crew. Leaving his wife behind, Joe worked the rest of the summer and
fall, returning with around $200 for the winter months. He earned a reputation
as a knowledgeable horseman. He raised and trained horses, later selling teams
to people in and outside Leola. It was not uncommon for horse buyers to come to
Leola on the train and visit Stephan's farm. Joe was particularly proud of a
dapplegray team he sold for $650, an extraordinary price for that period of
time. Most teams sold for $100 to $15()

        Howard No. 2 school pupils in 1942.

The Stephans raised three daughters who remained in the Leola region. They
retired, moving to Leola in 1927 and Elizabeth (their youngest daughter) and
Walter Kline moved on the homestead, farming there for many years.

Farming practices change and in the '80's larger farms are the trend. Howard
Township has around seven farms at the present time.

                Koto Township

Anticipating the survey of township subdivisions during the summer of 1883,
settlers of Koto Township began in May with the arrival of the following
families: J. Bergoff, B. E. Dexter, J. L. Dow, J. A. Kelly, F. L. Newman, and
F. Rolfe. By late 1884 claims had been filed on 70 percent of the available
township land. Of the 35 initial homesteaders in 1884, six finally purchased
their land while 16 became owners after living on the land for the full five
years. The remaining 13 claimants relinquished title to the homestead land.
Using the preemption method, settlers acquired 31 quarters by living on the
land for six months and paid $1.25 for each acre.

It is estimated that in 1884 there were 66 farm dwellings in Koto Township.
This is in contrast to the 12 active farms in 1984. The typical homesteader 100
years ago cultivated 40 acres of land while his home was about 400 square feet
in size. This is in comparison to the preemption settler who usually cultivated
15 acres and lived in a home of 270 square feet. The average claimant was 36
years old. Ten percent were women and nearly 60 percent of the men were
married, only a few were born in a foreign country. Settlers usually came from
states such as Wisconsin, Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio.

The town of Koto was established in June 1883 where Koto School No. 1 stood
until recent years (SW 1/4 of the SE 1/4 of Section 22) and also on the area
across the present east-west section line road (N 1/2 of the NE 1/4 of Section
27). The property was initially owned by Dr. Julius Bergoff but in April 1884
it was sold to Mary B. Dow. She was the wife of James L. Dow, a settler on the
NW 1/4 of Section 27. Originally Koto, which was platted with streets and
avenues by a Mr. H. Barnard, located on the SW 1/4 of Section 22, was 30 shown
by the land surveyors in July 1883.

The activity of Koto centered around Dr. Julius Bergoff, a Russian-born
physician and surgeon; James L. Dow, a bank cashier who came from Wisconsin
(and in May 1884 was named as one of three county commissioners appointed by
the outgoing Territorial Governor Nehemiah Ordway), and two lawyers--John A.
Kelley of Wisconsin and Zechariah Spitler of Indiana. In 1883 their primary
interest in the Koto community was the development of flourishing businesses
and law practices. All four had prospered, were politically active and were
well regarded in the town of Frederick prior to moving to Koto.

During Koto's existence, it had board walks, a post office, a large hotel, two
printing offices, two land offices, a blacksmith shop, two stores, a $1,400
schoolhouse that was built in August 1884, and several family dwellings. The
first postmaster, Oshea A. Fowler, was appointed June 22, 1883, and was
succeeded by Dr. Bergoff on October 3, 1883, who was followed by storeowner B.
H. Hoag. One of the printing offices, the McPherson County News, was founded by
Dr. Bergoff in May 1883; Erwin O. Blair edited the paper for the doctor. In
August 1884, Dr. Bergoff sold a half interest in the paper to Lyman T. Boucher,
an Illinois attorney by training, who became the editor of the News by
November.

In 1884 the location of the McPherson County seat was to be left up to the vote
of the people. In a tough campaign, Koto lost the election and began to fade.
By 1886, the principal businesses of Koto had closed and the people were drawn
towards Leola.

        Koto School No. 2 group of pupils in 1910-1911.

Koto Township was organized as a civil township on April 12, 1913. First
officers were Charles Fosler, John Lapka, and Peter Geffre as supervisors;
Hiram H. Yost, clerk; William H. Woodall, treasurer; Evan Jones, assessor; D.
R. Witte and Mark R. Warnick, justice of the peace; and Ed Hickman and Eugene
Morrison, constables. For nearly 50 years Koto operated three rural schools and
maintained its township roads . In August 1967 Koto ceased operating as a civil
township. An era had passed leaving as its only trace of existence a lone
marker on the prairie--a steel pole where the school playground once sported a
"Giants" swing.

                Leola Township

As a political subdivision of McPherson County, the boundaries of Leola
Township were first established by a surveying crew in 1880. However, it was
not until the first settlers began staking out their claims in 1883 that the
township was given a name.

According to statements by land claimants, the first settlement of Leola
Township began in May 1883. With the arrival of spring weather, five
individuals, John Murrie, Walter Cavanagh, Henry N. Archer, Agnes M. Thomas,
and Lilian F. Longee came into the territory to settle and claim their home
land. John Murrie led this group by settling on the NW 1/4 of Section 20, on
May 5. By July 2, Murrie, a single, 27-year-old lawyer, was appointed as the
community's first postmaster. When the surveying crew had completed its mission
in September of '83, 35 sooners were located on federal land. Their presence
was recorded on a township map by the surveyors, although the filing of claims
was not accepted until November 27, 1883.

H. Z. Moulton, S. P. Hardenbrook, Captain E. D. Haynes, J. Hooker, A. Williams,
and O. J. Roe all filed preemption claims for their land. John Darlington
became identified with Leola Township when he filed a timber claim on the SE
1/4 of Section 32. George Chamberlain was the first county commissioner elected
from Leola Township. This Illinois farmer homesteaded on the NE 1/4 of Section
30. Several others arriving in early 1883 in Leola Township included Henry
Young, Wilson Dively, and Tarquin Franklyn. Two other community leaders,
Charles N. Herreid and Wendell W. Cornwall, filed their preemption claims in
February and April in 1884. These two lawyers had accompanied H. Z. Moulton, J.
Darlington, S. P. Hardenbrook in the first effort to organize McPherson County
on March 6, 1884.

It was not until 1884 that the bulk of the township's settlers had arrived to
claim nearly every acre, outside of the land set aside for possible schools.
Homestead and pre-emption claims were nearly equal in number although the
timber claim entries did not exceed one per section. Of the homestead claims,
over one-fourth had been successfully proven for ownership by a five-year
residence requirement while one-third had been commuted to the Federal
government such as preemption claimants were required to do. Of the timber
claims filed by 1884, only one-third were granted to such people as the
Melvills, T. Franklyn, A. Pischke, Z. Spitler, A. Young (Jung). Diligent
efforts to raise a ten-acre stand of ash and box elder trees over an eight-year
period was usually thwarted by drought and frost.

A comparison of the Leola Township people who initially owned rural land in
1884 indicates that only five chose to make the Leola community a lasting home.
After satisfying residency requirements to acquire land ownership, a number of
the early claimants moved elsewhere, and rented their land or began selling it
to later arriving settlers. By 1911, the population of Leola Township had been
materially transformed with the immigration of farmers from Iowa, Illinois, and
Missouri such as the Crouchs, Shafers and Turnwalls.

Economic and physical survival of the settlers during the 1880's was no easy
task. Small grains like wheat, oats, barley, and flax and garden crops did well
the first few years. Total crop failures due to drought and insects in 1886,
1889, and 1890 were the final blow to many settlers. Between 1889 and 1905 the
population of Leola had declined from 300 to 176.

The construction of the M & St. L Railroad in December 1906 to Leola gave the
community a big boost. This was followed by the arrival of the many immigrants
seeking land and a demand for merchants to service the rural community.

The educational facilities of the entire township were located within the
village of Leola except for the years that a rural school operated south of the
Otto Hauffe homestead on Section 3 around 1907. To develop improved rural
roads and other matters of the entire township, a civil township was organized
on October 2, 1917, which ceased in 1967.

Leola Township's resident writer was Edwin C. Torrey, who lived in Ordway
before establishing his claim. Torrey settled on a homestead claim on Section
23 in May 1884 next to his apparent aunt, Lydia Torrey, who had been there on a
preemption claim since July 5, 1883. In his 1925 book of Early Days In Dakota,
Torrey wrote several chapters about life and events that affected the early
developments of eastern McPherson County and the Ordway-Columbia area.

                Lincoln Township

It was in 1874 that Ed. D. Palmer ran the first survey line in the county. It
ran along the south line of Lincoln Township, then up its west line and up to
the southwest corner of Carl Township. Lincoln was one of the earliest
townships to be homesteaded. Some of the early settlers were John Walkey,
George Martin, Aaron and Richard Dillinback, Elmina A. Cotton, Edward Lapham,
Horace F. Scott, John W. Daly, William A. Boyle, John E. Torgerson, W. H.
Maupie, John W. Weaver, John Rooney, Sadie M. Freckenhaus, Nettie S. Huntly,
Norman H. Farnhaus, Fred A. Hicks, Jacob and William Nattress, George L.
Farnham, George R. Lewis, Martin Maloney, Henry Harrison, William H. Robinson,
William Brearton, Jerry Lewis, John Bussey, John Kirnan, Wm. W. Long, Amos R.
Cornwall, Mary E. Barnes and James Barnes, Sr., Walter M. Savage, and Henry and
Jeremiah Royle. Most of their homesteading was done during the year of 1883.

The first school in Lincoln Township was organized in June, 1885 with the
following board members: G. W. Martin, clerk; Charles Anderson, chairman; and
M. Stone, treasurer.

Within Lincoln's boundaries lies Wetonka town. The town was established in 1906
on the homestead of George Kirnan, 14 miles southeast of Leola. E. B. Friel,
postmaster for many years, built the first residence in Wetonka. This house
served as a post office until it burned in 1910. The Wetonka public school was
founded in 1907 when two schoolhouses were moved in from the country, and Mrs.
Will Leighty was hired as the first teacher. Wetonka grew by leaps and bounds
for a short while, but throughout the past 25 years it has dwindled to a
population of 22.

There are six farms plus the Long Lake Hutterite colony in Lincoln Township at
the present time.

Lincoln disorganized as a civil township May 1, 1979.

                Long Lake Township

The name of Long Lake could well have been established by the U.S. Postal
Department. A mail station had its beginning by that name and was located at
the home of Frederick Bittner on September 11, 1884. Jakob Schaeffer took over
on August 20, 1898. It was then located at the home of Joseph Heyd on March 26,
1900. Later, on July 19, 1901 a mail station was located east of the present
site of Long Lake, in the Ludwig Orthwein store. They were paid $127 for their
services. Mr. Orthwein hauled supplies for his store from Eureka, and also
hauled the mail. The Orthweins sold their business in 1913 and moved to Eureka.

Christian and Carolina (Teske) Fischer farmed a short distance north of Long
Lake, where they had a store and also a post office station, beginning November
27, 1909. In 1929 the Fischers moved their store to the present site of Long
Lake.

On January 2, 1930 it was taken over by Karl Meier at the present site of Long
Lake. Merle Meier presently serves as Postmaster.

In 1918, Edward Zelmer established his farm three miles west and one mile south
of Long Lake. This area was first homesteaded by Andrew J. Layton in 1896. Mr.
Layton had a Long Lake post office station also.

Some of Long Lake township's pioneers were: Jakob Hoffman, Friedrich
Schumacher, John F. Feiock, Andrew J. Layton, Jakob Burkhardt, Friedrich Klooz,
Johann Zumbaum, Nickolay Smolnisky, Fredrich Zelmer and Wilhelm Schumacher.

Fredrich Zelmer was among the first settlers to organize the first township
school in 1890. The first officers were: Christian Hetterle, chairman; E. D.
Haynes, clerk and Fred Junge, Sr., treasurer. Eventually Long Lake had four
schools, in sections 8, 11, 26 and 29.

Wilhelm Schumacher arrived in Long Lake Township in April of 1889. The family's
first home was a sod house with a ship-lap finishing on the inside. A feature
of this structure was a temporary stove of sod and rocks, built into the
ground, which was used during their first summer to cook the food. Many times
Wilhelm told how the early pioneer families would assemble in private homes and
conduct church services. The ways of traveling to these meetings were far
different than our mode of travel. Sometimes the pioneers would hitch an ox or
horse to a stoneboat, and the family would be hauled to church in this manner.
At other times an ox or team of horses would be hitched to a hay rake, and the
family conveyed to church while sitting on the teeth of the rake.

        Long Lake No. 2 around 1931. Left to right: Edna Straub, Oscar
        Schumacher, Mathilda Schumacher, Hulda Straub, Edmund Schumacher,
        Elenora Schumacher, Hildegard Schumacher, Olga Straub, Henry
        Schumacher, Delores Schumacher and Violet Straub.

Wilhelm served on boards of education for a number of years but did not seek
public office. However, two of his sons achieved prominence in the political
field in the county. Ludwig Schumacher represented Dist. No. 4 as commissioner
from 1920 to 1929, during the time the present day courthouse was built. August
Schumacher was elected mayor of Eureka city.

At one time Long Lake Township was well populated. Now there are 11 farms shown
in the McPherson County Rural Resident Directory.

                Moscow Township

Moscow Township 126-70 is located in the central part of McPherson County.
Homesteading began as early as 1884 in Moscow Township. The early tax list
shows Johanes Stoller, Carl Martel, Friedrich Jakober, Michael Binder, Philip
Weisz, Johannes Kranzler, Peter Hauck, Martin Brosz, Christian Wolff, Jacob
Job, Jacob Muhlbeier, George Rueb, Michael Pietz, and Jakob and Ludwig
Ketterling as taxpayers.

Jacob Jakober, Sr. was also among the earlier pioneers. Jacob Sr. came to
Moscow with his parents, Friedrich and Christiana Jakober, when he was nine
years of age. He spent most of his life on the farm his father homesteaded.
Jacob Sr. owned threshing machines and hired a crew of 16 men to operate them.
They threshed throughout a large area.

Martel Post Office was started February 24, 1896 with Carl Martel as
postmaster. It was located on Section 2. Later it was moved to Section 22,
where Martin and Helena Brosz combined the post office with a country store.
The post office was discontinued in 1919.

The first school in the township was organized in 1890, with the following
board members: Friedrich Jakober, chairman; Jacob Muhlbeier, clerk; and Michael
Binder, treasurer.

        Pupils at Moscow Township No. 1 around 1926.

Some of Moscow's citizens were not only farmers, but served in other
capacities. Jacob Muhlbeier was such a man. He was one of the county's earlier
sheriffs. Among his duties was the settling of boundary disputes which
sometimes arose between neighboring farmers. Jacob later became a state
legislator.

        Moscow Township School No. 1 (1926).

Many of our early day settlers can truly say they had hard times. Life on the
farm meant many hours of hard work. For their winter supply of fuel, a large
stack of "Pioneer Lignite" (mist-mistholz, meaning manure wood) was put up for
use. During the winter months, the manure from cattle was hauled onto a small,
well-drained area, and spread about a foot deep. The following spring or early
summer, usually after the mass started to dry, a process of packing the manure
bed was started. Horses were used to trample it into a solid mass. The horses
were led around the manure bed in a circle several times. Rollers were made out
of the threshing machine cylinders and used in the final operation. After it
was dry enough it was cut with a spade, into pieces about a foot square. These
were then set on edge to cure. The cured squares were then carefully placed in
large stacks. After stacking, fences were placed around it to protect it from
being thrown over by livestock. The squares and dried corncobs were the only
kinds of fuel used by the pioneers during the winter. Most of us living in
electrically heated homes in 1984 cannot comprehend what a winter would be
like, living in a sod house, heated by "pioneer lignite," trying to endure a
Dakota
blizzard.

There are about 14 farms left in Moscow Township. Those who stayed in Moscow
made history, and left a legacy for their children.

                Spring Township

Spring Township was organized as a civil township by election on January 31,
1890. The settlers held the election at A. Hafer's home, electing William Hill,
Daniel Milbrandt and Carl Breitag as directors; Fred Arndt as treasurer; and A.
Hafer as clerk. The group took into consideration the fact that the township
had at least 12 to 14 natural water springs located in it, consequently naming
it Spring Township.

Some of Spring's early homesteaders who helped to build the foundation for
sound township government were: Carl Breitag, Frederick Jasmer, Jerome S.
Davidson, Merrit E. Goodspeed, John H. Luce, Clarence L. Becker, Fred
Glaesmann, William H. Lohr, Fred Breitag, A. Hafer, Fred Arndt, August Arndt,
Daniel Milbrandt, William Hill, T. Bohmke and Karl Glaseman. Most of these men
took their turns serving on the township and school boards throughout the first
quarter of the century.

Due to Spring Township's neglect to hold an annual election, the first school
board was appointed by the county commissioners July 14, 1890. Those appointed
were: William H. Lohr, Carl Breitag and Daniel Milbrandt, directors; and Fred
Arndt, treasurer. At a special township meeting the settlers finished the
organization of the school board by appointing William Lohr as chairman and A.
Hafer as clerk. The board voted to have school held in the Fred Breitag house
for a term of two months, for which Fred was paid $4.00 per month. Ida Hafer
was hired to teach the children.

        Back row--left to right: Anna Stephan, teacher; Marabell Becker, and
        Alvena Becker. Third row: Alvena Jasmer, Minnie Joireman, Reuben
        Breitag, Robert Jacobson, Harold Becker, Eric Jacobson, Sigmund
        Stickel, Arnold Becker, Albert Walker, Rudolph Stoecker, Albert
        Breitag. Second row: Esther Jacobson, Albert Jasmer, Edgar Jasmer,
        Alfred Joireman, Clara Breitag, Ida Jasmer, Wilma Stickel. Front
        row: Walter Jacobson, Gregor Breitag, Malita Glaser.

A special election was held to decide the issue on whether to bond the township
$300.00 to build a school. It was unanimously voted for. The citizens decided
to build a school on the northwest corner of Section 26, and August of 1891 it
was completed. School started August 25 with Ida Hafer as teacher. The school
term was four months and Ida's salary was $20.00 per month. Later they moved
the school to another location (Section 22). The school board set the school
terms and it is interesting to note the difference in years. In 1895, they had
six months and in 1896, four months (two in the spring and two in the fall). In
1898-1909, the terms were six months.

An election was held September 5, 1911 to vote on bonding the school district
$800.00 for building another schoolhouse on the SE 1/4 of Section 10. It passed
and another school was added in Spring. By 1914 the township's schools were
having eight month school terms, but in 1915 an election was held and voters
made their wishes known when they voted to
have six months of school.

Progressive city schools gradually led to the closing of the township schools
in 1958, which in turn led to the disorganization of the township itself in
1966.

Two of Spring Township's homesteaders have descendants living in the township
at the present time. Gerhardt and Don Breitag are descendants of Carl Breitag.
Richard Jasmer is a descendant of Frederick Jasmer. Richard is farming on the
same land that his great-grandfather farmed.

                Wachter Township

The Fort Sisseton-Fort Yates Military Road crossed the northeast corner of the
county through Wachter Township. It was down this road that John Weber and
other settlers first entered McPherson County in 1882 and 1883. Among the early
settlers were Anna M. Wachter, William Wachter, and Katherina Wachter. It is
most probable that the township was named after the Wachters. Other early
homesteaders were: Thomas O. Hanlon, Frank P. Cross, Holden E. Stafford,
Alexander Ludwig, William Brown, Benjamin H. Marshall, Martin Jacobson, Ole G.
Anderson, John R. Hays, Thomas F. Churchill, Agnes J. Fleming, C. J. Hubbard,
H. E. Helgerson and the Hart family.

Jacob Wachter and his family homesteaded on the northern part of the SW 1/4 of
Section 5 on May 4, 1883. Jacob and two of his sons, Henry and William farmed
in Wachter many years. William served two terms as McPherson County
Commissioner. He served during the time the present county courthouse was
built.

        Alpha post office.

In the spring of 1883, James R. Hart filed on land in the SE 1/4 of Section
7-128-66, later known as Alpha, SD. Alpha was the earliest post office in the
county. Mrs. Anna Hart was appointed postmistress November 8, 1887 and she
served until February 23, 1906, when the office was discontinued and the mail
went to Forbes, ND. James R. Hart hauled mail, one day from Ellendale and the
next day from Leola. He was paid $1.53 per trip. In the early days the Harts
had several Indian scares. Caravans of Indians passed down the Standing Rock
Trail every few weeks, but always proved to be friendly. About 1890, it was
rumored that several hundred Indians were on the war path and that they had
left the reservation heading in their direction. The family lived in suspense
for several weeks until they heard that it was a hoax. The Harts described the
fire which destroyed about half of the village of Koto. One of the Hart girls,
Etta (Miller), was teaching the Koto school at the time. The day the town
burned, the dust was so thick she and her pupils didn't know part of the town
had burned until the next morning. Abner Hart recalled how the men would get
together on Saturdays and haul their grain to town. While they were gone, the
womenfolk would burn up the men's chewing tobacco in an effort at discouraging
"the habit." They never seemed to realize the futility or waste, for the men
always made sure
a fresh supply was stowed away before they started for home.

The first school was organized in 1890 with the following officers elected: C.
J. Hubbard, chairman; H. E. Helgerson, clerk; and Mrs. Anna Hart, treasurer.
Prior to that, many of the children attended school in
Weber Township.

The 1982 Rural Resident Directory shows there are 17 landowners left in Wachter
Township.

                Wacker Township

Eighteen eighty-five was the year homesteaders arrived in Wacker Township. Some
of the first to arrive were Karl and Phillip Wacker, Jacob Ehresman, Ludwig
Gienger, Philip Ehresman, Sr., George Feickert, Jacob and Gottlieb Rau, Jacob
and Konrad Ehresman, and Jacob Wagemann. It is probable that the township was
named after the Wackers.

Around 1890 the first township school was organized. As the township grew, two
more schools were added.

Karl Wacker, an early citizen, shared his story with his grandchildren who in
turn shared it with others. Karl Wacker brought his family to Wacker Township
around 1889. After a fire destroyed his house and barn near Yankton, he and his
family took the train to Eureka (end of the railroad), then headed northeast
and chose some land in what became Wacker Township. He built a sod house and
barn, dug a well and took cattle on shares to keep debt free. Karl told of
eight years of drouth, with wheat yielding only five to eight bushels to an
acre. Wells went dry, discouraging some of Karl's neighbors and some left the
area. Karl bought one of the farms for $500.00 and moved to it. He sold 160
acres of his land for $750.00 which he
used to pay off the new farm.

School classes, as well as church services, were held in the homesteaders'
homes. Karl Wacker was well educated in Russia; consequently he knew the value
of education. He insisted that his children learn to read and write both
English and German. He taught school when they were without a teacher. He told
of blizzards when the teacher kept the children in school overnight. A lot of
the children walked several miles to and from school. One blizzard started in
the afternoon and the teacher insisted the children stay. He informed the older
boys, who had plans of starting home, that they had to mind him when they were
in school, thus keeping all of them together in the schoolhouse. They burned
wood, ate what was left in their lunchboxes and stayed around the stove all
night. The teacher made sure that they drank water and told them stories to
keep their minds occupied. The next morning the smaller children cried and were
hungry. By late afternoon two of the fathers came with a sled and took everyone
to one house where they were fed and cared for. There is no doubt that the
teacher saved their
lives.

Wacker Township was not organized as a civil township until 1942. An election
was held in 1943 with the following elected: Edwin Feickert, clerk; Phillip
Ehresmann, treasurer; Christ C. Wolf, Jacob Feickert, Jr. and John Rohrbach,
supervisors. Wacker is still an efficient organized township with the following
1984 officers: Milbert Kappes, clerk; Ronnie Ehresmann, treasurer; Harvey
Shafer, Alvin Wacker, and Reuben Wagemann,
supervisors.

                Washington Township

George A. Kline brought his survey crew into Washington Township in the first
part of August, 1883. They found at least 53 individuals, claiming 40 percent
of the land. Eighteen eighty-three real property tax lists show that the
township had 13 women homesteaders among the early group.

The first rural land deed filed was from one of Washington's landowners. It was
recorded June 2, 1884 in the first county deed book, on page five. It shows
that Belle Grierson deeded land to C. N. Hazelton.

The 1884 tax list shows every section of Washington Township taxed. Some of the
early settlers were: Nathan Pierce, Gottlob Pade, Sr., Jennie Hoffman (formerly
Hummel), Robert Hill, Henry Young, Thomas Crompton, Arthur Chute, Frank Boyle,
the Huntley family, Anna Russell, Ida and Laura Warren, Rosell Anderson, J. H.
Darlington, and Hamlin Garland. The tax record shows J. H. Darlington owned
only one quarter of land in the township. It was on this NE 1/4 of Section 36
that five men gathered in a shanty to organize McPherson County. The land
description is noted in the first book of the
McPherson County minutes.

        Hamlin Garland.

Hamlin Garland, renowned author and poet, arrived in Dakota Territory at the
height of the land boom in the spring of 1883. He was 23 at the time. His
parents had come to the Ordway area in 1881 and homesteaded two miles northwest
of Ordway, SD. Hamlin joined his parents and helped them in the store that they
were operating in 1883. He intended to secure a claim by preemption. The
conditions of a preemption claim demanded a visit to one's claim every 30 days,
and the trips to the SW 1/4 of Section 32 were especially hazardous during the
February and March blizzards. The agony of nights alone in his shanty, besieged
by 70 mph winds, and waking up to 40ø F. below zero inspired Garland to put his
emotions and feelings into the writing of poetry on the walls of his shanty. He
scribbled notes on the four walls, from floor to ceiling and wherever space was
available. Three successive blizzards influenced him to permanently end his
adventure on the Dakota plains. He described his feelings in "Son of the Middle
Border" with the sentence, "Winter! No man knows what winter means until he has
lived through one in a pine board shanty on a Dakota plain with only buffalo
bones for fuel." After proving his claim, he mortgaged it for $200 and set out
for Boston. A short time later he began his literary career. He later
acknowledged this time of his life to be a turning point. His experiences on
the prairie influenced his writings throughout the rest of his life. He became
famous for his realistic portrayals of the harsh life of the prairie
homesteader.

According to the 1884 tax records, personal property tax carried a higher levy
than real estate. Hamlin Garland's land value was $575, taxed at $1.43; Thomas
Crompton's land value was $650, taxes were $1.62; Gottlob Pade, Sr.'s personal
property was valued at $170, taxed at $7.65; Arthur Chute's personal property
valued at $245, taxed $9.80; and Henry Hoover's personal property valued at
$700, taxed at $23.36.

Washington Township was organized as a civil township in 1911. The first
officers were Matt Patterson, Thomas Crompton and Gottlieb Pade, Jr.,
supervisors; John Heibel, treasurer; Charles Hill, clerk; and Ernest Leberman,
assessor. The township became unorganized in 1966.

The first school in Washington Township was called the Chute School, later
known as the Nelson School. It was located seven miles south of Leola, on the
Wetonka corner. The second school, called the Crompton School was located about
three miles east of the Chute School. Both schools were built in 1884. The
third school, the Pierce School, was located 1 1/2 miles from the Nathan Pierce
farm (five miles from Leola) and this school was started around 1910. It was
later known as Washington No. 2.

        Pierce school children, Mr. Bishop, teacher.

A post office was started January 13, 1885, with Herbert Chute as postmaster.
It was discontinued in 1886.

During the 1930's depression, drouth, dust storms and grasshoppers caused many
farmers to loose their farms, but later good crops and fair prices enabled most
of the people in the township td redeem their farms.

                Weber Township

If one were to describe the land in Weber Township, it would be summed up just
as it was done in the 1959 Jubilee book. They told us that Weber Township has a
range of hills running through the middle from northeast to southwest, with the
part lying east of the hills being fertile agricultural land, while the part
west of the divide is virgin prairie, used exclusively for grazing and hayland.

John Weber, the first settler in McPherson County, came to this untamed prairie
land in the summer of 1882. It is probable that the township was named after
him. He and his family came from Boonville, MO and settled in Section 2. That
same summer, five others, including Samuel Preston Howell, settled in the
vicinity. During the winter of 1882-83, these families were the only settlers
between them and the Missouri River.

The township was surveyed in 1883 by George A. Kline and his crew. Some of the
settlers he found were: C. F. and John W. Burns, John Haberman, Fred and Elias
Howell, Dan Newell, Mortimer Swift, William Scot, James Jones, Abe Stark and
John Weber, Charles Hargitt, Floyd C. Webb, S. P. Howell, and
Andrew J. Stark.

Weber Township was organized as a civil township in 1884. The first officers
were: Samuel P. Howell, Charles Hargitt and John Weber. It is still an
organized township at the present time. The 1984 officers are Clinton
Kindelspire, treasurer; Lea Kindelspire, clerk; Sam Hofer, Lee Kindelspire and
Tom Thorpe, supervisors.

The first school in Weber was organized in 1884 with the following officers
elected: W. A. Barden, chairman; F. D. Pepper, clerk; and Samuel P. Howell,
treasurer. The school was located south of the state line in Section 12, and
Irene Brewer was the first to teach in it. Her first term lasted three months.
Mrs. Joe Weber of Forbes, ND told of a dance that was given in the new building
before the seats were fastened down. She attended the dance, but was a child at
the time. The school quickly became the center of the community, where many box
socials and children's programs were held. Since it was the only school for
miles, children who lived several miles away had to be brought by teams of
horses. They seldom had more than five months of school during the year. When
County Superintendent, C. J. Collier visited the school in 1887, he recorded in
his school minutes that he found Weber School to be one of the best in the
county. This same schoolhouse was later moved to Forbes, ND where it was
rebuilt into a family home.

        Left to right: Walter Hammrich, Duane Bain, Dianne Hammrich, Viola
        Hammrich, Bob Kindelspire, Judy Kindelspire, Barbara Hammrich
        Darlis Bain, Kelly Kindelspire, Jolaine Breunig, and Lee Kindelspire.

Weber Township now has seven ranchers and farmers plus the Spring Creek
Hutterite Colony.

                Willow Township

The first homesteaders to file entries to land in Willow Township in 1883 were
Harriet Lowry and Frank Horning. The Frank Horning land is the only land in the
township to stay in the same relationship all these years. This land is owned
and operated by Henry Heagley, a nephew of Frank Horning. By 1886, Peter
Albrecht, Gustave Mundt, Charles Kruger and Robert Valentine were settled in
Willow.

Willow Township was organized as a civil township on April 24, 1886, by
electing the following officers: A. W. Hunt, clerk; James A. Wells, treasurer;
Frank Mincks, assessor; M. J. Benjamin, overseer; Hope Carpenter and P. T.
Lamb, supervisors; James Tooker and T. S. Hunt as Justices of the Peace; and
Frank Horning and F. M. Wertz, constables.

Not long after organizing, a special meeting was called to vote on a tax of one
percent on all taxable property in the township. This tax was to provide money
for building roads, bridges or any other expense of the township. Apparently
everyone was in favor of the tax for there were no votes against it. Each tax
payer had the option of paying the special tax or working so many days with
team and scraper to fill old cellar holes, old wells and low spots on the
roads.

Everyone was invited to attend trotting races held in Willow Township on June
5, 1890. The first meeting of the Willow Township Trotting Association was held
the same day at the race course, which was on Section 25-126-66. They had four
categories: three minute trot--$35.00 purse; Farmers trot--$10.00 purse;
running horses--$25.00 purse; and free for all running--$100.00 purse. The
racing started at 1 :00 P.M. It is said that the races provided many hours of
enjoyable entertainment.

The homesteaders were just as aware of noxious weeds as our modern day farmers.
In 1886 every person or corporation owning land in Willow was notified that all
noxious weeds such as cockleburs, Canadian thistles and mustard must be
destroyed by pulling or plowing before July 14, 1886.

Washington No. 2.

The school districts of the township were organized March 3, 1885. June 1,
1885, the first school board of Willow was elected, consisting of J. W. Tooker,
chairman; J. A. Wells, clerk; and T. S. Hunt, treasurer. The first school in
the township was opened on February 26, 1886 and named Willow District No. 1.
Nellie Tap was the first teacher.

        Students on YCL convention trip to Pierre (1957). Left to right:
        Karen Durheim, Joanne Heagley, Lyle Weiszhaar and County Supt. Otto
        Strobel.

Willow Township disorganized in 1968 as a civil township. The 1982 McPherson
County Rural Resident Directory lists 24 farms in Willow Township.

        Howard
