JOE and ELSIE BREUNIG

Joe Breunig, son of Henry and Elisabeth (Kurt) Breunig, grew up on the family
farm ten miles northeast of Leola. He lived with the Albert Breunig family
until 1935 when he purchased the Gamble Store in Bowdle, SD.

Joe married Elsie (Weisgram) of Java in 1943. They bought and moved to a farm
ten miles north of Leola. They had five children: Jolaine (Mrs. Curt Johnson)
of Apple Valley, MN; Linda (Mrs. Gary Milbrandt) of Buffalo, ND; Kurtis,
Billings, MT; Lana of Fargo, ND and Sharon (Mrs. Tom Hieser) of Leonard, ND.
The family moved to Lisbon, ND in 1959.

In 1973 Joe returned to Leola where he assists his brother, Albert in the OK
Hardware Store.

        Elsie, Joe and Jolaine Breunig.

Joe delights in his large garden and the produce that he raises.

HENRY and ELISABETH BREUNIG

The first ancestor of the Breunig family who came to America was Martin Breunig
from Bavaria (a German state). Martin settled in Wisconsin and married
Margareta Ganser, whose family came from Trier, Germany. Eight sons and two
daughters were born to them. Two of these children moved to South Dakota in
1888. They were Annie, who married John Mack, and her brother Henry. Both
purchased land ten miles northeast of Leola.

After two years of farming in South Dakota, Henry returned to Wisconsin to
marry Elisabeth Kurt, in 1891. Elisabeth (Liz) Kurt was born July 4, 1873 in
Dane, WI. Her parents had migrated from Alsace Lorraine (France). Henry and
Elisabeth returned to Leola to continue farming.

Nine children were born to Henry and Liz: Albert, Joe, Martin, Lorene, Natalia,
Carl, Henry, Arthur, and Eddie. All are deceased except Albert and Joe, both of
Leola, Martin, the oldest, of Coos Bay, OR, and Lorene. Martin married Dorothy
Beard, and they have two children: Franklyn and Virginia. Lorene married
Charles Hubbard, and resides in Salt Lake City, UT. Their children are: Gerald,
Charles and Charlene.

Liz died at the age of 36, December 21, 1909, leaving Henry with eight children
under 16 years of age. Three boys died soon after their mother. Henry never
remarried.

Henry once stated, "After coming to South Dakota I could never return to
Wisconsin to live. It is too humid there and I don't like cutting all that
wood." He loved the open prairies, rolling hills, and the morning mirages. They
could see the smoke from the train 17 miles away, as it traveled from Aberdeen
to Ellendale. Henry passed away March 17, 1946.

Looking back through the years, special incidents remain in the memories of
Albert and Joe. They remember going 17 miles to Frederick to church on Sunday
with a team and buggy. This was before the new church was built five miles
south of the home place. Joe recalls that if they could see in a blizzard, they
went to church! Remembering the death and burial of their mother on December 24
Albert, age 11, and Joe heard their father ask Art Mack to purchase candy,
nuts, and oranges for the children for Christmas. In spite of their great
sorrow they were known to be a happy family.

GEORGE and MAUDE BROADBENT

George Broadbent was born May 31, 1883, in a sod shanty on a tree claim, where
his parents, Mr. and Mrs. William Broadbent, had settled in Franklin Township,
Brown County, Dakota Territory.

George married Maude Evans from Lake Andes, SD, at Leola, SD, October 23, 1907.
At the time of their marriage, George was running a dray line and Maude was
teaching school in the Leola area.

The Broadbents lived in the home built earlier by his father, William
Broadbent. Here were born seven of their ten children, the older ones attending
Leola Public School.

Later the family moved to a farm east of Leola, where they ran a threshing rig
and a cook car for many years.

The children and spouses of George and Maude Broadbent are: Dale Ivan, married
to Mary Peck. They had three children, one deceased. They reside in Sioux
Falls, SD; Blanche Lenore, married to Andrew Ratajzeck. They had three
children, one deceased. They reside in Redondo Beach, CA; Harriet Lucy was
married to Glen Morris. They had three children, one deceased. They reside in
Minneapolis, MN; Edgar Dean was never married. He died March 14, 1975; Dorothea
Delores married to Charles Von Eschen. He died June 27, 1967. They had five
children, one deceased. She resides in Aberdeen; Ione Maxine married to
Clifford Green. They have one son. They reside in Aberdeen, SD; Ward Evans
married to Eleanor Backous. They have three children and reside in Westport,
SD; Betty Lou married to Leroy Pierce. they have four children, and reside in
Bloomington, MN; La Verna Gayle was married to Adam Biffert. They had one child
and reside in Bell Flower, CA; Doris Jean married to Wayne Donahue. They have
two children and reside in Sioux Falls, SD

Maude Evans Broadbent was born October 23, 1886 and died November 11, 1955.
George Edgar Broadbent was born May 31, 1883 and died March, 8, 1966. They were
residing in Aberdeen, SD at the time of their death.

DELLA BROADBENT (MRS. FRED GREISER)

Della Broadbent, daughter of William and Harriet Broadbent, was born November
19, 1896, in a sod shanty on a tree claim in Brown County.

In 1906 she came with her parents to Leola where she attended school. Her
father, a carpenter by trade, built the family home a block west of the Court
House on the south side of Main Street. Della attended school in Leola and
worked as a waitress in the hotel dining room. Later she went to Eureka to
work. There she met and married Fred Greiser in 1917. Fred, like most young
men, served in World War I.

The Greisers nad four children: Woodrow Arnold, Gordon and Gwendolyn. The three
boys served in World War II and are now deceased. Gwendolyn (Mrs. Chet
Erickson) lives in Marietta, GA. Since the death of her husband, April 23,
1953, Della has made her home with Gwendolyn.

JOHN and ELLA BROADBENT

John Broadbent was the oldest son of Mr. and Mrs. William Broadbent, born in
Kempton, Ford County, IL, in 1877. At the age of three he, with his parents,
homesteaded on a tree claim in Franklin Township, Brown County, where they
lived for several years, moving later to the Wetonka area.

In 1901 he married Ella Huntley. They settled on a farm between Westport and
Leola. In addition to farming, Mr. Broadbent drilled wells, ran threshing
machines and worked at odd jobs during his lifetime.

They were farming in the Westport area at the time of his death, September 13,
1938. It was then that Mrs. Broadbent with her eight children moved into
Westport, where she lived until her death, June 12, 1962.

Their children and spouses were: Lilliemay, married to Charles Montag;
Adelbert, married to Mildred Heygood; Fren, married to M. Matteson, later to
Wm. Hechler; Glenn; Gertrude, married to Martin Hove; Ruth, married to William
Rohwedder; Orpha, married to Walter Ochs; and Leota, married to Carl Ewers.

WILLIAM and M. HARRIETTE BROADBENT

McPherson County can boast very few settlers of English descent, but William
Broadbent was one who had pioneer blood in his veins, eventually settling in
Dakota Territory.

William Broadbent was born at Ashton in Surrey County, England, April 9, 1848.
He was three years old when his parents immigrated to America in 1851. They
settled west of Chicago in Kendall County, IL, which was then considered the
Great West. Here he grew to manhood, and at the age of 20 he left his parental
home, moving further west and settling in Ford County, IA.

In 1876, he married Mary Harriette Hose at Champlain, IL. A few years later Mr.
Broadbent again heard the call of the West. With his family, he headed west,
traveling by train to Ordway, Dakota Territory. There they settled on a tree
claim in Franklin Township, Brown County, living in a sod shanty where several
of their children were born. From there they moved to McPherson County, where
they were among the first pioneers of the Wetonka area.

In 1906 they moved to Leola, where Mr. Broadbent employed his talents as a
carpenter, erecting a number of buildings. Some of these are still standing,
including the original Broadbent home, which later became the Gutjahr home.

To the Broadbents were born nine children, five boys and four girls, all of
whom grew up and married in this area. John married Ella Huntley; Laura married
Mike Scherman; George married Maude Evans; Frank married Pearl Howell; Iva
married Clarence Ayres; Arthur married Tillie; Charles married Gusta Turnquist;
Della married Fred Greiser; and Olive married Thomas Lohner. All are deceased
except Della, who is living with her daughter in Marietta, GA, and Olive who
resides in her home in Aberdeen.

Mr. Broadbent died in 1917 and Mrs. Broadbent in 1923 Roth are buried in Green
Mound Cemetery at Leola.

DAVID and DOROTHEA BROSZ

David Brosz was the eighth of 13 children born to Martin Brosz Sr., and Helena
W. (Schlechter) Brosz. He was born March 7, 1900, in Martell, SD, (Moscow
Township, McPherson County). Two children died in infancy and all are deceased
except David, who currently lives in Leola, SD; Mrs. Henry (Lydia) Quaschnick,
93 of Garden Grove, CA; and Mrs. Gottlieb (Freda) Weisz, 86 of Minneapolis, MN.

David's family moved to Leola in 1908. The family lived in the house built by
his father, now occupied by the Marvin Bonnet family. David, age eight,
attended school in the first brick building in town. David remembers it being
48 degrees below and running to school, standing around the radiators until
noon trying to get or stay warm. At that time the only house between their home
and the school was the Frank Pierce house, now owned by Terry and Mary Hoffman.

David spent much of his time helping his older brother John and Jacob Muhlbeier
at their livery barn. He also worked for Gross and Mankoff in the grocery
store. He helped his folks with the work at the hotel; cleaning about 25 lamp
chimneys each day, making beds and waiting on tables.

In 1916 he attended the Grand Island (NE) Business College. In 1917, Dave
taught school in Berdorf Township, near Long Lake, SD. In 1919, Dave went to
work in a grocery store in Mina, SD. Two years later, he went to work for his
brother-in-law at the South Main grocery store in Aberdeen (now known as Four
Brothers Market). Brosz & Quaschnick started the store.

In 1923 David returned to Leola where he and his brothers Arthur and Joe
started the Brosz Brothers General Merchandise Store and Cream Station.

        David & Hulda Brosz.

In December 1928, David was united in marriage with Dorothea Dusel from
Tolstoy, SD. The brothers' business had split up, so Dave and Dorthea moved the
cream station to the Brosz Hotel. On January 27, 1930, a daughter Joyce, was
born. They paid Idelette Lundquist $35.00, attendant at delivery, the fee being
all the money the Broszs' had at that time.

Dave remembers when threshing was done with horsepower. All the grain was
sacked and hauled to town with horses and wagons. Grocery prices for the '30s
were: cream ten cents a pound, eggs eight cents a dozen, chickens five cents a
pound, cow hides one cent a pound and horse hides $1.00 each. During the '30s
David purchased the old Darby Wheeler Plumbing shop from John Wageman. They
rented out the upstairs and had a barber shop downstairs.

At one time Frank Junge had owned the building and the first movies had been
shown in it: ten cents for adults and five cents for children. Dave remembers
when his brother-in-law bought tickets for him and brother Joe. They got scared
when the train in the picture came right at them.

In 1941 Dave and Dorothea started a Red Owl store and in '42 discontinued
buying cream. They purchased the Silverman building (presently the Apparel),
remodeled it and moved to this store. It was the first self-service store in
Leola. The building was sold to Calvin Hilgemann in 1956. During 1960-67, Dave
and Dorothea also sold Watkins products in north Brown County.

Their daughter Joyce, married Gerald Heibel, the son of Earl and Clixta Heibel
of Leola, SD, in June 1952. Dave remembers it as quite an event. Early in the
morning a thunderstorm came up and lightning struck the Brosz house. The power
went off and they had to store all the food for the wedding in the walk-in
cooler at the store. The day was not only Joyce's wedding day, it also was
Dorothea's birthday and Father's Day. Gerald and Joyce have three children and
one grandchild. They live in Monmouth, OR. At present Joyce works for the State
Board of Education, State of Oregon, in Salem. Gerald is retired.

David and Dorothea were members of St. Paul Lutheran Church. Dorothea was
organist and choir director for many years. David has served on the church
council, and has held all offices but one. He was a member of the City Council
for about 15 years, during the W.P.A. days.

David's mother passed away in 1958. David and Dorothea became the owners of the
Brosz Hotel. They took over renting apartments and rooms.

Dorothea died October 15, 1976.

Each having lost their mate in death, on March 7, 1979, David and Hulda
(Klingman) Fuehrer were united in marriage. They are living in the Brosz Hotel.

See Albert Fuehrer for Hulda's family.

MARTIN SR. and HELENA BROSZ

Martin Brosz, Sr. was born September 17, 1861, in Bessarabia, S. Russia, where
his parents had immigrated from the principality of Wuttenberg between
1820-1830. He was one of four children. In 1887 he married Helena Wilhelmina
Schlecter, born October 31, 1869, in Odessa, S. Russia. She was one of six
children.

Martin and Helena immigrated to the U.S. in 1889. bringing with them a
six-month old son, John. Their remaining 12 children were born in McPherson
County, SD. Upon arriving in New York by boat, Martin and Helena went to
Scotland, SD, and from there traveled to Eureka by train. They settled in
Moscow Township on Section 22, 16 miles east of Eureka. After first living
under their wagon, Martin and Helena later had a store and post office called
Martell, SD. Martin hauled the mail by horse three times weekly and Helena was
Post Master. The neighbors brought their eggs, butter, etc. there and got their
mail. In 1908 the Brosz's moved their store building to Leola. They were
involved in several businesses in Leola for the next 50 years, including the
Brosz Hotel. (See businesses for details.)

        Helena & Martin Brosz.

Martin died May 8, 1929; Helena died April 22, 1958. There are three surviving
children at this time: David (83) of Leola, Lydia Quashnick (93) of Anaheim,
CA; and Freda Weisz (86) of Minneapolis, MN. The other children were: John,
born 1888, married Emilia Haase, died 1973; Martin Jr., born 1892, World War I
veteran, died in 1951; Helena, born 1894, married R. H. Becker, died in 1969;
Jacob, born 1895, married Margaret Schlumbom, died in 1965; Joseph, born 1898,
married Lydia Valentine, died in 1975; and Arthur, born 1901, married Mary
Hamilton, died in 1980. Anna and Gottlieb died in infancy.

GRAN W. and MELLIE BURNS

Gran W. Burns and his wife, Mellie, and young son Claron moved from their
Missouri home to their new home, northwest of Leola, in April 1909. To their
dismay their house turned out to be a tar-paper shanty. The farm was located in
township 126 and contained approximately 190 acres. Claron, then four years of
age, was unhappy with the prairie shanty and homesick for his Missouri home.

Four more children were born to Gran and Mellie in their South Dakota home.
Nina Mae followed Claron on September 9, 1912. G. W. Jr. (Dud or Duddy) was
born May 28, 1914. Then came John R. (Jack) on July 2, 1917. Then another
daughter Elizabeth Ann (Betty) arrived December 8, 1919.

Mr. Burns farmed and raised Hereford cattle. He also bought and sold mules,
sometimes shipping them to Missouri by the car load. Old timers will remember
Gran Burns as the man who always wore a hat, even in the South Dakota sub-zero
temperatures.

Sorrow came to the Burns family when their mother died of cancer in March 1929
in Missouri. After the funeral, the family returned to Leola and lived there
until the fall of 1937.

        The Gran W. Burns family. Back: Claron H. and G. W. Jr. Front: Betty,
        Gran W. and Jack.

All of the Burns children were graduated from high school in Leola. Claron
taught rural school for a time. He also attended business college in Aberdeen.
On October 6, 1928 he married Helen Pierson, a highly successful math teacher
in Leola High.

Nina Mae graduated from Leola High School in 1930 and then attended Northern
for one year. She taught in Washington Township one year and then married
Kenneth Ferguson of Aberdeen in June 1933. She died there the following
February.

Brothers Claron and Dud left Leola in 1936, going to Seattle, WA, where they
were later joined by Claron's wife.

Jack, Betty, and Father Gran now moved back to Missouri in 1937, having lost
their farm in the drought and depression.

Jack, who was graduated from Leola High School in 1935, and Dud, who was
graduated in 1933, now enlisted in the armed services in World War II. After
their discharges they each spent a year with their father in Missouri. They
then returned to Olympia, WA, where all three brothers still reside.

Betty married Paul Williams Jr., of Ethel, MO. They have one daughter, Jane Ann
Britt. Betty's husband is a retired employee of the A.T. and S.F. Railroad.

Jack married Helen Jones of Olympia. They have two sons.

Dud married Ruth Gill of Olympia. They had two sons, Patrick and Larry Gill of
Olympia. Dud's wife is deceased.

Gran Burns served on the school board of Leola. He and his family were assets
to the Leola Community.

Mr. Burns died in Missouri on March 31, 1949.

Claron and his wife, Helen, lived in Leola a few years after their marriage. He
worked for Standard Oil. They reside in Olympia, WA.

ADDISON GROVE and JAMES SHERMAN CLAYTON

Addison Grove Clayton and James Sherman Clayton, sons of Samuel and Jane
Rebecca Lyle Clayton, were early settlers in McPherson County, having
immigrated here from Nance County, NE in the 1880's. Addison Grove arrived
first, marrying Mildred Augusta Gregory in February of 1885. Mildred was the
daughter of Douglas and Cynthia Ann Busnell Gregory, who at the time of the
Leola fire of April 1889 were living eight miles east of Leola. Addison and
Mildred had five children: Clara Belle, who married William Harrison DeWitt in
Leola; Lyman Morton; Beryl Melba, who married Charles W. Kelley; Floy Mae, who
married Grover Roundy and later Herschel W. Keener; and Myrtle Mae, who married
Elwin Hancock. All of the children were born in Leola and later moved away.
Addison died in 1922 and Mildred died in 1947.

James Sherman followed his brother, Addison, to McPherson County and in 1891
married Myrtle Mae Gregory, the youngest sister of his brother's wife, in
Leola. They also had five children (the first and last born in Leola, the
middle three in Eureka): Della, who married Theodore Reue and died in 1947;
Mildred, who married Wallace Harris Ward and died in 1975; Lyle Gregory, who
married Mary Leverman and died in 1969; James Wayne III, who died in 1973; and
Hollis Reva, who married Stanfield Possehl and later A. H. Dankert and died in
1976.

Myrtle May Clayton died in Leola in 1932 and James Sherman died in 1948 in
Aberdeen, SD.

CLAUDE and HELEN CHITTICK

Claude Chittick was one of the early businessmen of Leola. He was born in
Dundalk, Ontario, Canada on February 10, 1878. In 1889 he came with his
parents, Mr. and Mrs. William Chittick, three brothers and one sister to
Hosmer, SD. (His father served about four years in the Civil War and acquired
ranch land near Hosmer as a part of his services.)

Claude married Helen Caroline Mikkelsen of Bowdle, SD. They moved to Leola in
1909 where Claude worked in stores--butcher shops. A few years later he put up
ice, delivering it in the summer to business places and residents who owned ice
boxes. He had a large building insulated with shiplap siding on the inside. In
the fall he ran about two inches of water on the ground several nights in
succession to freeze until there was about one foot of ice on the bottom of the
icehouse. Ice was sent by the car load (via M & St. L railroad) from Lake
Kampeska near Watertown, SD. Ice blocks were about one cubic yard in size. The
blocks were well packed in sawdust with a large supply of saw dust on top of
all the ice near the top of the building. During the summer, ice was delivered
in a wagon drawn by a team of horses. He would saw and chip the blocks to the
size his customers needed, wash the sawdust off, weigh it and then place it in
their ice boxes.

        Claude Chittick.

In 1912-1913, Claude and Helen taught rural schools near Eureka for five to
eight months in order to raise "capital" to start the first moving picture show
in Leola. They lived in a sod house, half of which served as a school room
where Helen taught. Claude drove four miles each day to teach a neighboring
school.

Claude and Rod Ronayne started the first silent moving picture show in Leola,
in November, 1913. They gave performances Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday
evenings of each week with a matinee on Saturday afternoons. A large cylinder
gas engine with fly wheels (about a yard in diameter) pulled a dynamo to
furnish electricity for the moving picture machine. The vibrations from the
engine were felt by the spectators throughout the building. The venture proved
to be successful. The business was sold later to Pete Schuchardt.

Claude took an active part in the social life of the community. He belonged to
a Literary Club and participated in debates, worked as city assessor, was a
member of the volunteer fire department and a member of the Masons.

In 1912 Claude and Samuel Bosanko wrote civil service examinations at the Leola
post office and became mail carriers. Claude was substitute carrier until
December, 1914 when he was appointed rural mail carrier for Wetonka, SD. He
carried mail in Wetonka for 27 years. He stayed active in the affairs of the
county seat.

The Chitticks had three sons:

William Douglas Chittick, born at Bowdle, SD in 1906. He married Bernice
Herther in 1936, while he was serving as County Superintendent of Schools
(1933-1937). He later became High School Supt., then Deputy State Supt. of
Public Instruction and Director of Curriculum and Research in Pierre. He served
as Professor of Rural Sociology, teaching and research at SDSU for 28 years. He
is serving his second five-year term as City Finance Commissioner for
Brookings, SD.

Ellsworth Chittick was born at Leola in 1908, and married Althea Hohman,
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. John Hohman of Leola. Ellsworth was rural mail carrier
in Wetonka. and later in Aberdeen, SD. Later he was in business in Mesa, AZ.
They are now retired and live in Nalcrest, Florida.

Malcolm (Dude) Chittick, born at Leola in 1914, married Grace Klinger of
Aberdeen. He worked in Gamble stores in Midland, MI and Fort Dodge, IA, then
traveled for Pfizer in western Iowa and eastern Nebraska until his death in
1967.

Claude passed away at his home in Wetonka in 1942 and Helen passed away in
1967.

PERRY and NINA CONAHAN

Perry Anthony Conahan was born August 16, 1898 in Amboy, IL. His grandparents
had migrated to Philadelphia, PA from Ireland when it was having a potato
famine. Perry's father John M. Conahan was born in Philadelphia and his mother
Theresa (McGovern) Conahan was born in Amboy, IL where they were married
October 13, 1887 and made their home. They had a family of eight boys and two
girls. Two boys and the two girls died in early childhood.

Perry was the second to the youngest in age. He and his brother Bryan had
become acquainted with Mr. and Mrs. S. D. Frost, whose farm was within walking
distance of Amboy. Here they spent many happy hours.

When South Dakota was receiving an influx of settlers from Europe, the S. D.
Frosts also moved to Leola and bought land in McPherson County. Mr. Frost was a
cattle buyer and rancher. Mrs. Frost operated a hotel located on the lot where
the present Lechner Hotel stands.

Perry's mother died at a young age and his father moved to Cody, WY to farm.
Perry, being one of the younger children, was raised in Denver, CO in an
Orphans' Home which was under the supervision of Catholic Sisters. He received
his education in Denver, a part of which time he attended Sacred Heart Academy.

He came to Leola after leaving the Home and stayed with the S. D. Frosts and
worked on their ranch.

In 1917, Perry enlisted in the Army and served through World War I. After his
discharge from the Army, he traveled to Los Angeles, CA, where four of his
brothers lived. He obtained employment doing restaurant work, learned the
business, and later operated a cafe there.

In 1924, he made a trip to Amboy, IL and then to Leola to renew old
friendships. He stayed at the home of Mrs. M. Blanche Frost.

The Luncheonette on Lot 17, block 6, operated by Mrs. Karolina Krause, was for
sale. Perry bought it in 1925 and began its operation, naming it Perry's Place.

Perry married Miss Nina Martinson of Ellendale, ND on June 2, 1926. She was a
teacher in the Leola school system. She had taught seven years in North Dakota,
her last year being at Marmarth. She came to Leola at the suggestion of her
Leola friends, the Dr. E. A. Gillette family. She joined the teaching staff
September, 1925.

Nina was born October 11, 1901, rural Ellendale, ND. Her parents John and
Elizabeth (Muckala) Martinson were pioneer settlers in Dakota Territory in
Dickey County, ND. Their native land was Finland. They were members of the
Apostolic Lutheran Church. Nina was confirmed in the same faith.

        The Perry A. Conahan Family. Back: Walter and Lee. Front: Perry and
        Nina.

Two sons were born to Nina and Perry: Walter Charles on April 20, 1927, and Lee
Eugene on January 26, 1930.

Perry, with the help of his wife and sons, continued operating the restaurant
for many years. Perry was active in civic affairs, and local politics, and
vitally interested in education. He was a member of the Local American Legion
Post and belonged to the Elks Lodge in Aberdeen, SD. His church preference was
Catholic.

In April of 1947, he was elected Mayor of Leola, serving one term. He decided
against serving another term.

Nina was a member of the American Legion Auxiliary, the Disco Study Club, and
the Star Extension Club. She was a member of St. Paul's Lutheran Church and
Ladies Aid.

On Sunday morning, March 7, 1954, Perry died from a coronary thrombosis. He was
buried March 10, 1954 in the cemetery south of Leola. Perry's death marked the
end of the longest period in Leola history (30 years) in which a local
restaurant was operated by the same individual. Both sons returned home to
assist their mother in the cafe. Nina, realizing that her sons' interests lay
elsewhere, decided to sell the business. Keith and Vera Durnil bought it in the
fall of 1955 and assumed proprietorship December 1st. Nina had an auction sale
and left Leola. She enrolled at the State Normal Industrial College at
Ellendale, ND and completed the requirements for a Bachelor of Science degree
in education, which was granted to her on August 1, 1958. She taught in
LaMoure, ND, then continued her education at Syracuse University, NY, came back
to LaMoure where she taught another year. She then accepted a position at
Clinton Elementary School, Prince George's County, MD and taught there for ten
years. She retired in 1968 but lived on in Clinton until her sons decided to
leave the Washington vicinity. She moved to Brookings in September of 1978 and
still resides there. Nina is an active member of Mt. Calvary Lutheran Church,
Ladies Aid and Golden Age. She belongs to the Brookings Area Retired Teachers
Association, Memorial Art Guild and does volunteer work there once a month. She
is also a member of the Brookings Hospital Auxiliary.

LEE and JEANETTE CONAHAN

Lee Conahan was born January 26, 1930 at Leola, SD. His parents are Nina and
Perry Conahan. Jeanette Walth Conahan was born May 23, 1933 to Gottfried and
Lily Walth in Bowdle, SD. Lee and Jeanette were married June 26, 1955 in St.
James Lutheran Church in Leola.

Both Lee and Jeanette graduated from Leola High School. Jeanette graduated from
Northern State and Lee from SDSU in Brookings.

Lee worked in the family cafe in Leola following the death of his father, for
one year. Jeanette taught in Brookings while Lee worked at the Brookings
Register.

Lee and Jeanette have four children: Cary Jay, born July 1, 1959, living in
Houston, TX; Kay Ellen, born June 4, 1961, also living in Houston; Peggy Jean,
born February 4, 1963, who passed away November 6, 1977; and Kelly Ann, born
March 21, 1965. While attending John Foster Dulles High School she was listed
as an outstanding High School Athlete.

        The Lee Conahan Family. Back: Kay and Lee. Front: Jeanette, Cary and
        Kelly.

Due to Lee's employment they have lived in many cities: Brookings, SD,
Arlington, VA, Rockville, MD, Oklahoma City, OK, Houston, TX, Missouri City,
TX, Sioux Falls, SD, and Manchester, MO. They are now back in Missouri City.
Lee is the present owner of a recruiting firm in Houston, TX. Jeanette is
presently employed as a pricing coordinator for Handy Den Improvement Center in
Houston.

WALTER C. and MARJORIE CONAHAN

Most Leolans can remember a young man, Walter C. Conahan, working in a
family-owned restaurant during the '40s and early '50s. Walter, son of Perry
and Nina Conahan was born April 20, 1927 at Leola. He attended grade school and
high school in Leola and SD State University in Brookings, SD. Walt served with
the U.S. Army in the Philippine Islands and received an honorable discharge in
1947. He returned to South Dakota to begin work toward a bachelors degree in
journalism. After graduation he became Associate Editor of the Clear Lake
Courier in Clear Lake, SD, working until 1955 when he resigned to assist in the
family restaurant in Leola. In November of 1955 he was appointed Staff
Assistant to U.S. Representative Harold O. Lovre, Washington, DC, followed by a
1957 appointment to Rep. R. Walter Riehlman, Washington, DC. In 1958 Conahan
started a 14-year stint as press secretary for the late Karl Mundt. Since then
he has held numerous appointments and been the recipient of many honors and
awards.

Walt married Marjorie Dean October 27, 1957 at LaMoure, ND. Marjorie is a
native of LaMoure, ND, and was a member of Senator Milton Young's staff in
Washington, DC, where she met Walt. Her parents farmed near LaMoure and her
grandparents were Dakota pioneers. Walt and Marjorie have one child, Christine
Mary, who was born October 5, 1958. Christine is married to Roger Barthelman
and lives in Sioux Falls, SD.

        The Walter C. Conahan Family. Back: Son-in-law Roger, Marjorie and
        Christine. Front: Walter and Nina.

Walt has many fond memories of Leola. He is particularly proud of being manager
of the 1948 Leola Independent Basketball team, which won the State American
Legion tournament championship representing South Dakota at the national
tournament in Jeffersonville, IN. Walt was commencement speaker for Leola's
graduating class of 1976. (Bicentennial year.)

Walter was elected State Senator to the SD Legislature from 6th District,
Brookings County, November 1982. He is serving on numerous committees on state
affairs. Walt and family reside in Volga, SD.

JOHN H. and MARY ANN CONLON

John H. Conlon was born July 9, 1868 at Morris, IL. Mary Ann was born August
15, 1870 at Emmetsburg, IA. They were married in Iowa on April 21, 1890.

In 1908 they and their family moved to McPherson County, SD. They came by train
to Wetonka and brought their stock, machinery and household goods by immigrant

        Mary & John Conlon.

IRA K. and ETTA MAE CRIST

Ira K. Crist was born at Montgomery, NY, on November 12, 1874, and while yet a
small boy moved with his parents to Waverly, KS. There he grew to manhood.

        Ira & Etta Mae Crist.

He married Etta Mae Jennings on March 27, 1901, and soon afterwards moved to
Winfield, IA, where he was engaged in farming. He moved with his wife and five
children, Deo, Esther, Lee, Wayne and Eva to South Dakota in the spring of
1909, and settled on a farm in Willow Township, six miles east and two miles
south of Leola. Besides farming he raised cattle and hogs. Mr. Crist served on

He resided on the farm until he passed away on June 16, 1931. Of the five
children only Deo Crist of Golden, CO, and Eva Crouch of Sturgis, SD, survive.

THOMAS and LYDIA CROMPTON

Thomas Crompton was born in Attica, WI, May 31, 1857. Tom Crompton filed on a
homestead of three quarters of land, four miles east and six miles south of
Leola in 1882. By 1889, the place was paid for and the deed signed by Benjamin
Harrison, President of the United States.

Some of the lumber for the house he built was transported from Wisconsin.

The first Registered Hereford cattle in the area were owned by Tom.

The second artesian well in the area was drilled on the farm about 1904 and a
small flow is still running.

The children of Thomas Crompton and Lydia (McKinney) Crompton, who was born at
Attica, WI, in 1864, are: Myrtle (Boyle), Orin Robert (known as Demmie),
Frances and Pearl.

The children of Thomas Crompton and Caroline (Mattatall) Crompton, who was born
at Tatamagouche, Nova Scotia, Canada, in 1878, are: Mary Ann, Hazel (Averill),
Bessie (Stephenson), Lloyd Thomas, known as L. T., Max, Lee, Lewis, Brian,
Alice Madeline and Marie (Wells).

Tom leased a piece of the NW 1/4 and a schoolhouse was built. The Boyles and
Crpmptons comprised the biggest attendance, as Tom had 13 children and Myrtle
Boyle, his daughter had ten children. School location--25-125-67.

He traded in Leola and Aberdeen until Wetonka was built.

In 1928, Tom, Carrie and two of the children moved to Molalla, OR, to a 20-acre
farm, leaving the place to be farmed by two sons, Max and Lee, who later moved
to Oregon. It was then farmed by the oldest son, L. T. At the present time, the
farm is owned by L. T.'s son, Tom Crompton. The original house is still
standing but the rest of the buildings have long gone.

L. T. and FERN CROMPTON

Lloyd Thomas Crompton was born September 4, 1902 at Wetonka, the son of Tom and
Caroline Crompton. He spent his boyhood and youth on the farm that Tom Crompton
homesteaded in Washington Township. He attended country school until the sixth
grade when work on the farm made it impossible for him to continue formal
schooling.

L. T. and Fern (Hamilton) Crompton, who was born in Duluth, Minnesota, had five
children. They are Josephine Lucille, Lewis Lloyd, Mary Lou and Leo. An infant
died at birth.

Lucille was born in 1924. "Jo" married Jack Green from Wetonka and has five
children: Judith (Westover), Clark Allen, Patricia Ann, Kathy Jo and Virginia.
Lucille is now Mrs. George Goodfellow living at Lebanon, SD

Lewis Lloyd was born in 1927. He married Jennifer Weicken and has a daughter,
Heather. They reside in California.

        Lloyd T. & Fern Crompton.

Mary Lou was born in 1930. She is married to Marvin Kamm. They have four
children: Tony, Sandy, Terry and Casey.

Leo was born in 1933. He married Viola Liedle. He has two stepchildren and
three grandchildren.

Mrs. Crompton died in 1935. In 1937, L. T. and the children went to Oregon to
spend the winter. He returned to the farm in the spring, leaving Lucille and
Lewis with relatives in Oregon.

L. T. and Grace LaBay, who was born at Brentford, SD, in 1917, were married in
1938, making their home in Stratford, SD. Later that year, L. T. went to Oregon
to bring his children home.

They started their journey home in a 1935 Chevrolet truck, the children bedded
down in straw in the truck box with a canvas covering the top of the box. The
children were not feeling well when they left Oregon, but an Oregon doctor
assured L. T. that their ailments were minor.

As their journey progressed across dirt roads and rugged mountain passes, the
children became more ill. When they arrived home with very sick children, the
doctor diagnosed "scarlet fever" and the family was quarantined for six weeks.
Although some of the family members were critically ill, all survived.

In the spring of 1939, L. T. and family moved to the family farm in Washington
Township and they lived there until 1946 when L. T. purchased the Hutton farm
in Lincoln Township two miles north of Wetonka, and moved there in the fall. He
farmed the land on both farms.

During the drought years of the '30s, L. T. worked various ways to earn income
when the farm would not produce. He trucked hay and grain and hauled coal from
Firesteel, SD. He trapped fur-bearing animals and sold their pelts.

In the '40s, after W.P.A. built the Wetonka Dam, he "put up ice." With an ice
cutting machine, large blocks of ice were cut from the frozen creek. Albert
Beilke, Wetonka, SD, hauled the ice to Leola where it was sold to Rod Ronayne
and customers. The ice was stored in straw-insulated buildings to be sold to
use in "ice boxes" to keep food cool in the summer.

Four children were born to L. T. and Grace. Dorothy, born in 1938, married
Gerald Hoffman and has three children. Jackie Ray was born in 1941. Jack passed
away in 1964 after a long struggle with muscular dystrophy. Caroline (Kelli),
born in 1942, married Richard Waltman and has three children. They live on the
Crompton farm at Wetonka. Thomas Richard, born in 1944, married Susan Lott from
Kent, Washington. They have two children. Thomas and Susan have served as
missionaries in Ghana, Africa since 1981. One of their children (James) was
born in Africa.

L. T. died July I, 1964. In 1969 Grace married Martin Waltman and now lives
near Aberdeen.

DAVID NELSON and ELIZABETH CROUCH

David Crouch was born in Tennessee, on June 18, 1853, and at a young age moved
with his family to Missouri, going up the rivers in flat boats with their
livestock and family possessions. He remembered having slaves, and several, not
wanting to be left behind went with the family to Missouri. He spent his early
years in Missouri, teaching school and working in a merchantile store, which he
later purchased and managed for several years.

        David Crouch.

He married Elizabeth Hurt in 1883, in Humphrey, MO. Elizabeth taught music
lessons and was very active in the Christian Church. David served two terms in
the legislature. When ill health forced him to leave the merchantile, he traded
the business for land in South Dakota and in the spring of 1908, he moved with
his wife and one son, Joseph Elwood Crouch, to McPherson County, settling on a
farm two and a half miles north of Leola, in Leola Township. He engaged in
farming and ranching.

The family had the misfortune of losing their home and all of their belongings
in a fire, while the family was in town. They moved in with a family living a
half mile north until a home could be moved from the town of Leola. A few years
later a tornado took the barn.

David was one of the founders of the Leola Equity Exchange Elevator and served
on the board for several years. In 1920, they rented their farm with the
intention of spending some time visiting in Illinois and Missouri. When word
came of the elevator having financial difficulties they returned to Leola,
renting a home in town until they could move back to the farm. David served on
the South Dakota Legislature during 1925 and 1926. In the spring of 1940, they
moved from the farm north of Leola, to the Art Hickman farm in Weber Township,
north of Leola, where they resided until he passed away March 5, 1944.
Elizabeth had passed away in 1941.

JOSEPH ELWOOD and EVA CROUCH

Elwood was born in Humphrey, MO, on November 26, 1900, to David N. and
Elizabeth (Hurt) Crouch. In the spring of 1908, the family moved to Leola,
where he grew up, attending school in Leola and Mitchell, SD. He married Eva
Crist, on August 5, 1926, and on March 7, 1927, Margaret June (Shafer) was
born. Audrey Mae (Geffre) was born on January 7, 1931 and their only son James
Wesley was born on May 19, 1932.

        Eva & Elwood Crouch.

They survived the "Dirty '30s," when there was no rain, just dust storms. There
were many days when the kerosene lamps were lit during the day. The dirt
covered fences as high as the fence posts and the grasshoppers ate what little
garden they tried to raise. Cow chips were gathered from the pastures and used
for fuel. They also used straw burners to keep warm during the winter. Prices
were so low, Elwood hauled a triple wagon box of corn into town to sell to buy
coal, and being unable to sell the corn, he hauled it back home and they burned
the corn in the hard coal burner that winter. Eva remembers when eggs sold for
five cents a dozen.

They lived in the Leola area until 1949, when they moved to Havre, MT, where
they worked on a ranch until 1968, after which they moved to Sturgis, SD.
Elwood passed away July 4, 1977. Thirteen grandchildren, 14
great-grandchildren, and one great great-grandchild are descendants of Elwood
and Eva.

JOHN and DOROTHY DALY

to Leola that same year and have made their home here. John teaches Industrial
Arts at the Leola School and Dorothy works at the Leola State Bank. They have
three children: Christopher, age eight; Rebecca Ann, age six; and Stephanie,

BELA E. and SUSAN DEXTER

Bela E. Dexter (born June 10, 1836), his wife Susan nee Bump, (born September
25, 1838), and three of their children were the first known settlers of Koto
Township and among the first to settle in the Leola community. Like John Murrie
in Leola Township, Dexter arrived on his preemption claim on May 5, 1883. The
Dexters were an established family of Gowanda in western New York (40 miles
south of Buffalo), whose principal livelihood came from the operation of their
sawmill and the sale of maple syrup .

Bela, in his mid-twenties, served in the Army during the Civil War. He became
seriously ill with diphtheria and was discharged. Through the patient and
attentive care of his wife, Susan, Bela, unlike most who had the dreaded
disease during the war, did not die. Two of their small children contracted the
contagious diphtheria and died. Only William, the eldest, survived. Subsequent
to this adversity, three other children, Dollie (1873), John (1878) and Edith
(1881) were born to the family.

A year after Edith's birth, Bela still suffering the aftereffects of his
illness, thought a change in climate would be helpful. He and a friend heard
that virgin land was being made available to the public in the Dakota Territory
and took a train to Frederick, SD. Bela found land 19 miles west of Frederick
that would be surveyed during the summer of 1883. After persuading his
45-year-old wife to move, Bela sold the family sawmill to their oldest son,
William, and began the long journey to the Dakota Territory in the spring of
1883.

After finding temporary housing for his family in Frederick, Bela purchased
lumber and building supplies. On May 5, he began construction on a two-story
house on the NE 1/4 of Section 26 in Koto Township, 1 1/2 miles east of the new
village of Koto. In 1884, Bela increased his land holdings by filing a timber
claim entry on the SE 1/4 of Section 23 which was successfully patented in
1898.

The family returned to Gowanda, NY for the winter months. This provided an
opportunity for Dollie and John to continue their education since neither Koto
nor Leola had schools in 1883. Susan was a proficient organist and the Dexter
home was one of the few homes of that day equipped with an organ. Susan taught
daughter Dollie to play. Over the years many early settlers and their children
learned to play the piano and organ through the mother and daughter' s
instruction . Their musical talent was especially appreciated at Leola's
Methodist church where both were active in religious affairs.

In the beginning days, farm life was made much easier through neighbor helping
neighbor. In most cases, cooperation meant the difference between success and
failure. Bela and his neighbor, Carl Schuchardt, began working together the
first summer in 1883. Lacking a threshing machine, they threshed grain through
the use of oxen walking continuously in a large circle over cut grain. In order
to purchase the first McCormick binder, when it became available in Koto and
Carl townships, Dexter agreed to let it be used to cut all the small grain in
the two townships. Because the community need for the binder was vast, it was
used around the clock as long as good harvesting conditions prevailed. In the
fall of 1884, threshing machines became available to the settlers. Because of
the Dexters' generosity, 30 or more spirited men gathered at Dexters and
threshed 220 bushels of grain by hitching themselves to the doubletrees, and
powered the threshing machine with manpower.

Bela Dexter was a willing public servant right from the start of McPherson
County's organization in 1884. During that year he served as the county's
central area justice of the peace, as Road District No. 2 supervisor and as
election judge in the central area, along with James L. Dow and Zechariah
Spitler. He continued to be of public service over 20 years.

Each of the Dexter children married spouses who were neighbors. Dollie married
Charles W. Schuchardt and had five children; John married Mary Lapka and had
three children; while Edith married John Lapka and bore nine daughters and
three sons. The children grew to adulthood in the Leola area.

At the age of 67, on December 19, 1903, Bela Dexter died of a stroke and was
buried in the St. Hyacinth's Catholic Cemetery (SE 1/4 of Section 25) in
southeastern Koto Township. Susan Dexter, died at age of 80, on July 2, 1919,
while living with her daughter. At Susan Dexter's request she was buried at
Gowanda, NY, next to four of their children who died in infancy before the
family moved to Dakota Territory.

OTTO and EVA DOCKTER

ALBERT and LYDIA EICHELBERG

Albert Eichelberg was born on February 12, 1909 in Arena Township, McPherson
County, 13 miles west and one mile north of Leola, the son of John and Pauline
Eichelberg. He attended elementary school with his sister Adella, who was one
year older, in a small, one-room schoolhouse in Arena Township. School was in
session only seven months of the year. After finishing the eighth grade he
attended Leola High School and graduated in 1926 in a class of 11 students. The
total enrollment in high school that year was 54. After graduating from high
school, he attended Northern State College at Aberdeen SD. It was then known as
Northern Normal and Industrial School. He then taught school several years in
Arena Township, one year in the same school that he attended when he was a boy.
He also taught in the adjoining township of Moscow.

In 1930 Albert married Lydia Schaffer from Glenham, SD.

        Lydia and Albert Eichelberg.

In 1932 the couple settled on a farm in Moscow Township and started farming.
This was just at the beginning of the great depression and also the beginning
of the drought of the '30 s. Crops in 1932 were good but the price of farm
products continued to decline. John Schlagel, manager of the Barzen Grain
Elevator at Leola, saved a card with price quotations of grain for many years.
The quotations on this card were: spring wheat, 25 cents per bushel, rye, 15
cents per bushel, barley, 11 cents per bushel, oats, six cents per bushel,
shelled corn, two cents per bushel and ear corn three cents less. Prices for
other farm products were not any better. Yearling calves brought from two to
three cents per pound, eggs were taken to the grocery store and traded for
groceries, for which the grocer allowed six cents per dozen. At these prices it
was almost impossible to make a living and pay operating expenses. Some farmers
burned barley and ear corn in the space heater to heat their houses. Cow chips
were gathered in the pasture and used as fuel in the cook stove. In 1937 and
1938 grasshoppers became very numerous and devoured much of what little crop
there was.

In order to supplement the farm income, Albert would teach school when there
was need of a teacher in a school close by. He remembers teaching school in
1935 at $40 per month and in 1937-1938 for $50 per month.

By 1940 the severe drought had ended and the economic conditions improved.
World War 1 also gave the economy a boost.

The Eichelbergs had one son, Floyd, born in 1932, who resides with his family
in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas.

In 1956 Albert and Lydia discontinued farming and moved to Leola. Albert was
employed by Ed Rueb, proprietor of Rueb Chevrolet, dealer of Chevrolet cars and
trucks and Oliver tractors and farm implements. After almost six years in the
employ of Ed Rueb, when Mr. Rueb passed away, Albert went to teaching school
again. He taught school several years, two of which were again in Arena
Township. Later he was employed by Leola Equity Exchange, Oil Department, as
bookkeeper.

In 1973 the Eichelbergs moved to Spearfish, SD, where they presently reside.
Albert operates his own janitorial supply business, visiting Leola two or three
times every year.

Albert and Lydia are members of the Seventh-Day Adventist Church. Albert has
served as youth leader, treasurer and deacon and is presently serving as elder
in the Spearfish Seventh-Day Adventist Church.

CHRISTIAN and KAROLINA EICHELBERG

Christian Eichelberg, son of Johann and Rosina (Engel) Eichelberg was born June
2, 1890, Gluckstal, South Russia, where the parents lived and the father worked
as a blacksmith.

The family immigrated to the United States in 1900. Christian had five
brothers: John, Fred, Gottlieb, Jacob and John and two sisters Rosina (Lechner)
who died during the flu epidemic, and Katherina (Ott). One elder brother John
died in Russia and Jacob died of the flu during the travel to the United
States. It was a common practice at that time if the older son died, the next
son would carry the same name.

The family homesteaded in Moscow Township, McPherson County. The father passed
away in March 1901 and was buried on the homestead. The mother and children
continued to live on the homestead in a two-room sod house. With no one to help
support the family, she was forced to hire the children out. In those days,
they herded cattle to keep them out of the wheat fields, as there were no
fences. The children walked over a mile to school, and many times in winter
their lunch would be frozen. The one-room schoolhouse consisted of a pot belly
stove and desks. The children received formal education only to the second or
third grade.

As a young man, Christian worked with the threshing crews for several years. In
1916, Rosina purchased a home in Leola. Christian and his mother each lost some
of their savings when the banks failed in 1925.

On February 6, 1912, Christian married Karolina Ketterling. Four sons were born
to this union: Emil, who died in infancy, Erwin, Oscar and Christian Frederick.
Karolina passed away November 3, 1918, during the flu epidemic, as well as
infant son Christian, born at the time. Burial was in the Salem Lutheran
Cemetery, Moscow Township, 15 miles west of Leola.

Christian moved to Leola and was a cream buyer for several years and served as
City Alderman.

He remarried January 17, 1921, to Lydia Koth and to this union six children
were born: Olive (Lafer), Verna (Barger), Alvin (served in the U.S. Air Force),
Martin (served in the U.S. Navy), Alma (Mittlieder) and Elmer (served in the
U.S. Navy). All the children attended Moscow School No. 1.

        Lydia and Christian Eichelberg.

In 1927, the family returned to Moscow Township where they built a new home,
and the current house was constructed in 1933.

In 1946, Erwin bought the farm and the parents purchased a home in Leola.
Christian did carpentry and plumbing work and also was City Justice of the
Peace.

Lydia passed away May 11, 1964 at the age of 66 and Christian on June 11, 1970
at the age of 80. Burial was in the Salem Lutheran Cemetery.

The present owner of the farm is Duane Fink.

GOTTLIEB and KATHERINE EICHELBERG

Gottlieb Eichelberg was born June 17, 1894, in Gluckstal, South Russia to
Johann and Rosine (Engel) Eichelberg. In 1900, Gottlieb, his parents, brothers
John Fred, Christian. Jacob. and one sister Rose came to the United States and
settled on the prairie to make a home 18 miles west of Leola, SD. Brother Jacob
died on the trip to America and was buried at sea. Within a year of their
arrival the father died and the youngest daughter Katherine (Mrs. Kate Ott) was
born. Growing up consisted of hard work with only a few months school in
winter. Gottlieb worked for farmers in the area until his marriage to Katherine
Leicht on February 29, 1916.

Katherine was the daughter of Christian and Katherine (Spitzer) Leicht, born
May 17, 1895. Her home was several miles south of Long Lake, where she learned
well the duties of cooking, cleaning and gardening. She became an excellent
seamstress, sewing for many wherever she lived. She had four brothers, Christ,
Jacob, Fred and Emil, and one sister, Magdalena Bertsch. Emil died as a youth.
Another sister, Katherine, died in infancy.

        David Thomas, Gottlieb and Katherine Eichelberg and Charlotte Thomas.

After their marriage they lived on the Eichelberg homestead where their only
daughter Leone (Mrs. David Thomas) was born. In 1925 they sold their farm, and
moved to Leola in 1926. Gottlieb worked in a garage for several years. He also
worked for John Heibel and Sons in the cattle buying business and did carpentry
until his retirement. Gottlieb died in January, 1980. Their two grandchildren
are David Thomas and Charlotte Thomas (Mrs. Robert Roe), and two
great-grandchildren David and Natalie Roe.

JOHN and PAULINE EICHELBERG

In 1901 John Eichelberg, then a lad of 17, came to the United States with his
parents John and Rosina Eichelberg. They came from the village of Gluckstal in
southern Russia. The family homesteaded in Moscow Township. Two years later
John's father died, and it was up to John to manage the farming operation as he
was the oldest of the four boys in the family. He also had two sisters. The
land where they lived was all prairie and very rocky. Before it could be
farmed, the rocks had to be dug out and hauled away. It was then broke up with
a walking plow and four horses. In this way 15 or 20 acres could be cleared and
broken up every spring. However, they did put up considerable wild hay, more
than was needed for the few horses and cows they had. In the winter John would
haul hay to Eureka, a distance of 20 miles, with a hayrack on the bobsled, and
sell it to the livery barn or to draymen for two dollars per ton.

When John reached the age of 21 he took up homesteading in the adjoining Arena
Township. This was mostly all prairie and had to be cleared of rock and broke
up in order to plant the crops.

        John and Pauline Eichelberg.

In January 1907, John married Pauline Heupel, who had come to the United States
in 1898 with her parents the George Heupels. They had settled in Arena Township
a few miles east from where John lived. John had put up a two-room house on the
land he homesteaded. A sod barn was also put up to house the four horses and
the few cows they owned. Every spring John would break up 15 or 20 acres and
plant it to flax. The following year this would be planted to wheat or oats.
Wheat was the main cash crop and oats was used for feed for the horses. The sod
barn was used for several years until it was replaced by a frame barn. Other
buildings were added as needed. In 1915 the Eichelbergs put up a two-story
house in which they lived until they left the farm and moved to Leola in 1939.
As time went on they were able to purchase additional land.

John and Pauline had three children: one girl, Adella, and two boys, Albert and
Arnold.

In 1939 they retired from active farming and moved to Leola. The farm was taken
over by the younger son, Arnold, who still resides on the farm.

Living in Leola, John continued to work, doing carpenter work, cement work, and
some painting.

John lived to be almost 90 years of age and passed away in 1973. Pauline passed
away a few years later.

REUBEN and BERNICE EHRESMAN

Reuben Ehresman was born to Philip and Christina (Rieger) Ehresman at Long
Lake. There were five children born to his parents, one deceased.

Reuben attended rural school and in 1951 formed a partnership with his father
until 1953 when his parents retired and moved to Ashley, ND.

Reuben married Anna Bernice Hoffman of Ashley, ND, on June 21, 1953. They have
three children: Linda (Mrs. Jerome Miles) of Aberdeen, Ronnie, who is in
partnership with his father, and Lanette, a student at Leola.

Reuben and Bernice still live on the same farm where his grandparents Jacob and
Louise (Rau) Ehresman took up a homestead in Wacker Township in the late
1880's.

ALFRED and NELLIE ETTLES

The late Alfred Ettles' father, George Ettles, emigrated from Scotland to the
province of Quebec, Canada, in the early 1870's. His parents and a sister
remained near Fochabers, in northern Scotland.

George married Mary Boughner, and the first three of seven children were born,
Lili, Chauncey and Wallace. In the late 1880's the family came to Turner
County, SD where Mable, Clyde, Olyve, and Alfred were born.

After the turn of the century, the family moved to a farm near Mina, SD. George
died there. In 1919, Alfred moved to the Byers and Anderson ranch southwest of
Leola. His nephew, George Hammond helped him operate it at first. Later, his
brother Clyde Ettles and family joined him for a time. Two rodeos were held
there.

Mary, his mother died in 1934.

In 1935, Alfred married Nellie Silver. Three daughters were born and grew to
share their parents' love of horses and of ranch life.

        George & Nellie Ettles.

The ranch became known as the Stockade. Alfred made many long drives, bringing
cattle and horses to summer pasture, and returning them to the owners in the
fall. A very efficient set of corrals, chutes, and a large branding chute had
been built to handle the herds. Later, an adjustable loading chute was designed
and built by Alfred to accommodate double-decker semi-trailers.

In 1942, Nellie's parents, Art and Clara Silver came from Edmunds County to
make their home with them. In March, 1948, Nellie suffered a broken back in a
fall from a load of hay, becoming instantly paralyzed below the level of her
chest, and spent over a year in hospitals. At 80, 'Grandma' Silver shouldered
the responsibilities of the home. Their fourth daughter was born in October and
was taken into the home of their dear friends, the Wilbert Engel's for a year.

Following that, Nellie and the girls were cared for in the home of her brother,
Raymond Silver and family in Madison, WI, for one school term. They had sold
the ranch to Paul Bollman. Alfred stayed at the ranch, and Mr. and Mrs. Silver
lived with their son Charles and family in Leola that winter. In the spring,
Alfred formed a partnership with the Bollmans, and after the Eph Jones house
was moved to the ranch, the family was together again. Mr. Silver died there in
1951.

In 1952 the partnership was dissolved. The older girls took active parts in the
ranch work besides caring for their mother, until they married and began their
own families.

The family retired and moved to Leola in 1965. In 1968, Mrs. Silver died at the
age of 100 years and six months. After a long illness Alfred died in 1982.

The daughters and their families are: Carol (Mrs. James Rempfer) of Winside,
NE, Mark, wife Jean, and Kate of Norfolk, NE, and Boyd, of Winside, NE; Mary
(Mrs. Adolph Zantow) of Leola, Alfred, of Chicago, Byron, Robert, and Marian of
Leola; Josephine (Mrs. Reinhardt Potratz) of Leola, Julie (Mrs. Wayne Meagher)
and Derek of Aberdeen, SD; Donna (Mrs. Rollin Stearns), Celeste, Michael, and
Susan, of Hecla, SD, Norman, and Lindsey of Webstel, SD; and Victoria of
Ipswich, SD.

JAMES and GERTRUDE FARLEY

The James Farley family lived in Lincoln Township but had several close ties
with Leola. Jim and Gertrude (Lorber) Farley moved to the Wetonka area to the
home of Gertrude's parents in 1930. Gertrude was born December 3, 1899, to
Louis Lorber who had come to Aberdeen from France in 1883, and Ellen (Carr)
Lorber. Gertrude was an only child but had an adopted brother John. Ellen
Lorber died in 1943. In 1945 Louis was married to Clara Farley (James' mother).
James Farley was born at Spencer, SD, April 18, 1900. Jim and Gertrude had been
living in Custer, SD, since their 1929 wedding at Wetonka.

        James and Gertrude Farley.

They were members of the Catholic Church in Leola. They became the parents of
four daughters. Joan, married September, 1962 to Clair Walter, is a registered
nurse in Aberdeen, SD. Jean married Joe Hauck, June, 1951, and works at Sacred
Heart School in Aberdeen, SD. Jean has three daughters and six grandchildren.
Patricia, married April, 1953 to Henry Waltman, works at St. Luke's Hospital
and lives in Aberdeen, SD. Pat had two daughters. Mary, married February, 1961,
to Rudy Cornay, is a registered nurse in Hot Springs, SD. She has three
children, two girls and one boy.

Jim spent many years involved with the A.S.C. office in Leola, much of the time
as manager. He left there in the late 1950's. During those years he became
acquainted with almost all the farmers in McPherson County. He was also
involved in the Better Leola Club. Gertrude had been a teacher previous to her
marriage. She returned to teaching in 1949 and taught in several township
schools (Washington, Willow and Wetonka schools).

The family continued their membership in the Leola Catholic Church where all
the girls were confirmed and Jean was married. Joan, Jean and Pat graduated
from Leola High School.

In 1959 Jim and Gertrude, together with Louis and Clara Lorber, sold the farm
the Lorbers had moved on in 1914 and moved to Custer, SD. Louis and Clara
Lorber both died in 1963. Jim was self-employed as a carpenter until his death
in Custer in 1965. Gertrude had taught in Rockerville and Hill City, SD, and
was teaching at Sanator, SD, at the time of her death in January, 1968.

JACOB and CHRISTINA FAUTH

Jacob Fauth was born January 6, 1874, in Bergdorf, South Russia and as a young
man migrated to the United States.

He met Christina Goehring in Eureka, SD, and they were wed December 17, 1896.

Christina Goehring was born in Marinburg, South Russia on November 8, 1876, and
then migrated to America in 1889 with her parents and brothers and sisters.

Jacob and Christina started a homestead about 15 miles northwest of Leola.

Twelve children were born to this union. They are: Christopher, born October 8,
1897; Albina, October 24, 1900; Magdalena, February 7, 1902; Jacob, November
16, 1904; Christina, January 25, 1907; Edward, March 10, 1909; John, December
10, 1910; Arthur, August 3, 1912; Elizabeth, February 13, 1914; Hertha, January
10, 1916; Jacob, February 9, 1918; and Oscar, born November 29, 1920.

Scarlet fever struck in the early winter of 1911 and within a week four
children died: Albina, Magdalena, Jacob and Christina.

Jacob and his family continued farming until 1943 when they decided to retire
and bought a home in Leola. Jacob passed away February 14, 1945, and Christina
continued living at her home in Leola until she passed away July 2, 1955.

ARTHUR and AMELIA FAUTH

Art and Amelia grew up in the Long Lake area. Art is the son of Jacob and
Christina (Goehring) Fauth, born August 3, 1912, at Long Lake, SD. Amelia is
the daughter of Christoph and Christina (Schumacher) Hoffman, born November 10,
1914, at Long Lake, SD.

        Arthur and Amelia Fauth.

Art and Amelia were married November, 1937, and moved to a farm in the Forbes
area on November 26th. October 15, 1945, they moved to a farm near Leola where
they still reside. They are the parents of one son, Myron. Myron married Sheila
Scheid and they have three children: Leisha, Launa and Jason.

The Fauths are members of the St. James Lutheran Church in Leola.

JOHN and LORRAINE FAUTH

John Fauth, son of Jacob and Christina (Goehring) Fauth was born near Long Lake
on December 7, 1910. He farmed with his parents until he was inducted into the
Army. He served some time in the Aleutians.

In 1949 he married Lorraine Steiger, daughter of Albert and Christina
(Stoecker) Steiger. She was born January 17, 1921, on her parents' farm
southwest of Leola. They made their home in Leola. John farmed near Leola and
Lorraine was employed as Deputy County Auditor and later as Deputy County
Treasurer.

In 1970 John suffered a heart attack and was forced to quit farming. In 1974 he
passed away following heart bypass surgery.

Lorraine continued to live in Leola. She was recently appointed County
Treasurer to fill the unexpired term of Ed Rall who resigned. She is a member
of St. James Lutheran Church, ALCW, Legion Auxiliary and Leola Ladies Golf
Club.

MYRON and SHEILA FAUTH

Myron Fauth was born on July 17, 1942, to Arthur and Amelia (Hoffman) Fauth. He
attended eight years of country school, then graduated from Leola High School
in 1960. He farmed with his parents five miles east of Leola. In 1964, Myron
joined the South Dakota National Guard for six years. He married Sheila Scheid
on April 18, 1965. Sheila is the daughter of Raymond and Velma Scheid of Long
Lake and was born March 15, 1946.

The Myron Fauth Family. Back: Leisha and Launa. Front: Jason, Sheila and Myron.

Myron and Sheila have three children: Leisha born December 24, 1965, a graduate
of Leola High School, Launa born February 9, 1968, a junior at Leola High
School, and Jason born April 27, 1970, a ninth grader at Leola High School. The
family still resides on the farm.

Myron and Sheila are members of St. James Lutheran Church of Leola.

ALBERT and VIOLA FEICKERT

Albert J. Feickert was born September 20, 1922, in McPherson County, SD, to
Jacob and Charolta (Wacker) Feickert. Viola Gienger was born April 15, 1925, in
McPherson County. She is the daughter of Gottlieb and Rosina (Walth) Gienger of

In 1946 they purchased a farm from Earl Henderson six miles east and one mile

        The Albert Feickert Family. Viola, Leland, Idella and Albert.

EDWIN and LYDIA FEICKERT

Edwin Samuel Feickert's father, Frederich came to America in 1892 with his
parents, John George and Christina Feickert, when he was 13 years old. They
homesteaded 13 miles northwest of Leola. Frederich married Christina Spitzer
and they had two children, Emma and Edwin. Edwin was born April 10, 1909, and
grew to manhood on the farm his parents homesteaded.

On March 19, 1931, Edwin married Lydia Docktor in McIntosh County, ND, where
Lydia was born and raised. She was born March 8, 1911. Lydia's father, Jacob
Dockter, born in Bergdorf, South Russia, 1875, came to America in 1905. Her
mother, Magdalena Wagemann, born in Neudorf, South Russia, 1879, came to
America in 1889.

Edwin and Lydia went to country school and some of their memories are of school
events such as Christmas programs, pie socials, picnics and every day lunches.
Many times they walked to school.

Lydia and Edwin lived on the farm his parents homesteaded until June, 1965,
when they moved to Leola. They were members of rural Hope Lutheran and later
St. James Lutheran Church.

        The Edwin Feickert Family.

They were the parents of two daughters: Lavina Iona, born April 24, 1932, and
Marcella, born January 4, 1939, both at Leola. Lavina married Elmer Hopf
December 30, 1950. They have four children. Marcella married Eldon Schock of
Elgin, ND, November 7, 1959, and they have six children.

Edwin passed away June 22, 1968, and Lydia still lives in Leola, SD.

ELVIN and CHRISTINA FEICKERT

Elvin was born to Frederick and Bertha (Wacker) Feickert in March, 1922, in
Hoffman Township, 12 1/2 miles northwest of Leola. Here he went to rural
Hoffman Hilltop School, continued farming and raised his family.

Elvin's father, Fred, immigrated to America with his parents in the early
1890's. His mother was born at Menno, SD, in 1884. Elvin has two sisters,
Amelia (Mrs. Lester Lambert), of Elk Grove, CA, and Freda (Mrs. Arthur Rau), of
Aberdeen. He also has three brothers, Edmund, Emanuel and Emil, all deceased.

        The Elvin Feickert Family. Back: Dennis, Roger, Elvin, David and
        Peter. Front: Sidney, Christina, Joyce and Philip.

In June 1946, Elvin married Christina V. Geffre at Leola. Christina was born in
October, 1924, to Joseph Andrew and Mary (Hartman) Geffre in Leola Township.
She went to school at Leola. She has seven sisters and three brothers. One
brother and one sister are deceased.

They have seven children. David, 36, married Jeannie Binfet at Ipswich. They
have two girls, Deanna and Roxann. David is Shop Foreman for Sheehan Equipment
Company in Aberdeen. Jeannie works for H&R Block.

Dennis, 35, married Shirley Forsting at Aberdeen. They have two children,
Rebecca and Jason. Dennis is a Lieutenant Fireman for the Aberdeen Fire
Department. He also does some farming. Shirley is employed at the South Dakota

Roger, 29, married Cathy Lemer at Leola. They have two sons, Matthew and
