Colleen (Moon) Wangsness was born and raised near Lake Benton, MN, where she
attended school, graduating from high school in 1966 and the Institute of
Medical Technique in 1968.

Marlin and Colleen were married on August 14, 1971. They are the parents of
three children: Eric David, born April 25, 1974; Ryan Daniel, March 31, 1978;
and Michael John, October 28, 1983.

MARK and DELLA WARNICK

Mark Rowe Warnick married Mary Adella Frost, daughter of Wm. S. Frost, a Civil
War Captain of Co. E. 15th Ill. Infantry. They left their home in Lee Center,
IL seeking a better climate for health reasons. They farmed in Kansas,
Colorado, Missouri and later in South Dakota.

        Mark & Della Warnick.

Don Frost, Della's brother, owner and manager of a hotel in Leola, encouraged
the Warnicks to move to Dakota land. A quarter section of fertile prairie land
at $7 per acre was purchased in Koto Township in 1909 and in March, the
Warnicks, with three children moved to Leola by M. & St. L. railroad. They
moved all their possessions in a railroad box car. Della and her three children
stayed in the hotel for three weeks while a temporary building was built to
house the family. They continued building, and a barn and new home were
completed the following year (1910). This home building is still standing in
its original spot of the "middle west" farm located five miles north and one
mile east of Leola. The home has been modernized, but shows evidence of its
original lumber, construction and care by the owners throughout the years.
Present day owners are Mr. and Mrs. Kevin Lapka.

Mark practiced diversified farming. If the crops failed, he met expenses with
livestock, cream and poultry, etc. He used a stone mill to grind hard wheat
which was used for breakfast food and flour for bread. One lean winter he went
to La Porte, IN, where he worked at the Rumley Oil Factory. He returned in the
spring to plant his crop, along with the agency to sell the Oil Pull tractors.
Many trade-ins were repaired by Mark and his sons, which they sold on a
commission basis.

Della accepted the chairmanship for the Koto Township WWI Red Cross volunteers.
She took "old Mose" and the buggy, traveling to Hilgemann's store (Leola) for
bolts of flannel and boxes of yarn, which she distributed to willing workers.
Her ladies sewed bed jackets, bed socks, gowns and bandages for the wounded.
Socks, scarves, sweaters and hoods were knitted and crocheted for the soldiers.
Ethel Woodal (Yost) taught girls (nine years and older) the art of crocheting
during recess and noon hours in the Koto School. All these articles were
collected and packed by Della, and shipped by railroad to the Red Cross
headquarters.

Following the war, Mark and Della traded "Middle West" for Turner's ranch at
the foot of the hills northwest of Leola, where he raised Registered Hereford
cattle. Mark was a promoter of the McPherson-Campbell County Fair. The fair in
the fall and the Chatauqua in June or July were family vacations.

Scarce feed due to lack of rain, high cost of wintering cattle and lack of a
good cattle market persuaded Mark and Della to sell and move to Leola in 1941.
Before remodeling of their house was completed, Della died in October, 1941.

Mark began another occupation after moving to Leola, as a result of one of his
hobbies. He became a carpenter, remodeling and selling homes. His last home was
in Aberdeen, SD where he and his wife (he remarried in 1945) lived until their
death in the fall of 1950.

The Warnick children are as follows. Donald married Ruth Cooper. They had four
sons: Wilbur, Herschel, Don and Marshall. Donald died in 1951 and Ruth in 1977.

Winfield and Grayce live in Columbus, GA. They have one daughter, Ann. Lucy
(Billey) lives in Ellendale, ND. She has one son, James and two grandsons,
Lloyd and Mark. Mary (Adrich) recently moved to Spicer, MN. Her husband,
Albert, died in 1977. They have two children, Duane and Jeane (Schmidt). Grace
married Gordon Holden. They have one son, Lee, and two daughters, Sally
(Porter) and RadyDell (Salkeld). They reside in Los Angeles, CA.

WILBUR and DEE WARNICK

On May 2, 1925 Donald Warnick married Ruth Ann Cooper, who had come from
Indiana to teach school in McPherson County in 1918. She was born November 4,
1898 at Dale, IN, the fifth child of Gifford and Sarah (Marshall) Cooper, both
of whom had been born in Indiana. Donald and Ruth's first home was the farm now
owned by Warren and June Shafer. Donald built the buildings on his own farm
north of there and the family lived there until 1936. Then they bought the old
Jones Ranch ten miles northwest of Leola, and moved there with their family of
four boys: Wilbur Kent, born May 24, 1926 in Aberdeen; Herschel Rowe, born
August 10, 1927, at their farm home; Donald Cooper, born February 9, 1930, at
San Antonio, TX, where Donald worked that winter; and Marshall Frost, born
February 20, 1936 at Leola.

Donald was very interested in horticulture, and attended South Dakota State
College at Brookings for classes in that area in 1920-21. He and his family
surrounded the barren ranch buildings with beautiful hedges, fruit trees and a
shelter belt, which were the inspiration for his neighbors to do the same. This
was done during the dry '30's when water was hauled with a stone boat to get
the trees started.

Wilbur Warnick served in the U.S. Navy during WWII, and in November, 1948
married Dee Jessen at Fort Meade, SD. They made their first home at Rapid City
where Wilbur was attending South Dakota School of Mines. Their two sons were
born there, David Lee on September 21, 1949, and Randall Mark on November 15,
1950. When Donald died February 14, 1951, they returned to Wilbur's home to
help Ruth with the Ranch. Herschel was in the Army, and Don in the Marines
during the Korean conflict. Wilbur and Dee's first daughter, Pamela Ann, was
born March 3, 1952 at Milbank, SD. The ranch was snowed in that winter and Dee
and their sons spent four months with her parents. In the fall of 1952, Wilbur
bought the Albert Stugelmeyer quarter and the family lived there until they
returned to Rapid City in 1955. Their second daughter, Janet Ruth, was born
July 17, 1959 in Rapid City.

In 1981 Wilbur retired, after 25 years as a Journeyman Ironworker. He and Dee
now live on a ranch near Clearmont, WY, which they purchased in 1978, in
partnership with their son Randy. They have four grandchildren. In 1961 Ruth
sold the ranch to Myron Schmidt, and she and Herschel moved to Rapid City.
Herschel married Leola Jean Stuver and went to work for the Boeing Company on
the missile bases. He retired in 1981 and now lives at Green Ridge, MO.

Ruth died July 11, 1977 at Rapid City, SD. She is buried in Green Mound
Cemetery in the Warnick lot.

HAROLD and JOSEPHINE WEISSER

Milford, IA was the birthplace of Harold Weisser. He was born July 15, 1895 to
Matt and Mary (Bailey) Weisser. He was 11 years old when he came to Eureka, SD,
with his father to get settled before the rest of the family joined them. They
stayed in a hotel until his mother, Helen, and Edith and John arrived two weeks
later. The family had filed on a homestead July 18, 1906, 19 miles east of
Eureka. Harold attended grade school in Highland Township and three years of
high school at Leola, SD.

Farm life meant long, tiresome hours of hard work for the family. The land was
full of rocks and hills. They were only able to clear eight to ten acres the
first year. The father had worked for International Harvester, selling mowers,
headers, grain binders and hay rakes.

When neighbors asked his father to teach school, he agreed. The school term was
about three to four months then, because most of the children had to stay home
and help with chores. Later, Harold's mother decided to teach school so her
husband could tend to the farming.

On November 19, 1925, Harold was united in marriage with Josephine, the
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. John Goeshel of Long Lake. They made their home with
Harold's parents until 1929, when his parents retired and moved to Leola.
Harold and Josephine began their married life farming with six horses, a mower,
rake, plow, header and binder.

        The Harold Weisser Family. Back: John, Josephine, Harold and George.
        Front: Ruth, Charles and James.

During the '30's Harold remembers selling wheat for 28 cents a bushel. As the
years went by, acreage of the farm increased to 1,240 acres. More cattle were
added, increasing the farming operation.

Five children were born to this family. Four are presently engaged in farming:
John and Charles of Long Lake, James of Roscoe, SD, and Ruth (Weisser) Lapka,
Leola. George died July 16, 1959.

Harold and Josephine continued farming until October 12, 1958, when they
retired and moved to Leola. Josephine died in 1961.

Charles, his wife Diann (Scheuffele) and family live on the homestead, which
consists of about 760 acres.

Harold married Othilda (Haas) Weber September 7, 1962--(see Harold and Othilda
Weisser history).

HAROLD and OTHILDA WEISSER

Harold Weisser and Othilda Weber were united in marriage September 7, 1962.

Othilda was born to Adam and Christina Haas of Zeeland, ND. She married Harold
Weber. They had three children: Pauline, Paul and Ottilia. There were seven
grandchildren and one great-grandchild. Her husband passed away and the family
moved to Aberdeen, where Othilda was employed as a cook at St. Luke's Hospital.
She did cleaning at Northern State College and also worked at the Dixie Kreme.

        Othilda & Harold Weisser.

Harold and Tillie are now actively involved in the Senior Citizens
Organization, and are members of the Methodist Church. Tillie was instrumental
in organizing the Senior Citizens Choir, which she also led for the first four
years. They are still singing some of the old German hymns. The couple was also
responsible for circulating the petition to begin Senior Citizen meals for the
many elderly members of Leola. They enjoy the work they are doing.

MATT and MARY WEISSER

Matt Weisser was born January 20, 1865, at Lancaster, NY. He moved with his
mother and family to Maringo, IA. Later in his years he migrated to Milford,
IA, where he was employed with International Harvester as a salesman. In
Milford he met Mary Bailey. Mary was born September 6, 1873 at Greenville, IA.
Mary attended grade school and also the Quaker Academy. She was employed as a
maid and waitress at the Chase House in Milford, where she met Matt. On
September 7, 1894, Matt and Mary were united in marriage at Sioux City, IA.

Four children were born to this union: Harold--(see his family history); Mrs.
Samuel (Helen) Bosanko, deceased; John (died January 23, 1975); and Mrs. Edith
Haugen, living in Cathlement, WA.

        Edith, Matt, Harold, John, Mary and Helen Weisser.

In 1906 Matt, Mary and family boarded an immigrant car on the Milwaukee
Railroad, bringing with them household goods, two horses, wagons, two pigs,
chickens, old lumber, 60 bushels of oats and 40 bushels of ear corn. They
arrived at Mitchell, SD at 12:00 noon. They stepped off the train and noticed
one of Matt's old friends. All went to dinner. While reminiscing over old times
they forgot to get back to the train. When they did get back to the depot, the
train had left and all their belongings were on their way to Aberdeen, SD. The
depot agent was kind enough to give them a pass on a passenger train which
arrived at midnight in Aberdeen, where they stayed at the Commercial Hotel.
Early the next morning they left Aberdeen for Roscoe and then Eureka, SD. Matt
was employed at International Harvester and also at the Eureka Bazaar Store.

The family located on a homestead where Matt had filed claim on July 18, 1906,
19 miles east of Eureka, but with the rough times and raising a family, to
supplement the family income Matt taught school in Long Lake Township, three to
five months a year. His wife also taught school and used her money to purchase
school desks for her school.

Matt and Mary retired in 1929 and moved to Leola. Matt died September 18, 1950.
Mary moved back to Iowa and later entered a nursing home. She died July 6, 1975
at the age of 101.

WILLIAM H. and EMMA WOODALL

William Woodall and Emma Treptow were married in Kingsley, IA in 1894, where
both resided at that time.

In 1902, William, his wife and two children, moved to South Dakota, settling in
the vicinity of Bryant, SD. Two years later they located in Dickey County, ND,
about 22 miles from Ellendale, ND, this being the nearest trading center. Their
means of travel was with wagon and horses.

A transient life seemed inevitable for the family and they moved again. In
1906, the Dickey County land was traded for a claim 8 1/2 miles northeast of
Leola, SD, located in Koto Township.

Mr. Woodall was active in organizing the township in 1913 and became the first
treasurer.

        William & Emma Woodall.

Like many of the early settlers, Mrs. and Mrs. Woodall put in many long,
tiresome hours of hard work in the early years of their lives.

The land to be farmed was broken up with a one-leigh sulky plow and two horses.
Wells were dug by hand. A box of wood was built and lowered into the well to
prevent it from caving in. Milk, cream and butter were placed in a bucket which
had a rope fastened to the handle. The bucket was lowered into the well, to
keep it cool. There was no refrigeration.

William and Emma were the parents of three children. Laurence was seven years
old and Ethel (Mrs. Donald Yost) was five, when the family came to South
Dakota. Harold was born in 1908. Mr. Woodall died in April 1933; Mrs. Woodall
in November, 1954.

LELAND J. and LOUISE WYLIE

Leland J. Wylie opened the first Vo-Ag Department at the Leola School. He
taught science, coached football and track.

On December 29, 1931, Leland was married to Louise E. Hayer.

A son, Leland James Jr., was born in Leola, May 2, 1933. He is vice president
of the Lutheran General Hospital, Park Ridge, Chicago. Leland and Louise also
have a daughter, who lives in Muscatine, IA. They have five grandchildren.

The Wylies left Leola about 1935. He accepted a position as superintendent,
Vo-Ag instructor at Orland Consolidated School in Lake County. He filled
positions as superintendent at Thomas, South Shore and Hudson, before moving to
Sioux Falls in 1944, where he worked as Minnehaha Soil Conservationist for four
years. In 1948, he entered the Sioux Falls School system, where he taught and
served as an elementary principal, until retirement in 1970.

Leland and Louise celebrated their Golden Wedding Anniversary on December 29,
1981. They reside in Sioux Falls, SD.

HIRAM and MINNIE YOST

One of the early arrivals in the Leola vicinity in 1884, was Hiram H. Yost,
coming from Erie, PA. He settled on a claim northwest of Leola.

In 1893, he was united in marriage to Minnie Moulton. She came to this
community before South Dakota was admitted to statehood

        Hiram & Minnie Yost.

Hiram and Minnie moved to a farm northeast of Leola, where they resided until
1917, when they moved to Leola.

Hiram worked for Montana-Dakota Utilities Co., for 20 years. He served as
Sheriff and Deputy Sheriff for 16 years. For a number of years he was the
Justice of the Peace and performed many marriage ceremonies. He was a member of
the Masonic Lodge and a charter member of the Modern Woodman Lodge.

Minnie, an active civic leader, was a charter member of the Civic League, an
organizer and charter member of the Disco Club and promoter of the first
library in Leola. She was a member of the Order of the Eastern Star and Royal
Neighbor Lodge.

Both Hiram and Minnie taught school in their early life. Both were members of
the Methodist Church.

This union was blessed with five children. A daughter, Leslie, became Mrs.
William Lindley. She passed away at her home in Leola, on August 25, 1983, at
the age of 94 years. Their sons, Harold, Donald and Raymond are deceased.
Robert lives at Holiday, FL.

On October 30, 1943, Bud was united in marriage with Phyllis (Phyl) Anderson.
Phyl was born September 24, 1918, to Herman and Esther (Randall) Anderson. Phyl
grew up and attended school in Arlington, SD, and college in Madison and
Aberdeen, SD. She came to Leola to teach second grade (1938 to 1941). Phyl
taught two years in Tyndall and one year in Aberdeen. She joined the Leola
School System in 1947 and taught first grade until retirement in 1980.

Bud was employed with the State Highway Department in McPherson County for 32
years. He retired in 1980.

Since July 1, 1982, they have made their home in Peoria, AZ. Bud and Phyl had
been married 40 years in October, 1983.

HENRY SR. and ELIZABETH YOUNG

Henry Young, Sr. was born in the village of Dreihausen, near Marburg, Germany
in 1859. His wife, Elizabeth (Schimpf), who came from the same area, was born a
year later.

Henry was known to have an adventuresome nature, which probably influenced his
decision to emigrate to America. He and his wife went to Waunakee, WI, where
they met up with his uncles, Andrew and Goddard, and his cousins, Charlie,
Lizzie and A. H. Between 1880 and 1884 they had all moved to Dakota Territory.
Most of them, including Henry and his wife, took up claims in Washington
Township.

In 1888 their first son, Frank, was born. By the time of the prairie fire of
1889, they also had a daughter, Anna. Like many other brave mothers, Elizabeth
saved the lives of her children and herself by pumping water from the well and
keeping them covered with it. Her husband had taken a load of grain to Ipswich
that day, and when he returned, his family was nowhere to be seen. His
buildings and livestock were destroyed. In despair he pulled his handkerchief
from his pocket to wipe his eyes. As he did so, the bill he received that day
from Germany, worth $500.00, came with it. The prairie wind whipped it forever
away. This was all the money he had. Later he was overjoyed to learn that
relatives had rescued his family.

In that same year as the fire, another son, Henry Jr., known to many as "Hank,"
was born. Approximately two years later George was born, but tragedy struck
again. In 1895 the young mother of Henry's four children died of typhoid. The
good women of the community helped him care for his children.

        The Henry Young Sr. Family. Back: Hank, Anna and Frank. Front: George
        and Henry Sr.

Henry moved to the farm 1 1/2 miles east of Leola to be nearer to town. Since
he had been well educated in Germany he now decided to enter public service. He
took a job of driving the stage which carried mail and passengers to and from
Leola and Aberdeen. This was a two-day trip with horses. From Aberdeen they
drove north to Westport where they took the Wetonka road. The half-way house
was on this road. Here they changed horses and ate their meals. They often had
to stay overnight during blizzards. In the morning they continued on to the
corner north of Wetonka. Here they turned right, following the rough road
through cow pastures, often to Leola. This was a dangerous trip, especially in
winter, when they sometimes became lost in blizzards.

Henry Young served as town constable in Leola, as well as several terms each as
sheriff and register of deeds.

The Youngs were reputed to have had extensive holdings in the Black Forrest in
Germany. They manufactured wagons, also. With this background, it seemed
natural that Henry's sons, Frank, Hank, George and Albert all entered the
lumber business. Frank's son, Dick, and Hank's son, Gene, are also in this
business.

In later years Henry married a second time. Elizabeth, known as Lizzie, became
his wife. To them were born May (Frey), Albert and Fred. They moved to Lodi,
CA, where Henry died in 1921. He was buried in Leola. Albert and his mother,
Lizzie, returned to Leola where Albert worked many years for the Atlas Lumber
Company. All of this family are now deceased.

Henry's first family is also deceased. Anna (Halpenny) died in 1914. Frank,
who married Margaret Kutschke, died in 1937. Hank married Iva McGee, who
survives him. Hank died in 1962. George, married to Carol Gillogly who survives
him, died in 1980.

Henry Young, Sr. had 13 grandchildren and a number of great-grandchildren.

HENRY G. and IVA YOUNG

The only member of Henry Young, Sr.'s family who lived permanently and
continually in McPherson County was his son, Henry G. (Hank). Hank never lived
more than two miles from Leola, and most of his life was lived in town.

Hank's brother, George Young and his wife, Carol lived in or near Leola for
several years. Carol taught in the Leola public schools and George farmed on
the old Young farm before going to work for the Central Lumber Co. in Leola,
until he became manager of their yard in Loyalton. They spent most of their
life in Minnesota. They had one son, Jack and a daughter who died in infancy.

Hank and his wife, Iva, reared a family of six children. All survive except
Howard, who was killed in an accident in 1966.

        Iva and Henry G. Young. Grandchildren: Kathy and Todd Young.

Lorraine is the oldest. She spent 4 1/2 years as a teacher in McPherson County
schools before moving to Minnesota for additional training. She did various
kinds of office work and psychometric testing for Mankato State University and
Mankato Board of Education. She never married and presently lives in Leola.

Gene and his wife, the former Luella Warnemunde live in Portland, OR. They have
a son and two daughters. Gene works as one of the special managers of a large
lumber distributing company in Portland.

George (Bud) married Phyllis Anderson. They are now retired. They live in a
suburb of Phoenix, AZ.

Ardith is married to Allen Hilgemann. They live in Aberdeen, SD and are the
parents of five grown children.

Marianne, the youngest, became the wife of Albert Neuharth. They have three
children. They live in Edina, MN where Albert works as an electrician and
Marianne, at the Methodist Hospital.

Hank Young entered the lumber business when he was about 25. He worked at it
until he retired at age 67 in 1956. He was Manager of the Central Lumber
Company for over 30 years. During this time he served on the Leola Board of
Education 20 years, was treasurer of Leola Township many years and was active
on many civic and municipal boards and committees.

He was an active member of St. Paul's Lutheran Church.

Henry and Iva have 13 grandchildren. Iva recently celebrated her 90th birthday.
She is at home in Leola at the present time.

GEORGE and LEOCADIA ZACHER

George Zacher, a native of North Dakota, was born July 25, 1917 in Strasburg.

        Leocatia & George Zacher.

George has held numerous occupations. He began teaching in rural schools in

PAUL and LENA ZANTOW

Paul Zantow was born March 23, 1883 in Posen, Germany, which is now part of
Poland. He came to America when he was 18, following his father and two
brothers who had come earlier. His mother and two sisters came later. One
married sister remained in Germany. The family first lived in the Watertown
area, but Paul soon decided that he wanted a place of his own, so set out to
locate a good place and to earn some money to buy it. After working in Canada,
on the Wyoming Cody Dam, and various places in North and South Dakota, he
decided that any place in America was a good place if one set his mind to make
a success of it. He settled on a farm nine miles south of Leola.

On December 26. 1917 he was married to Lena Krause at Summit, SD. She was the
oldest daughter of Carl and Mathilda (Kaaz) Krause. She had three sisters and
two brothers. Her parents were farmers in that area. Lena died November 21,
1937 leaving five children. Paul later married Kati Schnaible from Artas. She
died May 25, 1955. Paul spent the last few years of his life in Eureka and
Hosmer nursing homes. He died September 2, 1971.

        Paul Zantow.

The children of Paul and Lena were: Edwin, born January 15, 1919--(see his
family history); Hazel, born May 12, 1921--(refer to Zetterlund family
history); Alice, born December 29, 1924. (She is a graduate of SDSU. While
there, she met and married Ralph Kane of Akron, OH. He has recently retired as

                        McPHERSON COUNTY HERALD

1889-1900

Twelve comrades of the Union Army of the Civil War were mustered into the Grand
Army of the Republic (G.A.R.) Simon Cameron Post of Leola July 13, 1889 by C.
E. Johnson of Frederick. Officers were elected and installed.

Area farmers organized the Leola Creamery April 2, 1896. Articles of
incorporation were forwarded to the S.D. Secretary of State. Stock has been
sold to underwrite the project, which consists of a main building, storage
room, cooling room, ice house, and boiler room. The machinery required:
engines, boiler, cream vats, churn, delivering cans, separator and butter
worker. The creamery will be in operation by June 15.

The books were turned over from the Brown County offices to the McPherson
County officials on 29 November 1884. The first tax was paid 25 December 1884
by Mark Samby.

Dr. C. T. Gamble reports a diphtheria epidemic in the western part of the
county. Twenty-six children are dead and many more are desperately ill.
12-27-89

Our village school is crowded to its fullest capacity and still more pupils are
expected. Prof. O'Reilly informs us that 47 pupils are enrolled in one room,
serving the 3rd through the 7th grade and for him to teach that many is an
impossible task. 9-14-98

Mrs. Harry Sears is an accomplished amateur photographer, and much of her work,
including some reproduced herein, are part of the albums of Leola folks. 1-3-97

The Leola School opened September 13, 1889 with K. D. Kribs as teacher. The new
organ for the school has arrived.

Leola Gopher Story Becomes A Legend

The legendary gopher story of 1903 for which William Cochrane, a former Leola
teacher, assumed responsibility, is one that had grown by leaps and bounds with
the passing of the years. If the observations of the Herald a short time after
the advertisement appeared are to be relied upon, comparatively few of the
little prairie animals were involved. The story has and will continue to make
good reading as a sidelight in the history of Leola. The advertisement and
subsequent observations by the Herald editor follow:

Live Gophers Wanted --10,000

We will pay 25c apiece for female and 15c for male gophers delivered at the
Leola House on May 2, 1903.

The Australian Rabbit Extermination Co. 114 Randolph St. G. A. Tolbert. 4-23-03

Landlord Hawes of the Leola House is fully convinced that it pays to advertise.
As a result of an ad placed in the Herald by a Chicago firm he has several
hundred gophers in his care and the man that wanted them at 25 cents each has
not as yet put in an appearance. The only one ahead on the deal is the printer
who received pay for the ad in advance. The joke is on Hawes and the boys who
caught the gophers. 5-7-03

1901-1910

THE RAILROAD COMES TO TOWN

Leola was founded in the spring of 1884 and from the start the prospects of a
railroad seemed plausible. Work began in 1885 on a proposed line from Aberdeen
to Bismarck, ND via Leola. The grade was completed except for the laying of
track and optimistic citizens expected the ironing to take place in the near
future. This 20-year optimism kept the town alive.

On 12 July 1906 the Minneapolis and St. Louis Railroad selected the
railroad-yard site and the construction train completed laying the track to the
depot site at noon Dec. 21 and completed side tracks and "Y" in the railroad
yards at 3:00 Christmas afternoon in 1906. A Red Letter Day for Leola!

LAST HOMESTEAD FILED IN FEBRUARY 1906

The days of free homesteads in McPherson County have passed a filing having
recently been placed upon the last 160 acre tract of land in the county. 3-1 06

There is no indication in the papers to whom this last full quarter of
homestead land was awarded.

McPherson County Land and Loan Company has been organized. Members of the
company met March 7, 1907 and elected C. S. Acker, president; F. C. Junge, vice
president and general manager and F. J. Pietz, secretary and treasurer. This
company should do well now that Leola has the railroad. 3-14-07

Banker Charles Turner has purchased a Model F Buick automobile. As soon as the

Leola is entertaining a bunch of harvest hands in the jungle west of town.

for $3 per day, which is more than farmers around here will pay. Nearly every
train brings fellows who will work for going wages, so farmers are getting
nearly all the help they need. 7-23-14

Jacob Kulm and Jacob Glaser were killed by gas which had accumulated in a well
they were digging. The two men and Gottfried Stoecker were sinking a well with
a boring machine and at a depth at 65 feet, they encountered a stone. Jacob
Kulm was lowered into the well to dig out the stone, but in a few minutes was
overcome by gas.  His companions discovered his distress and Jacob Glaser went
down to rescue him, but after descending about 20 feet, he was overcome and
fell to the bottom of the well.  Help arrived too late.  6-3-15

1921-1930

A gas war in Leola started by two filling stations importing gasoline from
Aberdeen for less than it could be bought from local oil companies. This
allowed them to cut the price from 27c to 25c with a further cut to 23c. The
other stations, although unable to buy such low-priced gasoline from their
suppliers, cut their prices to 21c per gallon.

Some months ago a woman who resides elsewhere in the county pleaded guilty to a
charge of manufacturing intoxicating liquids. Part of the evidence used in the
preliminary hearing was a copper still, which was locked in the county jail
until its destruction would be decreed. Recently janitor Ludwig Martz
discovered that "the still" was no longer in the jail. Someone had broken in
and absconded with it. 1-4-23

Forty to eighty a day has been the record of swimmers since Lake Lundquist was
officially opened for bathing a few weeks ago. A safety area has been roped off
and a regularly employed lifeguard is on duty at specified hours.
The lake is fed by an artesian well drilled early last spring, which discharges
about 150 gallons of water into the lake every minute, sufficient to keep water
going over the spillway at all times. Last week 12,000 bluegills were deposited
in the lake by the State Game and Fish Dept.

Thanks to farmers Richard Jasmer and Earl Rott, some large round flat straw
bales were made last fall for the Canada geese to use as nesting sites in the
Leola area. A few weeks ago volunteers from the Leola Sportman's Club
distributed the bales to wetlands between Leola and Long Lake after wrapping
the bales with nylon twine and loading them on vehicles.
The bales, now situated in the wetlands, are expected to appear as islands
after the spring thaw. Canada geese are known to prefer islands for nesting, as
they are more secure from predators. Assisting with the bales were Kevin Lapka,
Leo Kindelspire, Byron Kindelspire, Ernest Jasmer, John Weisser, Julius
Guthmiller, Paul Bultsma, John Price Elwood Lechner, Bud Smalley and Harold
Haux. 1-21-82

                        McPHERSON COUNTY

McPherson County is located chiefly in the rolling glacial hills section of the
Missouri Coteau in north central South Dakota. It is bounded on the north by
McIntosh and Dickey counties of North Dakota, on the east by Brown County, on
the south by Edmunds County and on the west by Campbell County. The county
covers 1,151 square miles of rolling prairie with an average elevation of
approximately 1,600 feet above sea level. There are approximately 850 farms in
the county and the chief crops are spring wheat, oats, barley, flax, alfalfa
and wild hay. The terrain of the county ranges from flat to undulating in the
eastern portion, hilly and rolling topography in the central portion and to
gentle and undulating slopes in the western areas. The undulating
stream-terraces and basins in the north central, western central and
southwestern areas contain numerous wetland areas used for waterfowl
production.

McPherson County is one of the largest east river counties in the state,
ranking 24th out of the 67 counties in total land area, with 736,640 acres of
land. According to the 1964 U.S. Census of Agriculture report, 95 percent of
McPherson County is farm land.

State Highways 10 (east-west), 45 and 47 (north-south) are the main roads
serving the county. These highways connect with U.S. Highways 281, which serves
Aberdeen, and 83, which serves the state capital city of Pierre. U.S. Highways
83 and 12 combine with State Highway 10 to link the county with the city of
Mobridge. Railroad service to other communities in the county has been
discontinued and in some areas the trackage has also been removed.

Leola, the county seat, located in the east central part of the county, has a
population of 640, according to the 1980 U.S. Census of Population. Leola is
about 39 miles northwest of Aberdeen, 159 miles northeast of Pierre and 90
miles east of Mobridge. The largest community in McPherson County is the city
of Eureka, located in the northwest part of the county, with a population of
1,349 persons. The physical and geographic details of McPherson County do not
distinguish it from many surrounding counties. Like any area, the people and
events that have occurred there make it unique.

Traveling through McPherson County in the early 1800's would have been a
difficult trip. Indian trails twisting through the treeless, grassy, rolling
plains were few and far between. There is record of a white man having traveled
through the area in 1804, as noted in the journal of a white man being here
until 1820. It is commonly known that a fur trading post existed in the
vicinity at this time, located near the Elm River not far from the east
McPherson County line.

The first specific records of white men date to 1863 when a group of scouts
passing through from the Missouri River to the James River had stopped to camp
at a lake in the Long Lake area. During the night Indians drew near. Fearing
they were hostile, the scouts went out onto a peninsula that extends from the
east bank of the lake and fortified the narrow neck in expectation of attack.
They discovered at daylight that the Indians were friendly. Also in 1863, in
September, General Alfred Sully's whole command crossed the area en route to
Ft. Pierre after the battle of Whitestone Hill near Ellendale, ND. The trail
they followed would have taken the column close to Long Lake and almost exactly
through the present city of Hosmer. These were the only white people to travel
in the prairie land until 1883.

McPherson County in 1870 was a small part of a huge county the Territorial
Legislature had set up: an enlarged Buffalo County, its south border on Charles
Mix, its northern border Canada, and extending from the west edge of range 66
to the Missouri River and out to Montana Territory in the west. Its county seat
was at White Earth City, not far from Minot, ND. In 1873 the Territorial
Legislature decided to create new counties of the large Buffalo County. Two
other counties, Beadle and Mills, were created at the same time as McPherson.
Beadle, directly east of McPherson, was the boundary line until 1879, when
Brown County succeeded Beadle and Mills. The west boundary of Brown was set
between ranges 65 and 66, the eastern tier of the county was not a part of the
county until 1885. The Territorial Legislature, in establishing the new
counties, named them after famous people, particularly generals. McPherson
County was named after Civil War General James B. McPherson, who commanded the
army of Tennessee. Many western soldiers served in this army. General McPherson
fell on the battlefield in Atlanta in 1864.

        General James B. McPherson.

In 1880 the surveyors came into the county to set up the township lines. By
law, "rights could not be acquired in unsurveyed lands, but by common consent
all land offices recognized the rights of squatters who came in ahead of
surveyors, and surveys noted their location." The first settler in the county
was John Weber, who settled in what is now Weber Township in July 1882,
according to the monthly "South Dakotan" in July 1901. These early people were
called "sooners." Most of them settled in Washington, Leola, Carl and Weber
townships. The "sooner" would locate a section corner on the township line
survey. He would take a compass and tying a rag to a wheel, would proceed over
hill and dale on a straight line to a place that pleased him and would set up
his dugout, shack or some such shelter. The other corners were located with the
same method. Usually locations were made by men who had a basic knowledge of
surveying. Amongst the early surveyors was a man named George A. Kline. He and
his crew started their survey in August 1883, and discovered there were at
least 53 "sooners" who had claimed 40 percent of the available homestead land
before the surveyors got to Washington Township. Leola Township had 35 and Carl
had 15 "sooners" by the spring of 1884, and Weber, Wachter and Koto also had
their shares. One of the men who helped to organize the county was a "sooner"
by the name of J. H. Darlington.

As the surveyors (including a Mr. William Alley) worked westward, they found
fewer "sooners;" Howard Township had a D. A. Child and Spring Township had a
Charles W. Olds. Other townships in the same tier as Arena had none, while
Arena had three Daughterys and a Mr. Craig in October 1884. Although this area
was sparsely settled, there were well-defined trails leading into and across
the area.

The need for county organization became apparent in 1883 when a young settler
in Washington Township fatally shot another as a result of a quarrel. The
pioneers petitioned for organization of the county to Governor Ordway. The
governor then appointed Henry Z. Moulton, John H. Darlington and James L. Dow,
but governmental processing by territorial officials held up their commissions.
Apparently tired of waiting, Moulton and Darlington obtained certified copies
of records showing their appointments and proceeded with organization plans in
early 1884, but slow communications held them back. On March 6, before dawn,
five men driving two teams left Ordway (in central Brown County), a thriving
community in 1884, with Darlington's shack as their destination. Darlington's
residence was on the NE 1/4 of section 36, in Washington Township. The
traveling companions were Henry Z. Moulton, John H. Darlington, Shannon P.
Hardenbrook, Wendell W. Cornwall and Charles N. Herreid. The day was described
by Herreid as being bitterly cold, "a day which proved to be one of the coldest
of the winter, with a strong wind blowing from the northwest and practically no
road to guide them through the deep snow. After a desperate struggle with the
elements, they reached their destination. They had to shovel the snow out of
the barn in order to provide shelter for their weary horses. According to
Herreid, they had brought a sheet iron stove along and they set this up, built
a fire and prepared a frugal meal. With this accomplished, they proceeded with
the business at hand. The first commissioners' minutes record the date as
Thursday, March 6, 1884, the time was 8:00 P.M. The two commissioners, Moulton
and Darlington, took oath of office. Moulton was elected chairman and C. N.
Herreid was appointed County Clerk and Register of Deeds. Shannon P.
Hardenbrook was appointed Sheriff. Near midnight, having the county organized
according to law, they adjourned.

The next day, Friday, March 7 at 9:00 A.M. they reconvened and made further
appointments: Assessor, Joseph Worthy; County Judge, Wendell W. Cornwall;
County Surveyor, Ed D. Haynes; Justices, Henry Hoover and Andrew Williams;
Constables, David E. Collins and John W. Hooker. Commissioner Darlington then
introduced a resolution involving the location of the county seat. Because of
friction over the location, the town of Leola was not named, but rather the
description which is: section 17, township 126, range 67. The county was
divided into three equal portions of eight miles each from north to south and
extending from east end to west end of the county, constituting three
commissioner districts and numbers as follows: District 1--North, 2--Central,
3--South. The group decided its minutes should be published in one paper in
the county: the Koto McPherson County News. The office of C. N. Herreid was to
be considered the office of Register of Deeds and County Clerk. All other
officers were to use their own offices for county business. They adjourned
until March 17, when they met at the home of Henry Z. Moulton, which was to be
the seat of government for the time being. At the March 17 meeting supplies
were ordered. The problems of completing appointments of county officers and
division of road districts were considered. James L. Dow, who was the third
appointed commissioner and who had been absent from the initial meeting, was
again absent from this meeting. His home territory was around the town of Koto,
which was considered to be a rival of Leola for the county seat. The
commissioners, as an apparent appeasement move, took this into consideration
and appointed E. W. Howell of Weber Township, Treasurer, (quickly succeeded by
Samuel P. Howell and later Orvin J. Roe) and Zechariah Spitler, a resident of
Koto, as Coroner. (Koto was a platted town with a post office manned by
Postmaster Oshea O. Fowler as of June 22, 1883, ten days earlier than the
appointment of Leola's postmaster.) Bela E. Dexter and George W. Kemp, who
lived near Koto were appointed Justice and Constable for the central area;
Samuel A. Bordan and William Roberts were named Justice and Constable for the
northern area.

At a June 6 meeting, Mr. Dow finally appeared and took his oath of office. The
board was reorganized and once again Moulton was chosen chairman. Once again
they located the county seat in Leola. The Pioneer Banner was also listed as
the official newspaper. The school districts were set up by the new County
Superintendent, John A. Kelley. Polling places and precincts were appointed.
The county's first revenue came in July and on July 7 they paid bills which
amounted to $300.00.

The commissioners held more than one meeting per month during the early times,
and on July 15, 1884 they approved a tax roll, paid bills and passed a
resolution concerning the granting of liquor licenses. Commissioner Darlington
introduced the following resolution: "Whereas, the granting of license for the
sale of intoxicating beverages has come to be a question of grave interest for
our people, deeply affecting their financial and social conditions and whereas,
we believe that the granting of such license would be offensive and detrimental
to the substantial growth, the peace, good order, social advancement and
happiness of our people and deeming it our sacred duty to guard faithfully the
interests committed to our care, therefore, resolved, that we, the
Commissioners of McPherson County, grant no license whatsoever for the sale of
intoxicating liquors to be used as a beverage within this county." The county
remained dry officially until July 1887, when the board granted a liquor
license for the remainder of that year.

Many were listed on the first tax rolls, but these were inaccurate as many
original settlers had moved to other areas of the county and were taxed for
their former location. The commissioners set up a road poll of $1.50 and a
school poll of $1.00 to catch those with neither real or personal property. The
tax-paying man ages 21 to 50 years had the privilege of working the road poll
tax off by one day's labor on roads. With these tax problems settled, the board
felt the county wholly organized.

The pioneers in the east tier of townships, Wachter, Carl, Willow and Lincoln,
enjoyed a no-tax situation until the newly elected commissioners, George
Chamberlain, Orvin J. Roe and Samuel P. Howell, elected in November 1884,
decided to send Mr. Chamberlain to Bismarck to try to persuade the territorial
legislature to put range 66 into McPherson County. Apparently he accomplished
his mission, for a bill to re-bound the county was passed and signed by
Governor Pierce February 5, 1885. This gave the county four settled areas to
add to the tax lists. The 1885 census lists 156 dwellings and as many families
and 447 persons in those townships.

On April 6, 1885, the commissioners were presented a communication telling that
on November 4, 1884 ten citizens of the county agreed to give $1,000.00 to aid
in the construction of a courthouse in Leola. This was in response to a
proposal by Koto to be the county seat. The Leola citizens had held a meeting
in the Leola schoolhouse on March 30, 1885, attended by more than 60 people
from different parts of the county. At this meeting they decided it was not the
right time to erect county buildings. The commissioners abided by the wishes of
the people. Nevertheless, the $1,000.00 offer was accepted. The generous donors
who paid $73.75 were: Charles N. Herreid, Wendell W. Cornwall, L. H. Moulton,
S. P. Hardenbrook, E. D. Haynes, Tarquin Franklin, Walter Cavanagh, Charles
Turner, Orvin J. Roe, Henry Z. Moulton, Andrew Williams, and George W.
Chamberlain. F. E. Beach, Emmet C. and Stillman Moulton each paid $50.00 and
Fred Jung paid $15.00. On February 13, 1886, Wendell W. Cornwall appeared on
behalf of the donors of the $1,000.00 and informed the board that the money
would be ready and subject to the disposal of the commissioners any time before
April 1, 1886. The board accepted. On February 20, the board met and completed
the choice of the courthouse location: to be on block two of original plat of
Leola.

Plans for the courthouse building were adopted March 5, 1886. The commissioners
passed a resolution that day to hold a special election to raise $1,000.00 by
taxes to aid in the construction of the courthouse. They assigned polling
places and election officials. A vote was held and the measure was approved. On
May 28, bids for construction were examined. The bid of Walter Cavanagh to
furnish material and construct the courthouse for $1,750.00 was accepted. The
bid of Stillman Moulton to construct a stone foundation for $7.25 was accepted.
William H. Barnum was employed to dig the required trenches and cellar for the
courthouse at $.40 per cubic yard. Construction plans were completed. At this
same meeting, a representative from Ordway, Bismarck & Northwestern
Railroad Company appeared and informed them they would locate a depot and
construct a line into Leola. This railroad was to be completed by January 1887.
The courthouse was completed by September 11, 1886. Many meetings were held to
decide on furnishings.

        The Old Courthouse.

On July 9, 1892, a group of 528 McPherson County citizens petitioned the
commissioners to change the county seat location to Eureka by holding an
election on November 8, 1892. It was granted. This was the second of four
attempts to change the courthouse location, the first having been a
"half-hearted" attempt in 1888, which failed. The voters decided the county
seat was to stay where the first commissioners so designated. In the July 1896
meeting, a petition signed by 674 voters of the county was presented to the
board, again petitioning to move the county seat to Eureka by the election
process. The people voted in the General Election and again it was defeated.
From 1896 to 1900, the minutes show a large turnover in commissioners and
officers in the county. Some resigned and others filled in. New faces and
problems arose during the next few years. Many hours were spent on road
problems, township schools, elections and equalizing taxes. There were many
conflicts in the county and many had to be settled in court trials by juries.
Many trials required the use of interpreters.

September 1, 1914, a courthouse building fund was created. McPherson County was
fortunate in having some far-seeing commissioners in office at the time. These
five men, Fred Hilgemann, John Doering, John J. Hepperle, John Mehlhaff, and G.
B. Howell set a levy of 2/10 mill aside to be used for a building fund for the
future.

In 1916, there was a need for a jail house, so on May 9 the commissioners
accepted the bid of J. Lawson of $2,092.00 and the jail building was built
behind the courthouse.

Records show that on July 11, 1922, a resolution was introduced stating that
the courthouse was unsafe for reason of risk by fire, that the county now had
$55,945.54 in the building fund and after the year's taxes were collected they
would have approximately $76,945.54, and that the board would submit this to
the electors of the county for their determination at the General Election,
November 7, 1922. The voters would decide the question of "issuing its bonds in
an amount not to exceed $100,000.00 for the purpose of providing a proper site
and of erecting thereon a suitable courthouse building at the county seat of
said county." The people turned this down by a small majority, evidently
because of issuing bonds. After the election the State Fire Marshall wrote the
commissioners a letter condemning the courthouse and imploring them to take it
upon themselves for the good of the county citizens to do something about the
situation. After much discussion, the board began plans to construct a
fire-proof vault for the courthouse and notified the State Fire Marshall.

A petition was again addressed to the board on July 1, 1924 for the purpose of
submitting the question of the removal of the county seat from Leola to Eureka
to the voters of the county at the coming General Election. The story goes as
follows: "The east really got organized under John E. Reagan, Leola banker."
Two men from Leola and vicinity were delegated to watch each west-end precinct
to see that all election laws were followed, that polls closed on time, etc.
The women stayed in Leola to get out the eastend vote. Eureka finally bowed to
the inevitable and even quit appropriating the county records from time to
time. Eureka has not been a total loser, however, since they actively take part
in the county government. Agriculture Extension work began in our county in
1924. A petition signed by 325 people was presented to the commissioners to put
the issue on the ballot in the General Election. It passed and the Extension
Department was born.

January 7, 1926, a resolution was introduced by Commissioner Kusler: "That for
the sake of economy and protection of county records and files and in the best
interest of the taxpayers, residents and voters of the county, a new county
courthouse be erected. " Since the courthouse building fund had been levied for
in 1914 and carried through the years, there was now a sufficient sum to pay
for all expenses incurred. The board called for an election to be held on March
23, 1926, for all voters to decide whether a sum not to exceed $100,000.00
should be expended from the courthouse building fund for the erection of a new
courthouse at the city of Leola. Around 200 electors of the west end of the
county presented a petition to the board in February, asking that they amend
the resolution to have the question of erecting a courthouse in the November
General Election instead of a special March election. The commissioners
rejected the petition. The special election was held as they planned in March,
with 1,685 votes cast in favor of building and 813 votes against. The board
declared the proposition carried. The commissioners went on a mini-tour on May
24-29, inspecting recently constructed courthouses in Ashley, Ellendale,
Forman, and Wahpeton, ND; Fergus Falls, MN; and Clear Lake, Hayti, Milbank,
Kennebec, and Aberdeen, SD. They had to know what they wanted before they hired
an architect. June 8, 1926, they secured the service of Messers Buechner and
Orth of St. Paul, MN as architects. July 6, they accepted plans submitted by
Mr. Orth and by August 7 all preliminary plans were completed. The board
advertised for construction bids of the courthouse, according to plans. County
Auditor Ray Sutherland had his hands full with all these extra duties.

September 7, the board accepted the bid of Majerus Company of Watertown, SD for
the general construction work of building the courthouse for $99,481.00.
Building commenced in 1927 and fixtures and furniture were purchased throughout
the year. January 1928 found the courthouse close to completion. They started
moving records to the new building. May 22 was designated as the dedication
date. They sold the old courthouse for $750.00 to J. H. Dalke. There were no
sidewalks around the courthouse until August 1929, when the board contracted
sidewalks for $1,000.00.

The next years were spent solving problems with township schools, building and
re-building roads. During these years the county paid many salaries to men who
worked on the roads; not only workers in construction and maintenance, but also
men who shoveled and hauled snow off the roads during the hard winters. Board
minutes show they even paid people who hauled the snow-shovelers. Wages for a
man and a two-horse team were 40 cents/hour, for road labor 25 cents/hour.
Times became increasingly difficult and in 1933 the commissioners urged the
people to "plant large gardens and resort to the tilling of the soil in order
to become again independent and self reliant." There were many on poor relief
at that time. There was a county emergency relief committee to help the many
needy ones caused by the severe drouth in 1935. The county helped families but
reserved the right to withdraw the help if people abused the aid. The example
abuse the board used was spending money on "shows" or "overindulgence in
intoxicating liquors." The commissioners resolved to cooperate with all the
federal programs that were in operation at the time. One bright spot in the era
was when Northern Power and Light Company constructed a transmission line along
certain highways in the county. This brought electricity to many town homes,
and with it came increased comfort.

In 1937, drought and insects destroyed most crops. Many of the helpful programs
continued. The commissioners paid hospital, doctor and food bills for many
during the years 1937-1939. On the positive side, the commissioners spent time
improving the county roads. In 1937 they urged the State Highway Commission, by
a resolution sent to Pierre, to oil at least five miles of Highway 10 through
Leola and five miles through Eureka. This was done and, naturally, improved
travel.

At the end of the 1940's, influenza swept the county and once again many
families needed county assistance with doctor and hospital bills. During the
'40's, the commissioners continued improving roads and continually helped the
taxpayers in any way possible. They continued to build their highway department
to serve the taxpayers. Along with the growth came many problems in
administration relating to the roads the taxpayers had to travel. As the people
demanded better roads for their tax dollar, new and better equipment was
required, and these issues consumed many hours of the board's time. These
concerns continued through the '50's.

October 2, 1951, the commissioners saw fit to appoint a Veteran Service Officer
for our area: Edwin Hilgemann. In 1952, they appointed another for the west end
of the county: Jacob Gehring. Gehring served the veterans in the county for 23
years and resigned in January 1975. Floyd Libis was then appointed Deputy
Veteran Service Officer for the county. Hilgemann still serves.

The '50's brought few changes. In 1953, improvements were made on the
courthouse grounds, made possible by cooperation between the commissioners and
the Better Leola Club. Landscaping was done and the grounds beautified. In
1956, the county participated in the establishment of a mental health center in
Aberdeen, SD. At that timeit cost $700.00 to become a member; currently it
costs $6,955.00. In November 1959, the commissioners adopted the South Dakota
Survival Plan under the South Dakota Civic Defense. McPherson County was
declared a drought disaster area that year and the Small Business
Administration granted loans to firms experiencing economic hardships. By 1960,
so many meetings dealt with road business that the board became known as "road
commissioners.

A water conservancy tax, at a levy of .10, was first paid by county citizens in
1961, amounting to a revenue of approximately $2,200.00. The current levy is
.38. The state sponsored the surplus commodity program in 1962 and McPherson
County took part. This program continued for several years and was replaced by
the Food Stamp Act in July 1968, which is still in operation. January 3, 1962,
the commissioners by resolution formed a civil defense organization for the
county and appointed a director, Robert Eiseman, Eureka. On February 8, the
courthouse was designated as a Civil Defense shelter. Eiseman resigned and
Richard Gross took over as director in October 1963. A fall-out shelter was
stocked in the spring of 1963. Preparations for a tower and equipment for a
radio communication system began in 1966. The site chosen was lot 3, section 18
in Wacker Township. In April 1969, Gross informed the board they could drop out
of Civil Defense on the state level. He told them it would cost the county at
least $1,500.00 per year to be eligible for a state reimbursement. If the
county dropped the state plan, Gross offered to perform duties for a small
salary. One commissioner had to serve on this committee and Christ Schanzenbach
was chosen. Changes occurred again in 1975, when the board decided not to join
the three-party civil defense program. In December 1975, the commissioners
appointed the auditor to be the civil defense coordinator for McPherson County,
simplifying matters greatly. The program is now called Emergency and Disaster
Service, and McPherson County is included in the membership of the South Dakota
Civil Defense Association.

Much of the business of the board of commissioners is repetition and there is
always the duty of keeping the courthouse and grounds an attractive historical
site. Changes have been made through the years as deemed necessary. In 1966,
the jail building was ordered abolished, as it had not been used for years. A
storage shed for the janitor's equipment now stands in its place, built in
1976. In order to make the courthouse offices more comfortable, 10 units of
air-conditioners were installed in 1967. In April 1973, they decided to buy
carpeting for four office-vaults, and in February 1977, they bought drapes for
the commissioners' meeting room. The courthouse grounds were improved greatly
by re-sodding the entire area in 1973. Shrubs and flowers were purchased, which
resulted in a more attractive setting. Much of the expense was paid by revenue
sharing funds, a result of the 1972 State & Local Fiscal Assistance Act. In
September 1978, combination windows were installed, and security lights for all
courthouse entries were purchased in November.

In October 1974, the commissioners decided to update the furniture in their
meeting room by purchasing five new chairs, at $109.00 per chair. The salesman
had brought a demonstration along and proceeded to show the qualities of the
chair. While demonstrating, he sat in the chair, exclaiming it was almost
impossible to tip it over backwards, and as he expounded on that fact, he
leaned backwards a little too far and promptly fell over. Needless to say, the
room rocked with hearty laughter.

Citizens of Eureka established a museum in 1976, and a group appeared before
the board to ask support from the county. They proposed to change the name to
McPherson County Museum from Pioneer Museum if the county would share in the
funding. In July 1976, the board granted the museum $5,000.00 per year as long
as the Revenue Sharing Act continued, on condition that it be named the
McPherson County Museum.

New programs were implemented through the years, and among the new ones was the
feasibility study on establishing a TV translator district in May 1976. The
county entered a joint agreement in October, which combined a five-county
district to bring more channels and better television reception to county
taxpayers. In 1976, the commissioners also petitioned the governor by
resolution to declare our county a disaster area, which in turn entitled county
citizens to receive federal and state aid. A soil survey was in progress during
that year, which was completed in 1979. "The survey recognized over 50
different soils. This many different soils in one county make McPherson County
one of the more complex in the state. What makes a soil different? To the
farmer, one of the most obvious differences between soils includes topsoil
thickness, surface texture, depth to sand and gravel, wetness, slope and depth
to and density of a hardpan, to name a few. There are over 150 different soil
samples on file in the McPherson County Soil Conservation office. The soil
survey was used in 1981 for assessment purposes."

In January 1978, McPherson County was declared a major disaster area within the
state, due to adverse weather and road conditions. Many hours of board time
were spent discussing snow problems in late 1977 and 1978. All through 1978
pressure was applied to join the Community Health Nurse program. The
commissioners voted to join the WIC (Women, Infants, Children) program in
October 1979, and they joined the Health Nurse program in January 1980, which
was implemented in July 1980.

In January 1981, McPherson County began administering an Energy Assistance
program to help people with fuel bills. Kristine Zandstra was the first
director for the county. In 1982 Gail Noble became the director and served
until September 1983, when she was succeeded by Doris Bell.

In April 1981, the county granted Northern Border Pipeline the re-zoning of a
tract of land from agricultural to industrial. Northern Border Pipeline Company
installed a pipeline crossing McPherson County, totaling 41.279 miles of
pipeline.

Nineteen hundred and eighty-two and 1983 saw no significant problems or issues
in the county. As it has in the past, the stability and effective functioning
of county government and operations will almost certainly continue into the
future.

Jubilee Journal, Leola, South Dakota, 1959.

                        COURTHOUSE MURALS

        Max Herzog's Courthouse Mural.

These four masterpieces of art were painted by one of the greatest artists in
America, Mr. Max Herzog, of Chicago. Mr. Herzog was born in Germany, studied
art in Berlin, Munich and Paris. He was awarded many gold medals, prizes and
high honors for his work in America.

The four mural paintings in the dome of the rotunda cost $500 each. They
represent in the north; the original American citizen, the Indians crossing a
stream, their tepees and a rough but beautiful landscape in the distance; in
the east, the new immigrant coming into the county in covered wagons, some of
them driving their cattle and sheep along the wayside; in the south, the new
settler building up homes in the county, some are plowing with oxen and some
with a horse and an old fashioned plow. The landscape in the distance is very
beautiful, fine fields of grain and nice homes, cattle grazing peacefully in
the pastures. This picture represents "Prosperity for All." Picture 4, in the
west represents "New Progress." It shows the Capitol at Washington, DC in the
distance, combined with a thrifty city of factories and steel works, trains
moving back and forth. In the foreground, the artist crowns this most beautiful
painting with an (advance) from early days hard labor to later progress by
showing a sunlit field of expression of happiness as a reward grain, a
beautiful horse and happy children.

Taken from McPherson County Herald, Jan. 5, 1928

                McPHERSON COUNTY HIGHWAY DEPARTMENT

It has been said that McPherson County has one of the outstanding road systems
in South Dakota. Cooperation between the Commissioners, Highway
Superintendents, landowners and the State throughout the years has made this
possible.

It was in 1919 that the concern for roads and bridges in the county became more
organized and road building began. During that year, they built approximately
300 miles of road according to the current equipment and standards. The
landowner paid his taxes and in turn demanded that his roads be made passable.
At the time, the county had enough money deposited in the banks to do road work
every year through 1933. Road projects were assisted by the federally funded
W.P.A. in 1933 and continued until 1936.

When the road construction began in 1919 there was a need for special
supervision which led to creation of the Highway Superintendent Office in the
county. This eliminated the township road supervisors who had been managing the
township roads since the county began. This new highway program seemed to work
well until the '50's which records show to be a time of unrest among the
citizens. The Commissioners had decided to run the highway program by employing
a secretary to take care of the office work and the road construction share
would be run by them. This became a difficult, trying decade. There were many
delegations registering complaints with the Commissioners. At times there were
bitter arguments among all concerned. A much needed improvement came in about
1960 when they hired a Highway Superintendent. They convinced Irvin Mutschler,
who was County Sheriff at the time, to give this job a try. Mutschler took on
the job of hiring a good crew and restoring a working relationship between the
taxpayers and the Commissioners. With the help of his able secretary, Vivian
Mack, he set up workable budgets. He spent hours preparing road projects for
future years, supervising his men and meeting with the Commissioners, ironing
out road and salary problems. The Commissioners in turn, put their trust in
their Highway Superintendent. This unity and cooperation built the Highway
Department into one of the most efficient in South Dakota. Mutschler's health
forced him into semi-retirement in 1977 and in 1978 the job was turned over to
Elvin Feickert who is diligently carrying on the work. This delegation of
authority over the road system has freed the Commissioner's time to be spent on
other issues and works efficiently when the Highway Superintendent and
department are given responsibility and freedom to function.

In 1962 a long held dream of a number of county citizens came into reality.
Construction of the final mile of highway through Leola as part of the State
Highway 10 project was finished in October. The first section of SD 10 was
placed in the State highway system by the Highway Commission in 1919; this was
a section between Britton and the Roberts County line. In the months that
followed parts in McPherson, Roberts, Campbell and Brown were added in that
order. In 1922-23 the three miles from Leola west, the Campbell County section
and project 132 from the west county line to five miles east of Eureka were
started. Nineteen hundred and twenty-four through 1925 work progressed from
Leola to the Brown County line. The final grading started in 1926-27 on the
section from five miles east of Eureka to three miles west of Leola. These
projects resulted in all of SD 10 being graveled by 1929. The first bituminous
surfacing came in 1938; it included one mile in Eureka and one mile in Leola.
Progress seemed to slow down in the '40's. In 1954 five men from Pollock, SD
and one man, Ray Neuharth, from Leola contacted all of the towns interested in
SD Highway 10. After contacting the Chambers of Commerce in all the towns and
finding that they were interested, the first meeting of the 'Highway 10
Development Association' was held August 27, 1954 in Britton, SD.
Representatives from the following towns were present: Pollock, Eureka, Leola,
Britton, Sisseton, Lake City and also Ashley, ND. They made plans to further
develop Highway 10 and elected officers. Raymond E. Neuharth, Leola, became
chairman and held this office as long as the organization remained active. The
officers worked with and through the State Legislators from the area to get
certain miles added to the State Highway systems. They were to travel many
miles and put in many hours before their work was completed. The group won mile
by mile until they had one of State's finest surfaced highways. Shortly after
completion of the final mile through Leola, a ribbon cutting ceremony was held
in Leola. By that time more towns joined and the association added Herreid,
Mound City, Artas, Long Lake, Barnard, Frederick, Houghton, Hecla and Browns
Valley to their group. Most of these attended the dedication ceremony in Leola
October 6, 1962. It was a big celebration starting with a morning meeting
attended by the public and the visiting cities' representatives followed by a
noon luncheon and the 2:00 P.M. dedication program which featured several
speakers including Gov. Archie Gubbrud. The ribbon-cutting ceremony culminated
the day's events.

In 1966, a new state law advocated a complete revision in highway construction
to meet changing times. As a result, the program for new highway construction
had to be revised to meet requirements for State and Federal aid. These require
that all roads must lead to the system which accommodates the greatest number
of travelers. In McPherson County, the traffic flows east and west, along
Highway 10. This cuts the county through the middle. Consequently the two main
county highways, 10 and 45 followed this traffic pattern. Interlacing this are
350 miles of county roads of which 186 miles are black-top and 625 miles are
organized and unorganized township roads.

Seventeen employees comprise the Highway Department labor force. These
employees diligently carry out their technical duties and daily
responsibilities. The Highway office is the basis for all budgeting and
accounting and any road questions are usually answered to the taxpayer's
satisfaction. The office staff consists of the Highway Superintendent, Elvin
Feickert and his secretary, Marva Lou Geffre.

McPherson County is most fortunate to have had men with vision and foresight
concerning road transportation throughout our history. Because of our
relatively sparse population our highway system has been and continues to be a
vital link connecting our citizens and enabling them to live lives of greater
ease and productivity.
