                Samual H. Ordway Nature Conservancy

The Nature Conservancy purchased 7,600 acres of prairie range and hayland in
McPherson County from LeRoy Hoffman in 1975. Five thousand and four hundred
acres of this vast prairie belonged to Tom Boylan before it was sold to
Hoffman. The Conservancy dedicated this as the Samuel H. Ordway, Jr. Memorial
Prairie in September, 1975 to commemorate a pioneer conservationist. Miss
Katharine Ordway, cousin to Samuel Ordway, contributed almost 1.5 million
dollars towards the purchase of the Ordway prairie. Katharine, referred to as
the lady who "saved the prairies," was a dedicated naturalist.

Headquarters for the Ordway Prairie is located nine miles west and one-half
mile south of Leola on Hiway 10. The Ordway is a mixed prairie of tall and
short grasses. It sits atop the Coteau, a range of hills (called the Coteau du
Missouri) which are parallel to and east of the Missouri River.

Among the rolling hills are numerous potholes and marshes. More than 400
wetlands can be found which is an excellent nesting place for wild ducks,
geese, and other waterfowl. About 2,000 mallards, bluewing teal, ruddy duck,
canvas back, and pintail nest among the cattails and marshes. Bitterns, herons,
cormorants, willets, plovers, and phalaropes share this nesting habitat.

Over 100 species of birds nest here on the Ordway and high on the hillside is
found the uncommon ferruginous hawk.

Numerous animals roam the prairies such as harvest mice, ground squirrels,
jackrabbits, badgers, white-tail deer, antelope, fox, sharp-tail grouse and
buffalo.

Plant life is rich with many species of grasses and flowering plants to cover
the prairie. This vast prairie with its diversified eco-system of plants and
animals is truly a "Nature's Bank." It is an excellent site for field trips and
is available to tours and research, by appointment, for those who wish to visit
the Ordway.

The Nature Conservancy was established to preserve natural lands of ecological
importance for scientific, educational, and aesthetic purposes. The
conservancy's main objective for Ordway was to re-establish the integrity of
the prairie system as it exists in McPherson County and throughout the midwest.
Utilizing grazing, haying, and burning as an effective and safe management tool
to maintain the productivity of the land.

A research station and home is located at the headquarters for the caretaker
and research participants. The present manager, Allan A. Steuter replaced Paul
Bultsma, who was manager from 1975 to 1982. Allan, Lois, and three children;
Camas, Matt, and John live at the Ordway.

Allen spends one-third of his time on conducting field studies and on research
projects. The balance of his time is spent on the management of the prairie and
its wetlands, handling grass leases, maintaining productivity of the grassland,
and acting as a representative of the Ordway Prairie Conservancy.

Allen will be holding Science Technical Workshops every other year at the
Ordway for individuals who can help improve the Prairie. These workshops
replace the Advisory Council that consisted of a local SCS agent, county
extension agent, local rancher, and someone from the local cooperative, along
with various water fowl and plant specialists.

                        OUR NEIGHBORING TOWNS

Eureka

Eureka was often referred to as the "end of the track" in the latter 1880's.
Many settlers boarded trains in the southern part of the state and rode the
rails to the end of the line which was Eureka at that time. Some English, a few
Jews but mostly German Russians, who were known to have persistence, thrift,
toughness which is often called stubbornness that is hard to beat.

Most Eurekans have feelings of gratitude to their forebears for enduring the
hardships they did for it is their descendants who have reaped the benefits.

These pioneers endured hardships of dust storms, blizzards, prairie fires,
loneliness and deaths while living on the prairie in a sod shanty. This race of
rugged individuals continued after a vicious tornado swept through Eureka and
also weathered the dirty thirties.

At one time Eureka was known as a "wheat capital," the world's largest inland
wheat center. In 1892 the train hauled 3,300 cars of wheat out of Eureka from
35 elevators and warehouses. The interest in wheat still prevails for in 1977
through the effort of Julius Wittmayer, a wheat strain was named Eureka.

The first school opened in 1888 with 47 pupils in attendance. Mrs. McKeever was
their teacher. Most of the students had no knowledge of the English language.

The oldest businesses still active are: N. W. German Mutual Ins. Co. which
started in 1896; Eureka Equity Exchange, started in 1915; Straub's Funeral and
Furniture, started in 1894; Northwest Blade, Inc., began 1893; Philip 66 in
1930; Lyric Theatre in 1935; NuWay cleaners in 1930; Oster Elevator, 1895; The
Luncheonette, 1928; Wolf, 1921; Slim's Plumbing, 1917 and Candy Service in
1935. Paul Kretschmar opened his law practice in 1927. Eureka has many
enterprising business establishments at the present time.

The Eureka Pioneer Museum of McPherson County, Inc. had its beginning in 1978.
A group of citizens mindful of preserving their heritage worked very hard
towards this goal. A grand opening was held in 1978 for the main building.
Additions since then are the schoolhouse, sod house and landscaping. The future
project is creation of a miniature of Eureka city and a building to house
antique machinery. The curator of the museum is Rev. Walter Kranzler. visitors
to the museum number over 3,000 for one year. The museum is also used for
research by college students from a large area. Displayed within the museum are
art and photography exhibits from the area's talented, changing as the entries
are offered. In the winter months museum volunteers use local art to make
stationery. They have compiled a pioneer cookbook and designed a pheasant
feather pin which they are offering for sale.

At the present time Eureka's citizens are in the process of preparing their
centennial celebration which will be held in 1987.

Greenway

Fond memories linger throughout the area surrounding the village of Greenway.
Some of the younger people listening to past descriptions of the village have
murmured "Greenway must have been a nice clean town."

In the early years Greenway had two stores, one owned by Lorence Schultz and an
unknown Jewish man, later owned by Henry Lutz and his son, Lorence. There was a
bank; post office, which employed Adam Lutz, Rose Lutz, John Schock, Emil
Ackerman and Audrey Ackerman; two grain elevators, managed by Emil Perman and
Ed Odenbach; a hardware and bulk station, which employed Mike Lutz, Jacob Lutz,
Emil Perman, and Karl Ottmar; Emil Diede delivered gas to the farmers; a cream
station and a puffed wheat factory, owned by Bill Weller and Oscar Isaak, who
delivered puffed wheat and rice to farmers.

Greenway had two churches, a Baptist and the Freidens Congregational church.
Later the Baptist church closed. The Congregational church was built in 1909
costing approximately $1,000 which was donated by members and friends. It was
dedicated in 1910. In 1952 the church was moved on a new basement and used
until its doors were closed in 1966.

School was held one-half mile outside of Greenway in the early years; later
they moved it into the village.

Greenway has had three reunions within the past 12 years. The first was held
June, 1976 with lots of former residents gathered to share their' happy
memories. The second was held June, 1980 and the last was held at Eureka, SD in
1982 with around 200 people present.

Hillsview

Hillsview came into existence in 1887. The treeless, virgin land soon attracted
the Black Sea German Russian immigrants and they needed a place for a town.
Hillsview was named so because of the view of the high hills to the north of
the townsite.

One of the reasons for establishing this tiny hamlet was that it was a shipping
point for the Milwaukee Railroad for grain and livestock between Eureka and
Hosmer. At one time there was a large stockyard in Hillsview and Lawrence A.
Wolf was the cattle buyer.

A cheese factory was started in 1897 operated by two Englishmen, Charles and
Henry Ritz. They also were the breeders of registered cattle. The factory was
located in the west end of town. The cheese was made and shipped out by train
to be aged. This factory was not in existence very long.

A fourth class post office dispensed mail continuously from 1886 to 1968,
usually in connection with some other business as the bank or store. John G.
Gross and Christ C. Gross were some of the first men to have the store and a
post office in the same building. Mrs. Theo. Wittmayer, the last postmaster
held the position for 30 years, until the office closed and mail was then
delivered by a rural carrier on Route I from Eureka, SD.

A lumberyard started by Matt Hammerschmidt of Eureka supplied most of the
lumber for the homes. During WWI business boomed, a new parish house and many
homes were constructed. During these years the town boasted a hardware store,
gas station, lumberyard, blacksmith shop, three general merchandise stores,
butcher shop, cream station, cafe, three elevators (always two in operation)
and a barber shop.

School was conducted in a two-story school building moved from Hosmer and
consisted of eight grades and a teacher for the four lower and one for the four
upper grades. This building burned down in the winter of 1959 and as families
had grown smaller they moved to a one-story rural school building and employed
only one teacher for all grades. Reorganization took place and the children
were bussed to Eureka to attend school.

In 1916 John Liedle, Philip Schamber of Eureka and John Heckenliable of Hosmer
filed to incorporate and founded the Hillsview State Bank. From 1916 until
August of 1922 this business was an asset to the town. In August, 1922, thieves
stole into town and blew the bank safe and escaped with $1,000 in cash. The
money was never recovered nor the thieves apprehended. C. E. Conradi was the
banker and George Imberi, assistant cashier. James Spencer, the depot agent,
could not call for help for the wires had been cut, the post office funds were
intact, however, for Louise Conradi, postmaster took them home every night.

During the depression years W.P.A. workers improved the streets and highway and
built a dam that formed a lake named "Hillsview Lake" a few miles from town
where citizens enjoyed fishing, boating and picnics.

This peaceful little hamlet never grew larger than 133 residents and has
dwindled to but two families, the Martin Malsams and the James Imberis.

Long Lake

The name Long Lake, so called for the lake by that name located about two miles
west of the present townsite, was very likely established officially by the
United States Postal Department when on September 11, 1884 a mail station was
started. The Post Office was located in various places until on January 2, 1930
when Karl Meier became the official Long Lake postmaster following the
dedication of the town on November 13, 1929. The present postmaster is Merle
Meier, son of Karl Meier.

The beginning of the Long Lake community certainly held promise for prosperity.
The railroad was a great inspiration and in the years following its
dedication in 1929, the town was bustling with new growth. Many businesses
sprang up the following spring and a school was built which firmly established
the community of Long Lake.

Religion played an important part in the continuation of this community, and
continues to be the main stay. Later the town was incorporated. The Town
Ordinances were officially approved on January 12, 1948 and signed by the first
duly elected officials under a Trustee Type governing board.

The officers presently serving on the Town Board are: Ruben Sandmeier,
chairman; Milbert Rath and Rudolph Heyd, trustees; and Floyd Heiser, finance
officer.

Wetonka

Wetonka, a small town eight miles east and eight miles south of Leola, lives up
to the meaning of its name--friendly people. Started in 1906 when the
Minneapolis and St. Louis railroad built a spur from Aberdeen through Wetonka
to Leola; a depot, section house, three grain elevators, and two lumber and
coal sheds were built.

When the depot was completed, the residents celebrated by having a dance. Mrs.
Tillie Kirnan played a small organ and her husband played the fiddle to provide
music. People from all around the country celebrated the occasion and many came
from Leola, with horses and buggies.

After using two small buildings for schools, the present school was built in
1911. The Presbyterian congregation built a cement block church in 1910.
Established in 1908 or 1909, the Wetonka State Bank was discontinued in the
1920's. A First National Bank operated and closed at about the same time. A
hardware store, barber shop, pool hall, shoe shop, and a livery barn were added
to the business area.

Wetonka was incorporated as a town in 1916 and added a city water system in
1921. The dirty thirties took their toll in Wetonka as it did in other
communities, reducing the business area to one store, a cafe, two elevators,
and several other small enterprises. Both elevators were in business until 1960
when the Wolff elevator closed and the Wetonka Equity elevator continued to
operate until 1968 when it was moved to North Dakota.

An increase in Wetonka's population took place in 1964 when a Hutterite colony
(the Long Lake Colony) was established nearby.

The '70's brought about a number of changes. The railroad ties were completely
removed; buildings were lost due to a fire; the school consolidated with Leola
thus dissolving the last school board: Carol Erdmann, Pat Beilke leaving the
post office (part of the store) on a contract base until July 1982 when it was
relocated in Westport, SD.

Wetonka celebrated its 75th anniversary in 1982.  Many former residents
returned to reminisce, making the celebration an enormous success. Newspaper
coverage of the anniversary shows Wetonka's population to be 24.

Epilogue

Their children now remain.
Slower and bent, they enter the stores and ponder today's price: hard to
believe
        --the cost of progress.
The First Ones wouldn't have understood, who bartered their time and labor
        in lieu of scanty cash.
Children's children and grandbabes now leave, seeking fortunes elsewhere;
        moving out from their womb to new horizons as did the First Ones.
